articles.title_orig: Qinwen Zheng makes history in winning China Open
articles.title_zh: Qinwen Zheng makes history in winning China Open
articles.content_orig:
Qinwen Zheng delighted a boisterous crowd of 15,000 as she became the first Chinese woman to win the China Open WTA 1000 on Sunday in Beijing.
Zheng earned her first 1000-level title with a 7-5, 6-4 win over fourth-seeded Mirra Andreeva of Russia. It was her first tournament win since her victory in Tokyo in late 2024 and her sixth overall.
The gold medalist at the 2024 Paris Olympics, Zheng captured her 14th career win over a Top 10 opponent in one hour, 43 minutes.
Zheng entered Beijing as a wild card, ranked No. 54 in the world after struggling much of the past year following elbow surgery.
But on Sunday, Zheng announced her return. Serving down 5-4 in the first set, she fought off three set points to even the match and then ran off eight straight points to take the opener.
In the second set, Zheng and Andreeva held serve until the ninth game, when Zheng went up 5-4 after winning the fourth break point of the game. She served out to win on the first match point, punctuating the victory with an ace.
This was the second career meeting between Zheng and Andreeva. The first also came in the China Open in 2024, with Zheng winning in three sets.

articles.title_orig: Mercedes posts record EV sales, but China slump drags quarterly sales down 6%
articles.title_zh: Mercedes posts record EV sales, but China slump drags quarterly sales down 6%
articles.content_orig:
© 2025 THE COOL DOWN COMPANY. All Rights Reserved. Do not sell or share my personal information . Reach us at hello@thecooldown.com .
Mercedes-Benz posted its strongest quarter ever for battery- electric vehicle sales, but a sharp downturn in China overshadowed that bright spot.
After the company reported third-quarter sales of 491,700 cars and vans, down 6% from the same period last year, its shares fell about 4% near 1 p.m. CEST on October 7, then recovered some of the loss, according to Euronews.
Mercedes-Benz's core car division delivered 407,200 vehicles worldwide in the quarter, down 8% from a year earlier.
Much of the pressure came from China, where sales dropped 31% amid "intense competition and challenging market conditions." Across Asia, Mercedes sold 132,300 cars, down 25% year over year, and Euronews noted that China accounted for nearly one-quarter of Mercedes-Benz's global car sales in the second quarter.
That weakness had already led Mercedes to cut its full-year outlook for car sales and group revenue in July. The automaker said tougher competition, softer demand, and changes to its model range in China had all hurt performance there.
Results were firmer without China in the mix. Euronews reported that group deliveries rose 2% and car sales increased 1%. Mathias Geisen, the Mercedes-Benz board member responsible for sales and customer experience, said, "Outside China, car sales increased for the third consecutive quarter in 2026."
💡These best-sellers from Quince deliver affordable, sustainable luxury for all
Electric vehicles were a major source of momentum. Worldwide electric-car sales climbed to 68,400 in the quarter, up 61% from a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Geisen said, "Mercedes-Benz Cars achieved the highest quarterly BEV sales in the company's history, led by the electric GLC, whose sales more than tripled compared with Q2."
Europe also marked a record quarter for Mercedes-Benz Cars BEV sales, up 78% year-on-year and 24% from the second quarter. Mercedes also said several new electric models in Europe are already committed, with orders extending into 2027.
Strong demand for the new electric GLC, CLA, GLB, and GLA has been helping in Europe, while North American growth provided additional support for the quarter.
To meet BEV demand, Mercedes said its plants in Bremen and Rastatt, Germany, as well as Kecskemét, Hungary, are operating on three shifts.
At the same time, the company remains heavily dependent on a small group of standout models in China. The GLC and E-Class together accounted for nearly two-thirds of Mercedes-Benz Cars sales there, Euronews reported, as the automaker tries to meet fast-growing EV demand in some markets while shoring up a critical region that has recorded two straight steep quarterly declines.
Geisen said, "Our new electric models GLC, CLA, GLB and GLA are sold out in Europe for the rest of the year, with order books extending into 2027."
These articles provide context for how Mercedes-Benz's mixed quarter reflects an EV market shaped by battery breakthroughs, fierce competition in China, and heavy reliance on Chinese supply chains.
• Mercedes-Benz and Factorial took a major leap toward solid-state EV batteries with far longer range.
• In China, EV price war pressures left about 70% of car sales unprofitable.
• Globally, just five EVs captured 20% of sales as Tesla and Chinese brands surged.

articles.title_orig: Taylor Knibb wins Ironman world title after leader collapses in dramatic Kona finish
articles.title_zh: Taylor Knibb wins Ironman world title after leader collapses in dramatic Kona finish
articles.content_orig:
Knibb overtakes Norwegian rival in final kilometer
Defending champion Løvseth collapses while leading
France’s Vincent Luis wins men’s title on Kona debut
American triathlete Taylor Knibb has won her first Hawaiian Ironman world title after one of the most dramatic finishes in race history.
With a mile left, Norwegian defending champion Solveig Løvseth led Knibb by more than a minute and looked rock-solid, having taken the lead from her inside the final 10km of the 42.2km marathon run.
But then Løvseth quickly developed a dramatic case of the wobbles and collapsed. Knibb passed her about a kilometre from the finish and the Norwegian eventually recovered from the meltdown to finish eighth.
It recalled the 1995 race, when Paula Newby-Fraser collapsed within just 500m of her seventh win and was passed by Karen Smyers.
In a twist of history, Smyers helped hold the winner’s tape for Knibb.
Vincent Luis of France won the men’s race aged 37, on his debut. It was just his third Ironman-distance race after Luis won Olympic bronze at Tokyo in the mixed team relay and claimed the 2019 and 2020 world championship series titles.
Grace Thek was the best-placed Australian, rallying in the marathon to finish 10th on her debut at Kona. Nick Thompson finished 11th among the professional men.
Essendon’s David Zaharakis joined a select group of former AFL players to finish Hawaii as an age-group competitor.
Knibb had to pull out of the race a year ago with only a couple of kilometres left, while in the lead.
But on Sunday (AEST), the American showed she had learned her painful lessons, staying composed when Løvseth passed her.
Knibb won the 3.8km swim, 180km cycle and 42.2km run event – triathlon’s most famous race – in eight hours, 36 minutes and 29 seconds. Germany’s Laura Philipp was three minutes back in second.
Løvseth was able to walk to the finish, smiling and high-fiving fans. Always a tough race, Hawaii this year was marked by particularly high humidity, and several contenders either did not finish or hit the wall.
This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue' .
“Last year played a huge part because ... I made a big decision and it was just, ‘take care of yourself’, because it was getting really hard,” Knibb said.
“Then when Solveig came back, I thought I can’t fight because if I fight, I’m going to lose, so I had to learn from last year to just get to the finish line, get to the finish line, get to the finish line.”
Luis had said before his Kona debut that he would also retire afterwards. He will now reconsider.
The Frenchman held off hard-charging Norwegian Gustav Iden, the 2022 winner, to claim the world title in 7hr 47min 27sec. Iden finished runner-up in 7:49:03.
“I said if I win, I will maybe not continue, but I went through some dark places in the last 3-4km – but 100% worth it,” Luis said.
“Let’s see, I have a few nights out to decide what to do with my life now.”

articles.title_orig: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire
articles.title_zh: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to what he described as an “energy ceasefire.”
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” the president said in a post to social media Sunday morning.
CNN has reached out to the White House and Kremlin for information on how the agreement was reached and what the next steps may be. A source close to Ukraine President Volodomyr Zelensky told CNN the announcement was news to them, but that they will agree if Russia does.
Asked about Trump’s post on Truth Social, another Ukrainian official told CNN, “We just read it as you did.”
The announcement comes days after Trump spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and the two announced a controversial deal to supply markets with Russian diesel fuel.
Talks with top Ukrainian and US officials, including Trump’s son in law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, got underway in Miami as the diesel deal was announced Friday, but Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky starkly criticized the news. Trump said as recently as Saturday that Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.”
It was not immediately clear what led to the Sunday announcement. In an interview earlier on Sunday, Zelensky also called for a ceasefire.
“OK, if they want energy ceasefire, we are open for this,” Zelensky said about Russia during an interview with ABC News. “Don’t attack us. Don’t kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel. And I think it’s fair, fair deal.”
CNN’s Victoria Butenko, Jennifer Hansler and Matthew Chance contributed to this report.
This is a breaking news story and will be updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
articles.title_zh: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire, but Zelenskyy says this is ‘news for me’
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.
The investigation into the networks that make up the White House TV press pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — is underway, and the department sent out “civil investigative demands” on Friday, according to a Justice Department official.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” department spokeswoman Emily Covington said Saturday.
The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording the president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The network performing pool duty then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets.
The New York Times first reported the investigation.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
ABC News said it has not received any notification from the Justice Department but expects to. Representatives for NBC, CBS and CNN declined to comment. Fox did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The investigation appears to be the latest move from the White House in its escalating feud against the press corps.
Last month, Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The other networks in the TV pool briefly declined to participate in pool duties after CNN was removed from its spot in the rotation.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued to block the ban, claiming it was a violation of the First Amendment. They were reinstated about a week later after a judge ruled that the administration had to temporarily restore their access for 14 days. A federal judge this week extended the order to Tuesday.
The five major networks released a joint statement at the time, saying: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
The pool system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.
During the time the outlets declined to provide pool coverage, individual TV networks, including NBC News, continued to provide coverage of White House events that were open to the press, outside of the pool.
Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the First Amendment protects the decisions news organizations make about coverage and called the investigation “another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”
Kelly O’Donnell reported from Washington, and Marlene Lenthang from Los Angeles.
Chief Justice and National Affairs Correspondent
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

TORONTO — Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:
Shareholders of Roots Corp. will vote on Tuesday on a deal that will see the retailer taken private by Marquee Brands, the firm behind Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli. Marquee plans to partner with Joseph Mimran, the Canadian fashion visionary behind Joe Fresh, Club Monaco and Alfred Sung, to help grow the Roots brand.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford will give a speech to the Empire Club of Canada on Wednesday in Toronto. Ford has been one of the loudest voices in Canada's trade fight with the United States.
Statistics Canada will release its building permits data for August on Wednesday. It will also publish its monthly survey of manufacturing and figures for wholesale trade in August on Thursday.
There are a pair of key data points for the Canadian housing market coming this week. The Canadian Real Estate Association will release its September home sales figures on Friday, while Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. is expected to release September housing starts the same day.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly will be at the Canadian Club Toronto on Friday to talk about the pressures facing Canadian industry. Last week, she sent a letter demanding that Stelco outline a plan on how its U.S.-based parent company Cleveland-Cliffs will honour its legally binding commitments made at the time of its acquisition of Stelco in 2024. articles.title_orig: Chicago Marathon women's wheelchair: Catherine Debrunner sets world record
articles.title_zh: Chicago Marathon women's wheelchair: Catherine Debrunner sets world record
articles.content_orig:
Catherine Debrunner breaks world record at 2026 Bank of America Chicago Marathon,a
Catherine Debrunner is back on top of the Bank of America Chicago Marathon podium -- and continues to be on top of the world.
The fierce Swiss wheelchair racer, who won the race in 2024, just soared to victory at the 2026 competition, shattering her own world record in the process.
Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
Debrunner set the world record in 2023 when she finished the Berlin Marathon in 1 hour, 34 minutes and 16 seconds. She finished Sunday in 1:33:16 -- exactly one minute faster.
"I don't think we have ever seen anything like this," analyst, Olympian and former Chicago Marathon champion  Amanda McGrory said during the NBC Chicago broadcast of the race. "This is a historical event we're seeing right now."
Debrunner has now won 12 major marathons, including in her U.S. debut in Chicago in 2023 and again in 2024.
The victory comes after she finished runner-up at the 2026 Boston Marathon earlier this year before capturing her fourth London Marathon title.
"I really gave all I could and when I saw the time at the finish … it felt great. It's unbelievable," Debrunner said after her victory.
Debrunner said she didn't enter the race expecting a world record, but credited the crowd and the conditions with helping her to a victory.
"I just wanted to give all I could, and that's what I did," she said.
Debrunner's victory came as defending Chicago women’s wheelchair champion Susannah Scaroni took the 2026 race off to welcome her first child.
Debrunner finished well ahead of a strong group of contenders, many of whom have won the division since 2015, including nine-time champion Tatyana McFadden and two-time champion Manuela Schär. McFadden finished second in a sprint to the finish with Schär.
Check back for more on this developing story.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo to have surgery after lump found on lung
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up.
"The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.
The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".
The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.
Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.
Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".
He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.
Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.
The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.
Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".
Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".
Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".
The Pope, born Robert Francis Provost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.
He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.
During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.
The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.
A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.
Most nodules do not cause other symptoms.

Steve Summers, Dolly Parton's creative director, joins Martha MacCallum on 'The Story' to discuss the opening of the 'Life of Many Colors Museum' and hotel in Nashville, Tennessee. The projects celebrate the legendary singer's rags-to-rhinestones legacy. Fans express emotional reactions to the immersive experience, sharing how they can feel her presence throughout the new building.
Kelly Clarkson is calling out a Brooklyn store after she claimed an employee mistreated her.
On Saturday, the singer and talk show host took to X to share details of her recent experience at Art of Play, a store known for its collection of toys, games, books, puzzles and other unique items.
"Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote.
KELLY CLARKSON WON’T LET HER KIDS WATCH ‘FROM JUSTIN TO KELLY’ AFTER BRUTAL ADMISSION ABOUT 2003 FILM
Kelly Clarkson described a recent shopping experience to one of Julia Roberts' character in "Pretty Woman." (Getty Images)
"Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale," she continued.
Clarkson then compared the encounter to a memorable scene from the 1990 film "Pretty Woman," in which Julia Roberts’ character, Vivian Ward, is dismissed by a boutique saleswoman who assumes she cannot afford the store’s clothing.
MICHAEL DOUGLAS' WILDEST HOLLYWOOD CONFESSIONS: FROM A-LIST ACTRESS BITE TO JULIA ROBERTS CLASH
"But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in ‘Pretty Woman.’ For sure, check it out," Clarkson added.
The singer’s description of the incident echoed the famous "Pretty Woman" scene, in which Vivian returns to the boutique after being rejected and tells the saleswoman, "Big mistake. Big. Huge."
Clarkson’s post quickly drew attention from her followers, some of whom defended the singer and criticized the store on social media. Several users also appeared to leave negative reviews on the business’ Google listing.
The singer called out Art of Play in Brooklyn for allegedly mistreating her. (Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame)

Art of Play so far has not issued a formal statement addressing Clarkson’s claims.

articles.title_orig: India’s ‘Cockroach’ Leaders Released as Small Protests Go On in Delhi
articles.title_zh: India’s ‘Cockroach’ Leaders Released as Small Protests Go On in Delhi
articles.content_orig:
India's Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has vowed to continue its protest seeking the resignation of top election official even as the city sees more demonstrations for a second day with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded.
Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders were arrested on arrival in Delhi on Saturday. They were freed on Sunday.
In his first comments after his release, Dipke said "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated".
Media reports said, 7,000 protesters were detained and released on Saturday. Hundreds have also been detained on Sunday.
The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.
It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.
On Sunday morning, Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were set free by a magistrate's court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year", police said.
After his release, Dipke posted on X , saying: "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India."
In another post , he said he was going to his village to attend his grandmother's funeral who died around the time of his arrest yesterday. He added that "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated".
Ranka and Das later told a press conference that the condition did not mean they couldn't protest.
"Peaceful protest is our constitutional right and Jantar Mantar is a desginated protest site, so this doesn't mean we can't do peaceful protest," Ranka said.
"Breach of peace is done by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and CEC Gyanesh Kumar," he said, adding that the CJP will continue to protest.
Saturday saw dramatic scenes as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed.
For a second day in a row on Sunday, much of central Delhi had roads barricaded and offices, shops and restaurants shut and internet services curtailed.
In Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest shopping and entertainment hubs, there are rows upon rows of bright yellow police barricades, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.
Protesters have returned to the area for a second consecutive day, but they are vastly outnumbered by security personnel and the BBC has witnessed many detentions.
Some were put into buses before being driven away. Some could be seen peering through the windows, others trying to push their way out while shouting "Gyanesh must go!" At one point, an entire bus reverberated with similar chants.
Every now and then, small groups of protesters managed to slip past the barricades and sprint through the streets, with police personnel chasing after them. Within moments, they were surrounded, detained and, in some instances, dragged across the road, before being bundled into waiting buses.
The most dramatic moment came during the detention of activist Neha Bora who was chased by police personnel before being caught and detained.
Some protesters also said they were feeling a little uncertain. One of them told the BBC that the absence of the CJP's top leadership on the ground was beginning to affect the movement's momentum.
"Without them, we're feeling a little lost," the protester admitted, before quickly adding, "But that doesn't mean we'll stop our fight."
The CJP had called for a protest on Saturday at Jantar Mantar - the road that the demonstrators had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms.
Police had refused them permission and the city was in a virtual lockdown with unprecedented curbs in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue.
At least 45 metro stations were closed and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route.
Internet was also curtailed in central Delhi for the entire day.
After the police detained the CJP leaders and other activists, lawyers and students leaders, the CJP called for more protests on Sunday.
On Sunday, the Indian Supreme Court held a special hearing to deal with complaints of shutdowns and detentions.
The court ordered the government to restore internet and ensure that metro and rail services functioned normally, unless there was disturbance to public order. The court also said that free movement of people should be permitted and there should be no illegal detention.
The row centres over a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - the commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.
At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.
The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.
Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.
Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister.

articles.title_orig: Georgia players, Kirby Smart had a lot to say about Keelon Russell
articles.title_zh: Georgia players, Kirby Smart had a lot to say about Keelon Russell
articles.content_orig:
The No. 2 Georgia Bulldogs got the job done on the road Saturday night, defeating the No. 6 Alabama Crimson Tide 20-17.
The game stayed close throughout. Georgia jumped out to a 10-0 lead but trailed 14-10 at halftime before holding Alabama to just three points in the second half.
Georgia rushed for 209 yards as a team, with Dwight Phillips accounting for 120 on 17 carries.
Quarterback Gunner Stockton also made plays when needed, completing 18 of 22 passes for 249 yards, one touchdown and one interception. He also rushed six times for 12 yards.
Georgia head coach Kirby Smart, who often shows his emotions on the sideline, made sure to celebrate with the Bulldogs crowd in Tuscaloosa after the victory.
However, his choice of celebration drew backlash from some college football fans.
As he ran off the field, Smart stopped and performed the classic "belt to [explicit]" celebration to mock Alabama.
Via Underdog CFB : "Kirby Smart pulled out the belt move when celebrating with Georgia fans after their win over Alabama."
Smart caught some heat on social media for his postgame celebration, with fans arguing that Georgia benefited from controversial late calls to escape with a victory.
"He knows he barely won with the help of the refs. What a clown," one fan wrote.
Someone else added, "First time beating Alabama in Tuscaloosa. This is how opposing coaches tend to act I suppose."
Another person wrote, "Dude won his super bowl. Let him have his moment."
"Surprised the refs didn't go celebrate with him," a fan commented.
One more added, "What a tool. ALL that help from the refs with the bad/no calls & still only won by 3."
Despite the emotional ending and his viral celebration, Smart spoke about his respect for Alabama and legendary coach Nick Saban during his postgame press conference.
"It's a hard place to play. I don't judge my happiness or success on how we play Bama. I got a lot of respect for this place," Smart said. "Nick [Saban] taught me a lot. Watching that show the other night… I have so much respect for him. We run our program a lot like that. The stuff going on in that show is going on in Athens right now… it's what he taught me and it's what we're trying to do."

articles.title_orig: A heroic, 7-day bike ride made this teen a global star. Where is she now?
articles.title_zh: A heroic, 7-day bike ride made this teen a global star. Where is she now?
articles.content_orig:
Jyoti Kumari holds a photo of her dad, Mohan Paswan. She became a global celebrity after news spread of her 700-mile bicycle ride, carrying her injured father on her bicycle, to get him to their village. Promises were made to reward her heroic feat. Were they kept? Deepak Paswan hide caption
Fame is a strange beast. It brings applause, attention and promises of a better life. But when the spotlight moves on, those promises are often forgotten. No one knows this better than 22-year-old Jyoti Kumari.
When she was 15 years old, during the peak of India's COVID shutdown , she shot to international fame for cycling over 700 miles, from northern India to her village in the eastern state of Bihar, with her injured father riding on the back of the hot pink bike she'd bought for $20.
Her dad, Mohan Paswan, drove an autorickshaw for 20 years in Gurugram, a city near Delhi , sending money to his wife and five children in the village of Sirhulli. After he suffered a debilitating road accident in January 2020, Kumari and her mom took the train to Gurugram to care for him.
Five months later, he still hadn't made a full recovery and his family was running out of money for food and rent. The family decided they would all be better off at home. But at the time, authorities had shut down public transportation for the pandemic lockdown. No one knew how Mohan Paswan could make the journey. That's when Kumari insisted she would bring him back home, riding on a pad attached to the main seat of her bicycle.
She cycled for seven consecutive days on a relatively empty stomach at the height of the lockdown to get him to safety. Even though it was a test of sheer endurance, Kumari discovered that she loved cycling — it came naturally to her.
लॉकडाउन था, सो अपने पिता को साइकिल पर बैठाकर गुरुग्राम से दरभंगा ले गई बेटी... वीडियो: मोहन भारद्वाज और सीटू तिवारी pic.twitter.com/Mc7hkmyB4O
Her epic ride grabbed headlines around the world. NPR's previous reporting noted promises of cash rewards, training for a career as a cyclist, even a movie deal.
That was in 2020. "Now — life is hard," Kumari told NPR in a phone call from her home in Bihar.
What happened to all the promises made — for financial support, especially to support cycling as a competitive sport?
Many promises were not kept, she says.
"The politicians who made promises, saying they would give money for my sports or education — nobody actually gave anything," she says. "Whatever reward money we collected back then [from individuals who extended help and a government award that came with a cash prize], we put it all into our house, rebuilding it. We had a brick house before, but it only had bare walls. Now we have completed it, added a toilet, a bathroom, and a running water connection. By doing all that, the house has finally become livable," she says.
This is no small achievement. An estimated 300,000 people are homeless in the state of Bihar in spite of government programs . For a family living in poverty, having a home can make a huge difference in the fight for survival.
For Kumari's family, making their house livable meant securing something that burst of fame had failed to deliver on — a more stable place from which to build their lives.
But they are doing so without her dad.
Mohan Paswan passed away of a heart attack in May 2021, just months after his daughter brought him home. Kumari says she felt heartbroken. After his passing, financial security has been precarious for the family.
At the moment, her mother works as a cook. Her meager income supports Kumari and her three siblings at home (an older sister has married and moved out).
"There are days when we go to sleep hungry," she says. "Our brother-in-law used to help us earlier, but now he also has a child, a wife and his father to take care of. He works a small job in the city — how much can he really do? So now he isn't able to help us much."
Still she holds out hope for a better future.
"Once my education is fully complete, only then will I be able to do something else. Only then can I prepare for things and look for a job," Kumari says.
But she has yet to pass the final exam required to complete Class 12, her final year of secondary school. That's an important credential to apply to university or qualify for certain jobs. It's a stepping stone to a better life, especially for disadvantaged students.
Finding time for her studies has been a challenge. Kumari's day begins at 7 a.m. She cooks and cares for her younger siblings after her mother rushes off to work. "I give my brothers breakfast for school and get things ready for my sister. Then, I clean the house, mop the floors, do the dishes, wash clothes by hand, take a bath," she says.
By the time she can turn her attention to her studies, she says it feels as if she has already done a gazillion chores. "There are days when I sleep because of the sheer exhaustion of it all."
Whatever the future holds, she is determined to stay in their native village rather than seeking employment in the big city, as her father did. His experience showed her how precarious day labor can be — he had no savings and no medical support after his injury.
Kumari is firm about living in their native village. "Whatever I do, I want to do from here," she says.
She says she still loves cycling as much as ever. She loves the wind in her hair, the feeling of going somewhere, of feeling free. That's what the bike represents to her. But she doesn't have the time to do it as much these days as she's bogged down by household chores and small but persistent everyday worries. She can't just cycle for the joy of it or train as a competitive sport. She only cycles to do errands for the family.
With her own progress on hold, the family has quietly set their hopes on her younger sister who will take her 12th grade exams in mid-2027. If she manages to pass and get into a good college, their prospects will improve once she graduates and starts working.
But Kumari hasn't given up. "When you're poor, fame doesn't help. Only education can help you out of your difficulties. Otherwise, life becomes a never-ending obstacle course," Kumari says.
Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times , The British Medical Journal , the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t .

articles.title_orig: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
articles.title_zh: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
articles.content_orig:
The UK does not support Donald Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin, which would see the US purchase millions of tonnes of diesel from Russia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House, he said the agreement had been done in the context of the US president facing elections in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living.
He argued that the US and other allies should focus on increasing pressure on Russia to shorten the war "and to secure Ukraine's freedom".
Trump's diesel deal is aimed at lowering fuel prices in America, which have risen following the US and Israel's conflict with Iran.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement would allow Moscow to raise funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
In response, Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader" who could reach a deal with Russia to end the long-running conflict between the two countries.
Streeting said it was a matter for Ukrainians to choose their leader but added that the country was "fortunate to have someone of his calibre, his courage and his integrity leading their war effort".
He added that responsibility for the war "lies squarely and solely with President Putin and his imperialist ambitions".
The defence secretary said it was not the first time there had been public disagreements between Washington and Kyiv, adding: "In these situations we see it as our role and our responsibility to try and bring our friends back together again."
He also sought to emphasise the US's support for Ukraine, saying there was "often an understatement" of how much help they had provided.
"We're seeing US support for Ukraine in a number of ways from the provision of weapons - and we do a lot of procurement through the Americans - through to intelligence support and through the diplomatic initiative that Washington is leading."
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Trump was "wrong" to call for Zelensky to go, adding: "The US is our closest ally but even close allies can disagree."
Speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he also criticised the diesel deal saying it "sends out all the wrong messages".
"If you want a peaceful world, you don't do that sort of deal - you properly fund defence and prepare for war."
Also appearing on the programme, Streeting said the UK had to plan its defence spending on the basis that there could be a Russian attack on Nato - the military alliance made up of 32 countries - by 2030.
He said the UK didn't "seek conflict with Russia" but added: "Strength is the best form of deterrence."
Earlier this year, John Healey - now the chancellor - resigned as defence secretary accusing Sir Keir Starmer's government of not providing enough money for defence and said the UK had to be spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.
Streeting said Healey would use the coming Budget to "plug" a £4.7bn funding gap to pay for the Defence Investment Plan.
He also said the government would set out a path to increase spending to 3.5% of national income by 2035 at next year's Spending Review.
Pressed on whether the government could commit to spending 3% of GDP by 2030, Streeting said he would "always push for more defence spending" but added: "We're not going to set out a spending commitment without showing how we will pay for it."
"If I were the chancellor to sit on your programme now and say '3% in 2030' without saying how we would pay for it, the markets would price in that risk and the cost of borrowing would go up."

articles.title_orig: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
articles.title_zh: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
articles.content_orig:
Riyadh airport attack was expected as the Houthis’ way to retaliate: Analysis
Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh international airport this week.
The victims of the attack on Saturday included four Saudis, two ⁠Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
It was the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.
The Riyadh airport attack came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by Yemeni government forces against the Iran-backed group.
Here’s a roundup of the global reaction:
US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), soon. He said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the Houthi attack killed an American and called for an end to “these reprehensible attacks”.
“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on X that he is “deeply shocked” and strongly condemns “Saturday’s lethal attack by the Houthis”.
He said attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violated international law and “must cease immediately”.
Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, said the deadly strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia represent “a grave escalation”.
“Such actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate cycles of violence and complicate even more peace efforts for Yemen,” he said in a statement.
The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “strong condemnation” of the Houthi attacks, denouncing their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Houthi attack, describing it as a “serious violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region, the safety of civilians, civil facilities and air navigation”.
It expressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Doha supported “all legitimate measures” the kingdom “takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and safety of its territories”.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the “heinous attack”.
“Attacks targeting civilians and vital infrastructure are utterly unacceptable and pose a serious threat to regional peace and stability,” Sharif wrote on X. He also reaffirmed Pakistan’s “steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity”.
Jordan’s King Abdullah offered condolences to Saudi King Salman and MBS over the attacks and expressed his kingdom’s full solidarity with Riyadh.
The country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the “brutal aggression” by the Houthis, describing it as a “dangerous escalation” and a “blatant breach of international law”.
The sultanate denounced the attack and emphasised the “necessity of prioritising the voice of wisdom and self-restraint, and avoiding actions that would expand the scope of escalation, in order to preserve the security and stability of the region”.
The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared “its full solidarity with the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia” and said it supported “all measures taken by the kingdom to safeguard its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its citizens and residents”.
Syria condemned the attack in the “strongest terms”, urging the international community to take “serious steps to stop the attacks that target civilian facilities and threaten the security of the region”, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs described the Houthi attack on Riyadh airport as “dastardly” and said attacks on civilians “are completely unacceptable and must cease immediately”.
Japan’s embassy in Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the repeated attacks by the Houthis, saying assaults on civilians “cannot be tolerated” under any circumstances.
Prime Minister Mark Carney described the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, particularly the strike on Riyadh airport, as “abhorrent”.
“There can be no justification for attacks on civilian infrastructure,” he wrote on X, adding, Canada “condemns these reckless acts of violence in the strongest possible terms”.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim “unequivocally denounced” the attack.
There can be no justification for attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure,” he wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating
articles.title_zh: Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating
articles.content_orig:
It’s like using cloud-based AI tools, but the privacy makes it more appealing.﻿
It’s like using cloud-based AI tools, but the privacy makes it more appealing.﻿
I’m embarking on a journey I’ve so far been hesitant to go on: actually using AI on the regular. Giving my most personal data to cloud services has been a major hold up for me, but it’s increasingly possible to run powerful models locally to see what they’re capable of. Is this tech so useful that it’s worth throwing gobs of money at a computer or a laptop with lots of overpriced RAM? I’ll try to help you find out. I’m not an AI expert, it’s going to be a journey for me, but maybe I can help you see if that journey is worth taking — and I’ll be posting my way through it.
A big part of Apple’s pitch for its new Mac desktops is how good they are for local AI, and there’s an entire line of new RTX Spark Windows machines landing imminently with up to 128GB of RAM aimed at using agentic AI. Local AI and agents are just, like, so hot right now. But, in all seriousness, the thought of having a little gofer living solely in the box on my desk that answers only to me and not overlords from OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, or Anthropic hits a bit different than trusting cloud services or subscribing to a chatbot. Don’t get me wrong, there’s still no way I’m gonna have it write for me, edit for me, or generate ugly fliers . But now, with some privacy on my side maybe I can finally think of useful busy work to “trust” it with.
So as part of my ongoing testing of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio , as well as experimenting on other Mac and Windows systems, I’ve installed some local LLMs and I’m beginning to tinker. Here’s how things are going.
I started by installing the open-source Hermes Agent on the Mac Studio. Hermes is a self-hosted AI agent desktop app that works on macOS, Windows, and Linux. It’s completely free to use if you stick to local LLMs. Since this M5 Ultra Mac Studio has 256GB of unified memory, I could run just about any model I want. This is how things quickly get overwhelming. There are more models out there than I can count , and some have specialized uses. Generally, models with many billions of parameters are able to do more than smaller ones with only a few billion. And since we don’t have to worry about paying for tokens when running a model locally, I figured I’d go big to start.
Using Hermes’ straightforward onboarding interface and model picker, I chose the Qwen 3.8 Flash Next model — a 125-billion parameter model that’s around 105GB in size. I also plan on spending some time with much smaller Qwen models on devices like an M6 Mac Mini, M5 MacBook Air, an Asus TUF Gaming A14 with AMD Strix Halo processor, and, eventually, RTX Spark. (Care to share what local models and hardware you use? You know where to leave your comments. 🫡)
It wasn’t long to get up and running with Hermes and Qwen, and even make them controllable via my phone by using a Telegram bot . But then, I was presented with my usual nemesis when it comes to using AI: the text box.
“What do I do with this thing?”
First up, to get things going, I followed some helpful YouTube advice and had Hermes make me a daily morning briefing — to just start small with a cron job and ensure things are working. It scans my email and calendar, tells me anything worth my immediate attention, and gives me a short weather report. It’s not all that useful, and you obviously don’t need a $12,000 computer to build it, but it’s something I can develop over time. The brief kept failing to generate at first, but then I eventually figured out that macOS couldn’t be asleep when the job fired up at 7:30am. Duh! It works like clockwork now, but I have to think of more info for it to pull for me to make the results more helpful.
A more useful task was reorganizing my Steam library. I have over 400 games on Steam, and I recently started categorizing them for when I want to play something new on a whim. Steam doesn’t categorize your games for you, so you instead have to do it manually, one-by-one. But here’s where an agentic lackey could fit right in. I asked, “Can you reorganize my Steam library?” Hermes could see most of my games by just viewing the already installed Steam client. It quickly came up with some organization options for me. I decided to have it organize my games by genre, but leave some of my own specialized categories(favorites, co-op titles, party games, games to play with my wife, etc.).
You have to give a local AI some permissions over your machine for it to take actions for you, and in the case of my game library I had to register a Steam web API key and give it to Hermes. Once it had that access, it only took a few minutes for it to churn through sorting all the games into categories. And the API key was easy to revoke right after, since I don’t need it further. The idea is for it to just do this heavy lifting for me once, and then I’ll file new games into the categories as I eventually buy them. It did a fine job overall, and now my Steam library is easily browsable.
Another simple thing I did was data analysis. I had Hermes take a look at financial records to crunch some numbers for me, and I also had it make me a spec comparison spreadsheet for a new laptop. These are small things, but they’re both tasks I cannot or will not trust with any cloud service — I don’t want to upload that sensitive data to the cloud, and in the case of a new laptop, that info was under embargo. Keeping them on my computer was the difference in me using this tool or not.
The bigger bit of automation I’m currently working on is a script to run a series of laptop benchmark tests. I run all our benchmarks manually, and tending to a laptop to run a dozen or so tests — three times over, to take the average — is incredibly time-consuming. I’d love to automate at least some of it. Even walking Hermes through all of the required procedures and getting it to spit out vibe coded Python scripts has been a bit of an endeavor, and it remains a work in progress. But I’m hoping to make some positive headway.
It’s still early days of me working with Hermes, and I’m hoping this is just the tip of the iceberg on the useful things I get it to do for me. But it’s also clear that even these powerful local models don’t make for a magical assistant that can do anything. Things still don’t always work as intended — my daily briefing already broke, multiple times.
I view Hermes and local AI as just a tool, a computer program to run on my computer. I don’t want a digital friend. I’m not saying “thank you” or “please,” or typing “sorry” when I change my mind on something. I’m remaining as stone-cold and indifferent when ordering it around as I am clicking a mouse around an operating system.
I hope to remain vigilant and cautious while I continue testing and learning with local AI. Let’s see where it takes me.

articles.title_orig: China’s Youth Has a Problem With History Too
articles.title_zh: China’s Youth Has a Problem With History Too
articles.content_orig:
The Tang era of imperial China is regarded by historians as the golden age of arts and culture, a period spanning nearly 300 years, recorded over a millennium ago, when some of its most celebrated poets and inventors lived. But what if it wasn’t real?
That’s the bizarre and apparently irresistible internet theory the Chinese government’s cyber police have been trying to shut down since the summer. Beijing has mobilized state media and public university resources to combat the conspiracy—and for good reason.
Nihilism is a deep skepticism about meaning, morality and truth; it can grow among society's marginalized and disillusioned. The West has seen some of the worst forms of this post-truth phenomenon, from Holocaust denial and 9/11 “truthism” to the glorification of the Paris terror attacks . It’s happening in China, too.
“Why do absurd arguments capture some youths?” the Communist Party’s flagship People’s Daily newspaper asked in August, trying to find the root of “cognitive misunderstandings” behind a line of thinking that could undermine the party's ideological and theoretical underpinnings. China’s leaders fear alternative interpretations of the past because anyone who turns their back on history can turn their back on the party.
“The Tang dynasty doesn’t exist,” read a viral hashtag on Weibo, China’s biggest microblogging website, and other social media apps in late April and early May. It was started by a vlogger on the video-sharing site Bilibili.
The user, whose accounts have since been banned, told his viewers that historians and politicians fabricated hundreds of years of Chinese history to create the Tang era of 618-907, based on his study of astronomy and calendars. He didn’t say why.
Everyone loves a good story, but the best storytellers weave in the zeitgeist too. The conspiracy took off by tapping into the nationalist sentiments of modern China and its majority Han ethnic group, which represents over 90 percent of its population today.
Historical accounts suggest the Tang dynasty’s Han rulers had mixed ancestry. Some of China’s ultranationalist Han supremacists may consider this impure and therefore easy to repudiate. After all, why shouldn’t they believe that a dynasty of intermarrying cultures and religions, often hailed as the peak of China’s art and literary history, was faked?
In case there’s any doubt: the Tang dynasty was real. A large body of historical records supports that, as do accounts from neighboring foreign powers at the time.
Although Han Chinese are the majority ethnic group today, the truth is that China’s long history was dotted with fiefdoms, kingdoms and entire dynasties that were ruled by people who Han nationalists would consider non-Chinese outsiders, colonists even.
Inconveniently, this would include the Manchus who led China ’s final imperial dynasty, the Qing (1644-1912), which overthrew the Ming (1368-1644) and its Han rulers, who overthrew the Yuan (1271-1368) and its Mongol rulers, who had supplanted the Han-led Song dynasty (960-1279).
The end of the Song era interrupted 1,500 years of Han lineage since the Qin dynasty (221-206 B.C.), which was founded by a man who called himself the “first emperor,” and who was later buried with a Terracotta Army in Xi’an, which is the modern name of the former Tang capital Chang'an.
The Chinese state’s rapid response showed the conspiracy had hit a nerve in Beijing’s political sensitivities. Internet censors purged unsanctioned views, and state news outlets boosted official rebuttals with help from history professors, academics and archaeologists. Now only posts debunking the theory exist.
Western pseudohistory and phantom time conspiracies have existed on the fringes of the Chinese internet for years. It was never a problem when self-appointed historians claimed that parts of ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome were fabricated or that the civilizations were built on technologies copied from ancient China , but the Tang dynasty conspiracy crossed a line.
Mistrust in the establishment can breed nihilism, especially amid socioeconomic hardship and general economic stagnation. The Chinese government is fighting a wave of quiet rebellion from those growing tired of the rat race, but it has long been worried about a particular brand of nihilism involving history.
For decades, the Communist Party has warned against “historical nihilism,” which it defines as interpretations of the past that deny or reject the party's legacy and its Marxist-Leninist socialist roots.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping said soon after coming to power in 2012 that Party cadres were not to dismiss the turbulent years under the late revolutionary leader Mao Zedong by pointing to the reform era led by successor Deng Xiaoping, and vice versa. To do so would undermine the foundations of the Party’s uninterrupted progress —look what happened to the Soviet Union after its leaders renounced those who came before.
A late-August editorial in Chinese Social Sciences Today , an academic philosophy newspaper run by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, spelled out the stakes for China’s leaders. David Cowhig, a former U.S. diplomat and now prolific translator of Chinese politics and culture, provided a translation on his blog:
“Pseudohistory erodes national cultural confidence and weakens national identity. China’s five-thousand-year-old uninterrupted civilization and the advances achieved under successive dynasties constitute the foundation of the Chinese nation’s enduring vitality , as well as a source of national pride and self-confidence.
“The spread of pseudohistorical arguments has spawned various misleading and erroneous historical narratives…. The ‘1644 view of history,’ in particular, treats ‘the fall of the Ming dynasty and the Qing army’s entry through the Great Wall’ as the ‘interruption of Chinese civilization,’ considers the Qing dynasty a ‘foreign colonial regime’ and blames all of China’s backwardness in the modern era on Qing rule.
“This erroneous historical perspective severs the historical development of the Chinese nation as a pluralistic yet unified whole…This diminishes national cohesion , centripetal force and pride. Allowing pseudohistory to proliferate will only marginalize the mainstream historical narrative and impede the inheritance and promotion of China’s fine traditional culture.”
Contemporary Chinese leaders found a way to reconcile the country’s multiethnic past long ago by claiming the Manchus, Mongols and others as native ethnic minorities under one China. The Han majority leads China, but it can’t afford to allow ethnic divisions to destabilize society, so it’s much easier to call everyone Chinese .
In 2017, during U.S. President Donald Trump’s tour of the Forbidden City in Beijing, Xi boasted that Chinese civilization had a continuous history of 5,000 years. The Communist Party's general secretary is never wrong.
The CASS newspaper said: “Pseudohistory encourages the pernicious trend of historical nihilism and endangers ideological security…Even worse, some engage in historical nihilism by reassessing the achievements of historical figures, repudiating major historical personalities, ridiculing historical figures, smearing revolutionary heroes, glorifying aggression and denying revolution.
“This poses a threat by denying the guiding principles of Marxism, the historical inevitability of China’s path toward socialism and the leadership of the Communist Party of China.”
In recent years, the Chinese state has accumulated various legal instruments to punish those who doubt official accounts of history or satirically interpret the deeds of historical figures whom the state considers heroes or martyrs. Since 2021, defaming these sacred individuals has been an offense under Article 299-1 of China’s Criminal Law.

articles.title_orig: Storm Isaias leaves 4 dead, thousands without power as it moves across southern US
articles.title_zh: Storm Isaias leaves 4 dead, thousands without power as it moves across southern US
articles.content_orig:
Storm Isaias has left four people dead as it moves across the southern United States , officials said Saturday.
Two of the deaths were in Florida, while the other two were in Alabama.
The storm originally made landfall on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida. It is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.
Florida, Alabama and Georgia have all declared states of emergency due to the storm. According to PowerOutage.com, over 500,000 customers are without power in Florida and Alabama.
The Florida Division of Emergency Management said approximately 5,000 Florida National Guard soldiers and airmen have been "activated to support impacted communities."
The storm brings heavy rainfall and powerfall winds, bringing the risks of flooding and tornadoes. It has ripped the roofs off buildings and downed trees in its wake.
The storm has weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and is moving over the southern US states of Tennessee and Kentucky into West Virginia, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
In its latest update, the NHC warned of possible flash and urban flooding and said "landslides are possible across the Southern Appalachians." It also warned of wind gusts along with additional power outages and downed trees.
In addition, swells from Isaias will continue to impact much of the Gulf coasts of the US, Mexico and western Cuba, and are "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions." NHC said a couple of tornadoes are also possible across eastern Georgia and the Carolinas.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon has hit Category 4 strength as it barrels towards Mexico's Pacific coast, where it is expected to make landfall on Sunday. The storm is expected to impact Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for American tourists.

articles.title_orig: ‘Special-forces’ travel: Chinese woman wins admiration after climbing 5 peaks in 5 days
articles.title_zh: ‘Special-forces’ travel: Chinese woman wins admiration after climbing 5 peaks in 5 days
articles.content_orig:
Challenge aligns with ‘special forces style’ travel trend that has surged in popularity among young Chinese people recently
A woman from southwestern China has climbed five famous mountains in five provinces in five days, earning widespread admiration on social media.
The climber, surnamed Peng, began her journey in her hometown of Guiyang, Guizhou province, on September 23, the Xiaoxiang Morning Herald reported.
She climbed Mount Hua in northwestern Shaanxi province the following day, then Mount Heng in neighbouring Shanxi province on September 25, Mount Tai in eastern Shandong province on September 26, Mount Song in central Henan province on September 27, and finally Mount Heng in Hunan province on September 28.
The five mountains are collectively known as China’s Five Great Mountains, celebrated for their natural beauty and historical and cultural significance.

articles.title_orig: How Taiwan’s military manpower shortage is undermining its ability to fight
articles.title_zh: How Taiwan’s military manpower shortage is undermining its ability to fight
articles.content_orig:
Concerns are mounting over its ability to recruit elite troops and whether it will be able to operate its new US equipment
Taiwan’s military is grappling with a worsening manpower shortage, with its volunteer staffing rate remaining below the 80 per cent target for a third consecutive year and concerns mounting over the impact on combat readiness, according to the island’s legislature.
A Legislative Yuan Budget Centre assessment of the government’s proposed 2027 budget warned this week that persistent personnel shortages could increase workloads and training demands on serving troops while affecting readiness.
Defence ministry figures cited by the centre showed that the number of staff positions successfully filled by volunteers peaked at 88.52 per cent in 2020 before falling below 80 per cent in 2023. It dropped to 75.93 per cent in 2024 and stood at 77.31 per cent at the end of last year.

articles.title_orig: Pope at Angelus: Christian joy is ‘gift of God for world’s salvation’
articles.title_zh: Pope at Angelus: Christian joy is ‘gift of God for world’s salvation’
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV prayed the noon-day Marian prayer of the Angelus on Sunday with pilgrims gathered in St. Peterâs Square.
As the Church celebrated the Twenty-Eighth Sunday in Ordinary Time, the Gospel reading recounted Jesusâ parable of a wedding feast prepared by a king for his son.
In his address, the Pope recalled St. Thomas Aquinasâ saying that âgoodness, by its very nature, tends to spread (â Bonum dicitur diffusivum sui â).â
Read the full text of the Pope's Angelus address
Like the king in the story, we too desire to spread our happiness with others.
However, noted the Pope, Jesusâ parable points out the lack of welcome the kingâs joy received.
âSome are annoyed, insult the kingâs messengers and even kill them,â he said. âUnfortunately, this can happen to us, too, for the good we offer to do is not always understood, recognized or appreciated.â
Yet, he added, we must not be discouraged when we face rejection but rather go ahead with our plans and invite others to share our joy, like the king.
Pope Leo then explored the question of whom the main characters in the story represent.
St. Jerome, the great 5 th -century biblical scholar, identified the king with the Heavenly Father, the bridegroom as Jesus, and the bride as the Church.
The Pope said we too are involved in the story, as we belong to the Church and are chosen by the Lord to share our lives with Him and His life with others.
âThe wedding feast is ours, and the banquet hall is our churches and homes, the places where we live and where the Kingâs Son, Jesus Christ, continues to declare His love for us and await our âyesâ,â he said.
In conclusion, Pope Leo XIV pointed out that Christian joy is not artificial but âprofound, concrete, and real.â
Our joy, he said, âis as beautiful as the faces of the people we meet. It is as genuine as the work, the smiles, the tears, the handshakes, and the acts of kindness that fill our days. It is a gift of God for the salvation of the world.â
Thank you for reading our article. You can keep up-to-date by subscribing to our daily newsletter. Just click here .
The Angelus is a special prayer recited by Catholics three times a day, at 6am, noon, and 6pm and is accompanied by the ringing of the Angelus bell. The name comes from the Latin word for Angel and the prayer itself reminds us of how Jesus Christ assumed our human nature through the Mystery of the Incarnation. The Pope recites the Angelus prayer in St Peterâs Square every Sunday at midday. He also gives a brief reflection on the Gospel of the day and often comments on some issue of international concern. The Popeâs words are broadcast all over the world on radio and television and widely shared on social media. From Easter to Pentecost the Regina Coeli is prayed instead of the Angelus. This prayer commemorates the Resurrection of Jesus Christ and, like the Angelus, concludes with the recitation of the Gloria three times.

articles.title_orig: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
articles.title_zh: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
articles.content_orig:
This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day
H umankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.
Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse , could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.
While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity – existential AI threats remain , as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating, global proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima, how much longer can our luck hold ?
Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putin recently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal , comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time, Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacks deep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.
Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “ annihilate the Islamic Republic ” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US is upgrading its nuclear arsenal of 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing a lucrative deal with Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.
Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’s status as a nuclear weapons state . South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim, whom he bizarrely terms a friend . “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit, is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow – which, at this rate, there may not be.
Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “ the most dangerous nuclear moment ” since 1989. Global military spending reached nearly $3tn last year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paper published by the non-partisan Arms Control Association (ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.
The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too, is the fast-developing contest for control of space , notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and others advances rapidly . Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.
If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator
