articles.title_orig: Baku 2026: Fourteen World Champions, a Thousand Stories and One Shared Passion
articles.title_zh: Baku 2026: Fourteen World Champions, a Thousand Stories and One Shared Passion
articles.content_orig:
These seven days have delivered a spectacle worthy of the occasion. Two weight categories each day, two world champions crowned, one woman and one man; this is the rhythm of the world championships, following the same format as the Olympic Games. It is a formula we never tire of. Every morning brings new expectations, every afternoon its share of surprises, and every evening two more stories enter the history books.
There are many lessons to draw from such an extraordinary week. Looking at the overall picture, Japan dominated proceedings with no fewer than seven world titles, exactly half of all the gold medals available. Add to that two silver medals and three bronze medals and the scale of the achievement becomes even clearer. Impressive, certainly, but hardly accidental. Behind these results lies a culture of constant self-questioning, an unwavering commitment to the principles of judo and an exceptional ability to produce the very best when the occasion demands it.
Hifumi and Uta Abe demonstrated once again that even when circumstances become complicated, they possess that rare ability to dig deeper and find solutions. Wakana Koga, Ryuga Tanaka and Akari Omori each illustrated, in their own way, the remarkable depth of Japanese judo. Haruka Kaju continued to astonish with her unbeaten record, while Sanshiro Murao offered a masterclass in technical purity, reminding everyone why judo can be such a beautiful sport to watch.
Yet Japan's extraordinary collective performance should not overshadow the achievements of the other world champions; quite the opposite. Their victories gave these championships their richness, diversity and emotional intensity.
Georgia climbed to second place in the nations' ranking, led by the thunderous performance of Tato Grigalashvili. Six consecutive world finals and a fourth world title; who can match that? There was also the long-awaited triumph of Ilia Sulamanidze, who finally reached the summit he had been chasing for so long. Asked to describe his day, he found a single word, "Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious!" Mysterious, extravagant, wonderfully joyful and perhaps the perfect expression of a happiness too immense for ordinary vocabulary.
And what about the host nation? Azerbaijan opened its world championships in spectacular fashion with Ahmad Yusifov's gold medal, one of the tournament's finest surprises. With seven medals in total, the country has every reason to be proud. From the organisation and the welcome extended to delegations, to the atmosphere inside the arena and the sporting results, Azerbaijan delivered on its ambitions. Interestingly, it was not always the most highly anticipated athletes who shone brightest, making the achievement all the more exciting. The Land of Fire has discovered new heroes, a generation of judoka now ready to stand alongside its established stars.
Spain celebrated an historic championship, crowned by the gold medal of Ai Tsunoda Roustant. Already a world champion at cadet and junior level, she has now completed the collection with a senior world title. She has joined the elite, just as 19-year-old Hyeonji Lee of the Republic of Korea did when she conquered the final women's category of the week. Youth was certainly not afraid to challenge experience in Baku.
Another extraordinary milestone came courtesy of Yelyzaveta Lytvynenko, who delivered the first world judo title in the history of the United Arab Emirates, across both men's and women's categories. This is a landmark achievement that will resonate far beyond the arena and may inspire an entirely new generation.
Last but certainly not least, Inal Tasoev (RUS) climbed to the top of the podium for the third time. His performance was a demonstration of technical and tactical intelligence, combining precision, timing and extraordinary sensitivity to his opponents' movements; a true craftsman of judo, capable of turning the slightest reaction into a decisive opportunity. That such finesse can be expressed in the heavyweight category makes it even more remarkable.
Of course, these are only the world champions. There would be so much more to say about every medallist, every athlete who came close to the podium and every judoka whose journey ended earlier than hoped. A competition of this magnitude is a remarkable concentration of humanity, a melting pot of ambitions, sacrifices, emotions and personal histories, each deserving to be told. There are winners and there are those who did not achieve the result they dreamed of, but does that necessarily make them losers? Every athlete leaves with something: an experience, a lesson, a clearer understanding of what must be corrected, improved or changed. Some delegations will undoubtedly return home disappointed, having fallen short of their objectives. That is the reality of high-level sport. Sometimes we win, sometimes we do not, but we always have the opportunity to learn.
The Baku World Championships will be remembered as a magnificent edition, one that brought crowds to their feet, filled the National Gymnastics Arena with extraordinary energy and captivated judo enthusiasts across the world. From the intensity of the contests to the enthusiasm of the spectators, from the emergence of new champions to the confirmation of established legends, these championships have reminded us why we love this sport so deeply.
And yet, we are still at the beginning of the road to Los Angeles 2028. So many stories remain to be written, so much sweat will be shed in dojos across the planet and countless hours of training, sacrifice, disappointment and joy still lie ahead. We will continue to follow these extraordinary women and men who dedicate their lives to a simple but powerful belief: through judo, we can push beyond our limits, overcome adversity, bring people together and, perhaps most importantly, become better human beings. That is what makes judo so much more than a sport. That is what made Baku 2026 so special.

articles.title_orig: A ferocious Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
articles.title_zh: A ferocious Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
articles.content_orig:
Workers place sandbags outside a restaurant as Hurricane Simon approaches Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Fernando Llano/AP hide caption
PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — The eye of Hurricane Simon was just off the Pacific coast of Mexico early Sunday and was expected to move inland later in the day as an extremely powerful storm.
Simon has strengthened to 155 mph (250 kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a Category 5 storm, the highest on the Saffir Simpson scale. It was about 60 miles (100 kilometers) west-southwest of Manzanilla and moving north-northwest at 6 mph (9 kph).
The hurricane could bring 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches (76 centimeters).
"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the center warned.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors were fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
Convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows Saturday, and few were walking the streets under overcast skies.
"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."
The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who along with his wife still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

articles.title_orig: Imran Khan's party's provincial government suspended by Pakistan president
articles.title_zh: Imran Khan's party's provincial government suspended by Pakistan president
articles.content_orig:
Authorities in Pakistan have announced a state of emergency in the northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
The state of emergency was invoked on Sunday under two articles of the constitution dealing with security. It effectively suspends the provincial government run by the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of jailed former Prime ⁠Minister Imran Khan.
President Asif Ali Zardari said in a social media post he had approved the recommendations made by the cabinet, which had held a meeting under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif earlier in the day.
A statement issued by Sharif’s office said cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.
Pakistan’s constitution allows the federal government to take over some or all provincial government functions ⁠during an emergency, though the president’s office did not specify how the province would ⁠be administered.
Shortly after the announcement, PTI lawmaker Junaid Akbar said Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, was arrested along with the party’s president in the province.
The move comes as the PTI has been preparing for a march on the capital , Islamabad, to demand the release of Khan, who has been in jail for more than three years but still commands widespread popularity across the country.
The march was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed until October 4 to allow talks between the government and the PTI leadership to take place.
The government, however, said it would not allow the march to enter the capital and has been preparing for weeks to prevent the arrival of PTI demonstrators in Islamabad. It has erected barriers using shipping containers to block main access routes to the capital.
PTI spokesman Zulfikar Bukhari said the decision to invoke the state of emergency would only lead to “further bloodshed, ‌instability and collateral damage”, the Reuters news agency reported.
He said there was room for talks, but the latest decision showed the government never intended to hold negotiations.

articles.title_orig: Puerto Vallarta boards up as Hurricane Simon hits Category 4 strength
articles.title_zh: Puerto Vallarta boards up as Hurricane Simon hits Category 4 strength
articles.content_orig:
Even after Hurricane Isaias plowed into the western Florida Panhandle on Friday night, causing widespread but non-catastrophic damage, the work of the NOAA/NWS National Hurricane Center was far from over. In an unprecedented onslaught, NHC found itself on Friday issuing advisories not only for Isaias but also for the U.S. Pacific coast and two stretches of Mexico’s Pacific coast, ahead of the projected weekend landfalls of Tropical Storm Rachel and Hurricane Simon. Both Rachel and Simon could produce significant, far-flung impacts, but in quite different ways.
Simon is by far the stronger of the two. After forming on Wednesday well offshore from Manzanillo, Mexico, Simon drifted westward as a tropical storm through Thursday night, then swung north while rapidly strengthening into a Category 4 hurricane on Friday and Friday night. As of 5 p.m. EDT Saturday , Simon was centered about 100 miles south-southwest of Manzanillo, heading north at 5 mph (7 km/h) with top sustained winds holding at 150 mph (240 km/h). Update : Yet another burst of strengthening pushed Simon’s top winds to 155 mph (260 km/h), just shy of Category 5 strength, as of 1 1 p.m. EDT Saturday . Simon was centered about 65 miles south-southwest of Manzanillo and was sliding northward at just 5 mph (7 km/h). As discussed below, it remains unclear whether the angle of this northward track will push Simon just inland, keep the hurricane just offshore, or hug the coast as the storm proceeds toward the general vicinity of Puerto Vallarta.
10/10 – Hurricane #Simon is nearing Category 5 intensity off SW #Mexico . Swells will affect portions of the southwestern and west-central Mexican coast over the next few days, bringing life-threatening surf and rip currents. More: https://t.co/Wk7xxBl094 #marinewx #GOESEast pic.twitter.com/LE1Spow8ut
The first hurricane-hunter flight into Simon at midday Saturday confirmed the storm’s Cat 4 power, finding an estimated central pressure of 933 mb and peak flight-level winds of 153 mph (246 km/h). The storm’s tiny eye on Friday night allowed for ferociously quick strengthening, followed by an apparent eyewall replacement cycle that gave Simon a larger eyewall and a somewhat broader wind field. The hurricane hunters found concentric eyewalls roughly 14 and 41 miles (23 and 66 km) in diameter.
#Now #Hurricane #Simon disrupts 11 airports. All commercial flights canceled at #Manzanillo ; @flyVolaris suspends services at #PuertoVallarta , #Colima , #Tepic & #Uruapan . @Aeromexico & @flyVolaris announce passenger protections. https://t.co/xk9yQ6AqcH
Simon’s general north to north-northwest motion was expected to continue, with weak but steady steering currents holding in place until the hurricane nears the coast of northern Jalico state on Sunday. That’s where the track and intensity forecast become unusually tricky, because Simon will be approaching the coast at a near-parallel angle, with the storm’s stronger right-hand (east) side closer to the coast. This means that only a slight leftward or rightward deviation in the track can produce dramatically different impacts along and near the coast. There was little help from Saturday’s forecast models in pinpointing those impacts, because the model suites included everything from tracks that keep Simon just offshore through Monday to coast-scraping solutions to tracks that move Simon bodily inland on Sunday well south of Puerto Vallarta.
Since hurricanes interact with the rugged coastal terrain of this area, they often angle further east than models expect, as NHC noted , so it’s safest to assume that Simon will move onto the coastline at some point this weekend. The rugged terrain, and drying from downslope winds flowing offshore into Simon, may induce some weakening prior to landfall, but Simon will likely be a formidable storm regardless.
As shown in Fig. 1 above, the official forecast track as of 5 p.m. EDT Saturday brings the center of Simon onto the southern Jalisco coast as a major hurricane early Sunday afternoon, and in the vicinity of Puerto Vallarta as a weakening minimal hurricane on Sunday night, likely slowing and dissipating by Tuesday. Note that the “cone” in this graphic is based on average forecast error over the past five years, and is designed to include about two-thirds of possible tracks. Simon could remain much stronger for longer if it stays just offshore, possibly bringing significant wind impacts to a longer stretch of coastline. Or it could weaken more quickly than expected if it angles further inland after landfall.
Regardless of these track possibilities, Simon’s heaviest rains will likely be well south of Puerto Vallarta, with totals near the coast as high as 12-16 inches in parts of Jalisco, Colima, and Michoacán states. The torrential rains could lead to life-threatening flash floods and mudlides. Huge surf and swells and strong rip currents are also expected, while the biggest wind impacts will hinge more closely on wherever the eastern and northern eyewall end up moving onshore.
A few hundred miles north of Simon’s encounter with the Mexican coastline, sprawling Tropical Storm Rachel will sweep onshore early Sunday, its center passing just south of the U.S.–Mexico border. As of 5 p.m. EDT Saturday , resilient Rachel’s top sustained winds were at 65 mph, a bit stronger than on Friday, with some help from the upper-level trough pushing the storm along. Tropical-storm-force winds extended out up to 140 miles (220 km) from the center, making Rachel a even broader gale-producer than Simon. However, Rachel was producing only limited rainfall, as its banding features were largely devoid of intense showers and thunderstorms (see infrared satellite image at top). Update : At 11 p.m. EDT Saturday , ill-organized Rachel was reclassified as a post-tropical cyclone with top sustained winds of 60 mph (95 km/h). No major changes have been made to the overall outlook or the expected impacts through Sunday.
10/10 – Rachel is now a post-tropical cyclone, but that does not mean the threat has diminished. Strong winds, heavy rain, and dangerous swells will continue to affect Baja California and the southwestern United States. More: https://t.co/Wk7xxBl094 #marinewx #GOESWest pic.twitter.com/cXlOHFybsM
Given Rachel’s brisk northeast motion (about 22 mph or 35 km/h on Saturday afternoon) and the size of its wind field, the storm could be packing sustained winds in the 40-50 mph range on Sunday across far northwest Mexico and as far inland as southeast California and southwest Arizona. By late Sunday, Post-Tropical Storm Rachel (or its remnant circulation) will be racing northward through Utah. Even as the surface winds spin down, upper-level winds will be slower to do so, and powerful gusts could occurs across the higher terrain of the Southwest into Sunday afternoon and evening.
A Haboob/Dust Storm with winds up to 55Mph spawned by Tropical Storm Rachel just went through Riverside County California. #CAwx #Rachel pic.twitter.com/Is1J9X4mpH
As Rachel moves onshore, the same frictional effects and higher terrain that will lead to its rapid demise as a tropical storm will help enhance rainfall. A corridor of 1-to-3-inch rains near Rachel’s path is expected on Sunday from the deserts of far southern California across the Las Vegas area and into southern Utah. Flash flooding could occur, especially where Rachel’s rains fall in narrow canyons and atop burn scars. The NOAA/NWS Weather Prediction Center has placed a moderate-risk area for excessive rain leading to flash flooding (level 3 of 4) around Rachel’s projected path from Sunday into early Monday.

articles.title_orig: Threats of Political Violence Have America’s Elected Officials Living in Fear
articles.title_zh: Threats of Political Violence Have America’s Elected Officials Living in Fear
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Capitol steps.  (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Violent threats targeted at least 70 U.S. senators, 185 House members, and 44 governors over the past two years, a New York Times investigation found, as candidates enter the final weeks of the midterm campaign.
The Times culled its tally from more than 100 open-records requests, court files, and law enforcement logs covering 2024 through August.
The threats hit Republicans and Democrats alike and reached more than half of the nation's secretaries of state, most of whom oversee their states' elections.
Official figures agree. The U.S. Capitol Police, which protects Congress, investigated 14,938 cases involving concerning statements, behaviors, and communications aimed at lawmakers, their families, staff, and the Capitol in 2025, up from 9,474 in 2024, a nearly 58% increase.
Yet the Times identified only 53 federal cases over the two years in which someone was charged with threatening a public official other than the president.
Former Capitol Police Chief J. Thomas Manger told the paper that fewer than 10% of the cases his investigators handled in 2021 resulted in charges.
Vague statutes, free-speech protections, and anonymous senders make many cases difficult to prosecute.
The cost shows up in campaign ledgers. Federal candidates spent roughly $6 million on security in the 2017-2018 election cycle and at least $25 million in the current cycle through Aug. 1, more than four times the earlier total, the Times reported , citing campaign finance records. That excludes officials' personal spending.
In Indiana, Rodric Bray, the Republican leader of the state Senate, became a chief target after his chamber voted 31-19 last December to reject a congressional map backed by President Donald Trump.
The plan aimed to eliminate the state's two Democratic-held congressional districts. At least 12 elected Republicans in Indiana faced threats or swatting attempts — false emergency reports intended to send armed police to a target's home — NBC News reported.
Bray, who plans to step down from his leadership post in November election, told the Times that bomb and death threats targeted his office and home, and he began varying his daily routine.
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., who left Congress in January after breaking with Trump over the release of files on convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, said in a May speech that when she texted Trump about threats aimed at her son, he told her "that it was my fault, and I deserve it," CBS News reported .
The White House did not deny the message's contents, the Times reported; spokesman Davis Ingle said Trump condemns political violence.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., drew a wave of threats last November after posting a video with five other lawmakers telling troops they need not obey unlawful orders, a message Trump branded seditious.
Someone swatted her parents' home while her father was dying of cancer, Slotkin said. "I signed up for this, but my family and my staff did not," she told the paper.
Capitol Police Chief Michael Sullivan told House appropriators in March that threats against Congress in 2026 were on pace to exceed the 2025 total, the Times reported .

articles.title_orig: Tech companies have an adorable plan to make you forget about AI's threat to jobs and humanity
articles.title_zh: Tech companies have an adorable plan to make you forget about AI's threat to jobs and humanity
articles.content_orig:
Jolly wants to help make your life easier — and be cute while doing it. The mascot for Meta's Muse AI is a slightly rotund, plush creature with rosy cheeks, big eyes, and a toothless grin. It can wear clothes or little headphones when he's "working" on tasks for you.
As someone who once went through some (embarrassingly) elaborate hoops to acquire a Labubu , I must admit that I was immediately enamored by the creature's debut . I'm not alone — much ink has been spilled on how cute the little avatar is . Jon Stewart even devoted a whole segment to debating the cuddly guy's true intentions.
Jolly joins a growing group of creatures vying for the hearts and minds of potential AI users. There are the round, mouthless dots of OpenAI , the fluffy Genspark lobster, and Grok users have adopted a little teal alien named "Groklet." All adorable, all plushy, and all debuting as the general populace was starting to worry that AI would maybe kill us all.
The idea behind Jolly and the rest of the mascots is simple: make us forget about all that AI doom-and-gloom and learn to love it. They play on our most human, primal instincts, distancing us from the fact that they represent something distinctly non-human. This round, fun little creature is your friend! He's going to work on your behalf! The fuzzy little charms also tap into our sense of nostalgia . Everyone I spoke to for this piece immediately had a connection to the Muse avatar: Some said it reminded them of a Tamagotchi, or MySpace avatars, or Baymax, the lovable robot from Big Hero 6.
"Seeing something cute stimulates the pleasure centers in your brain before you've even had a chance to think about it," Joshua Paul Dale, the founder of the niche academic field "Cute Studies," and a professor at Chuo University in Tokyo, tells me. "You're predisposed to act socially towards something that you find cute."
It's not the first time that cuteness has arisen in response to a collective sense of unease. In the past, the trait has been wielded as a comforting salve, a PR pivot, or to put a smiling face on something more complex. Cute has proven to be a powerful tool, and AI companies hope they can ride that wave into America's hearts — and computers.
The most visible — and successful — use of cute culture was in Japan following post-World War II. Fluffy mascots, manga, and stationery were used to shift the narrative about the country away from its aggressive, imperial history toward one of an approachable cultural destination. This shift is best personified by Hello Kitty , the now- ubiquitous cat-like mascot created in 1974 as an emblem of kawaii, the Japanese term for cute. Designed to appeal to Japanese women with newfound spending power — and their children — the cat avatar has since become a literal cultural emissary, bringing comfort to Japan's citizens and promoting the country's image elsewhere.
Beyond Japan, the deployment of cute as a culture-shaping force seems to repeat across the years. Gen Zers embraced Y2K nostalgia during the pandemic — a marked contrast to their Zoom-first era. Another 2020 hit was the video game "Animal Crossing: New Horizons," as gamers stuck at home clamored for the coziness of tending to animated life . Cultural theorist Sianne Ngai calls cuteness "an aestheticization of powerlessness" — for a consumer to feel something is cute, they need to feel they can wield power over it, giving them a sense of calm control. On the grim end, cuteness was used by Purdue Pharmaceuticals in its campaign for OxyContin: the company handed out plush toys to practitioners whom they wanted to convince to prescribe the drug. The Drug Enforcement Administration later said the tactic was "an indicator of Purdue's aggressive and inappropriate marketing."
AI companies clearly appreciate the persistent power of cuteness. It's easier for you to ask a question to your little buddy than a gray box — and why not buy a few more tokens so Jolly can book your next vacation or sift through your finances. For University of Iowa business analytics professor Thiago Serra, the branding has echoes of Tesla. Rather than consumers feeling like they have to take their eco-conscious vitamins and pony up for an electric car, Tesla made cars that looked and felt good — the environmental thing was a nice added bonus. For agents, adding a mascot shifts your thinking from the scary AI that might kill you or take your job to a cute buddy that can be helpful in your personal life.
Rebecca Kowalewicz, a digital marketing VP and millennial-Gen-X-cusper in Philadelphia, dabbled with a few AI platforms, but none were as fun as Muse. Jolly played on her sense of bygone days, reminding her of choosing a MySpace avatar. And Kowalewicz went one step further: She fed the software a photo of her late dog, Doctor Watson — a rescued coonhound pointer mix — and it quickly generated an animated version of him to replace Jolly. Now, Doctor Watson smiles at her, types, and moves his head. She's so endeared to the agent that she feels more inclined to stick with it.
"It's almost like having a work bestie," she says, except it won't push back and "you don't have to take it out to lunch."
In addition to personifying inanimate ideas or technologies, coziness and cuteness can also psychologically soothe us in uncertain times. Take Japan: already steeped in postwar cuteness, the country saw a renewed boom in coziness after its property bubble burst in 1990. People said it felt healing, Dale tells me, temporarily easing their woes amid financial and job-market upheaval. Similarly, agents can endear themselves to users by solving a task that causes dismay — with a little smile.
That's been the case for edtech consultant Tonja Brunn, a Gen Xer who — like many white-collar Americans — is on the job hunt. That search is how she and "Monkey," her Muse agent, first "connected." Monkey has "revolutionized the job search" for Brunn, and she's fallen in love with how cute her newest "employee" is. Seasonally appropriate, Monkey now wears a little shirt with a pumpkin and two cherubic ghosts.
A friendly avatar helping you plug away at all of the worst parts of the job search is the latest attempt by AI companies to target a new segment of customers: Everyday folks who were turned off by the early, austere chatbots and spooked by the rush of AI doomer news.
When Cole Benefield, the 25-year-old founder of Servo, an agentic firm for service businesses, first saw the Labubu-esque creature, he thought it was silly. Then he saw the promotional materials for Jolly, happily typing away at a keyboard. The business owners he works with probably wouldn't be too amused or charmed by the fuzzy guy. But the greater mass appeal of Jolly revealed something: While other AI firms signal their tech-industry bona fides with clever model names and sterile interfaces, Meta's years of honed consumer prowess have allowed it to reach a wider swath of consumers. Benefield says Meta's use of Jolly means non-technical users never have to think about what's happening under the hood.

Kaitlyn Murphy, a 26-year-old tech publicist in Massachusetts, questions how much AI agents could improve her day-to-day life — especially given the access they require. Despite the skepticism, when she first saw Jolly, she felt tempted to make her own version.
"I love the idea that I could watch it typing while I'm sending it on a task. I actually do think it's really cute," she sai

articles.title_orig: What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
articles.title_zh: What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
articles.content_orig:
A major energy conference is going ahead in Riyadh from Sunday despite a Houthi attack on the city’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Saudi ⁠Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said on Sunday that the 25th ⁠World Petroleum Council Energy Congress has begun ‌in Riyadh. The 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial will be held on the sidelines of the conference, called Riyadh Energy Week, which is to run until Thursday.
But Italy, the cohost of the IEF, will join the meeting via videolink. Nigeria, the other cohost, is sending a representative to the event.
The IEF brings together 68 countries that account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supplies and demand. Its members include Saudi Arabia, the United States and Russia. The meeting comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy flows and pushed governments to reassess their energy security.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at where the world’s energy comes from, how much is produced in the Middle East and which countries have strategic reserves to fall back on.
Energy heats our homes, fuels our cars, keeps the lights on and runs the factories that make what we buy. It comes from fossil fuels such as oil, coal and gas as well as nuclear power and renewables.
Despite rapid growth in renewables, fossil fuels still account for nearly 81 percent of global energy consumption. Oil is the largest source at 31.4 percent, followed by coal at 25.9 percent and natural gas at 23.5 percent. Traditional biomass, nuclear power and other sources make up the rest.
Production is concentrated in a handful of regions, so disruptions in any of them ripple through global markets.
The Middle East is the largest oil-producing region, and North America is the largest natural gas producer. Russia and Central Asia are also major producers of both.
The Middle East’s importance to energy markets is also about geography. Three narrow waterways connect its producers with consumers around the world.
Before the Iran war, about 27 percent of global seaborne oil trade and almost 20 percent of liquefied natural gas trade transited through the Strait of Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula.
On the peninsula’s western side, the Bab al-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. As the Iran war has spilled over into other areas of the Middle East and Yemen’s civil war has ramped up, traffic has been reduced through both the strait and canal, forcing some energy shipments on longer routes around Africa.
“That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a chokepoint,” said Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service.
He told Al Jazeera that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Gulf ports are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
Further down the supply chain, people and businesses are feeling the disruption through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries that rely on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf face higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find other suppliers. Even where deals have kept goods moving, the extra costs are being passed down the chain.
Eritrea and Madagascar are the most dependent on Middle Eastern oil, each sourcing about 90 percent of their supply from the region. They are followed by Pakistan (78 percent), Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Gas has been even harder to replace than oil because most of it travels as liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz.
Countries that depend on these shipments are paying more for fuel and electricity and competing for a smaller pool of cargoes. Poorer importers with little storage have struggled the most to find alternatives.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern gas are mostly in Asia. South Korea sources 31 percent of the gas it uses from the region, followed by India (29 percent), Pakistan (27 percent) and Taiwan (26 percent).
Countries keep emergency oil stocks for when supplies are cut off or reduced, and these have been the world’s main cushion during the war. That cushion is now wearing thin.
Western countries have little left to release, energy industry leaders warned, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1982.
“Estimates suggest less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today with the vast majority not practically available,” Amin Nasser, head of Saudi Aramco, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
The International Energy Agency, which coordinates emergency stocks for its members, released a record 400 million barrels of oil in March. It is now preparing to release another 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to ease soaring diesel prices although some of this may be oil from the March release that has yet to reach the market.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks in Saudi Arabia are now threatening supplies again, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Before this year’s releases, China held by far the largest reserves, an estimated 1.4 billion barrels, more than the rest of the list combined. The US was second with 413 million barrels, followed by Japan with 263 million.

Even if global warming is limited to 1.5 degrees Celsius, scientists warn China’s densely populated coastline faces flooding this century
They said gravitational shifts caused by shrinking Antarctic ice would redistribute water across the globe, causing higher ocean levels along China’s densely populated coastlines.
“Even if we limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit], the Paris Agreement’s most ambitious goal, Antarctica still has a 92 per cent chance of losing mass this century,” said lead author Lin Yucheng, an assistant professor at City University of Hong Kong’s school of energy and environment.

articles.title_orig: World Bank in talks with dozens of countries about crisis aid, Banga says
articles.title_zh: World Bank in talks with dozens of countries about crisis aid, Banga says
articles.content_orig:
Bangkok, Oct. 11 (SANA) The World Bank is in talks with around 40 countries about potential financial support to help them cope with the economic fallout of the Middle East war, particularly rising energy and essential commodity prices, World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters on Sunday.
Banga said the global economy had shown some resilience, supported by heavy investment in artificial intelligence and shifts in oil supply and demand. This had limited countries’ reliance on emergency financing made available by the bank after the US-Iran war broke out in late February.
The bank initially made $25 billion available to address the crisis and could provide an additional $35 billion by redirecting funds from approved projects, Banga said. More countries may seek assistance in the coming months as diesel and fertilizer prices remain high.
The bank is discussing financing options with several governments, some of which prefer to restructure existing projects to meet immediate liquidity needs rather than use its rapid crisis-response facility. Banga said the bank was prepared to expand support if conditions deteriorated.
He added that the bank could increase crisis-response financing to $100 billion if necessary, surpassing the roughly $70 billion it provided during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Last month, the bank reported mobilizing $112 billion in private capital in the year ending in June, up from $69 billion the previous year. It also invested $123 billion from its own resources, bringing total financing to $235 billion.
Developing countries face mounting pressure from higher energy and borrowing costs, with public finances already strained by the COVID-19 pandemic and inflation following the Russia-Ukraine war.
The financing push comes as official bilateral development assistance from Western countries has declined sharply, increasing pressure on international institutions to mobilize resources for economies most vulnerable to economic shocks.

articles.title_orig: Maximo Quiles: meet the 2026 Moto3 World Champion!
articles.title_zh: Maximo Quiles: meet the 2026 Moto3 World Champion!
articles.content_orig:
The #28 seals the deal with a win – get to know the newest Moto3 World Champion and future Moto2 star after a landmark season
Maximo Quiles (CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team) is the 2026 Moto3 World Champion! The #28 has shown incredible pace and expert racecraft all season to secure the crown, sealing the deal with a stylish win at the Pertamina Grand Prix of Indonesia. He’s only the fourth rider in history to ever win a Championship – in any class – with five races remaining, alongside Marc Marquez, Giacomo Agostini and Mike Hailwood.
The Spanish rider lifts the title trophy in Indonesia with five rounds to spare after a dominant second season in the World Championship
Quiles, born in 2008, began his racing career at a young age, making headlines on minibikes before climbing through the Spanish ranks. The #28’s talent was clear, as he found himself in the MotoJunior paddock, making his European Cup debut in 2021. Incredible. The only word that comes close to describing his rookie season. Three victories, five podiums and plenty of encouraging signs. Backing that pace up the following two seasons, Quiles returned to the top step in 2022 before setting up a title attack in 2023. The Spanish star joined Aspar, winning five times and proving he was the real deal; the #28 took the 2023 European Cup crown. There was a change of scenery in 2024 as he made the step up to the Moto3 Junior World Championship. Quiles impressed instantly, winning at the season finale and clinching third in the standings. Alongside his efforts in the MotoJunior paddock, he raced in the Red Bull MotoGP Rookies Cup for three seasons. Finishing third in the Championship on two occasions and picking up seven wins from his time in the class, Quiles’ name wasn’t far from the headlines. Aspar had seen enough, signing the #28 for the 2025 season – Quiles was Moto3 World Championship bound.
His rookie campaign was nothing short of incredible. His season didn’t get underway until COTA, with Quiles initially being too young to race in the opening two rounds. P5 on debut before a training crash forced the rookie to miss two rounds, returning in France. It didn’t take long for the ball to get rolling either, with Quiles earning podiums at Silverstone and Aragon before a maiden win at Mugello. Ending 2025 with three wins, nine podiums and two pole positions was an impressive addition to his CV, and set up a title attack…
2026 couldn’t have started much better for Quiles, winning four of the opening six races and standing on the podium a further two times. Further wins in Hungary and Assen only upped his Championship momentum – bringing his lead to 104 points – as we reached the summer break in Germany. However, it wasn’t all smooth sailing for the title leader, crashing in Q2 at Silverstone and sitting out the remainder of the weekend after a collarbone break. His comeback and response? Winning the next round at MotorLand Aragon to make his intentions clear – the title attack wasn’t over. Quiles carried his incredible form to Misano and Austria, making it three consecutive race wins, extending his lead to 131 points and setting up his first match point in Japan. His future might already be decided, with the Spanish sensation confirming the move to Moto2 next season, but his mission in Moto3 wasn’t over yet.
The deal wasn’t sealed just yet though. A second place in Motegi, under the pressure of his first match point, was impressive – but closest title rival David Almansa (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) made a stunning last stand to make Quiles wait for it. The #28’s moment in the spotlight then finally arrived at the Indonesian GP. Quiles was right at the front from the off, escaped a huge group scuffle for the podium and kept it calm to the line for his 10 th win of the season, crowning himself 2026 Moto3 World Champion.

articles.title_orig: Back in Bushong: Brothers and World War II veterans Jay and William Moreland returned to their home and family eight decades after their deaths
articles.title_zh: Back in Bushong: Brothers and World War II veterans Jay and William Moreland returned to their home and family eight decades after their deaths
articles.content_orig:
The Moreland brothers have been returned home.
Repatriation activities took place Saturday afternoon for brothers Sgt. Jay Moreland and Staff Sgt. William Moreland of Bushong, beginning with a ceremony and presentation from the Morelands’ youngest brother, Larry Moreland, inside Robert’s-Blue-Barnett Funeral Home. Following the presentation, the brothers received a formal escort from Emporia to Bushong, where they were laid to rest with full military honors.
Following the ceremony, Larry Moreland spoke with KVOE News and said it was important to him and his family to hold a funeral ceremony for his brothers.
Moreland noted that he was, to an extent, surprised by the ceremony’s size and turnout.
The Moreland Brothers enlisted in the US Army in February 1943 and, at their request, trained and deployed together as members of the 149th Engineer Combat Battalion. The brothers died on June 6th, 1944, during the invasion of Omaha Beach on D-Day when their landing craft struck an underwater German mine.
Jay Moreland was 21 and William 19 at the time of their deaths. Larry Moreland, who was only an infant at the time of his siblings’ passing, says their military careers were indicative of how “inseparable” his brothers were throughout their lives.
As mentioned, Saturday’s ceremony was a largely attended affair by both residents and veterans, including a half-dozen chapters of the American Legion Riders who helped provide the brothers’ escort, alongside local law enforcement. American Legion Post 5 member Clay Childs says this turnout symbolizes the unity and camaraderie amongst military personnel regardless of their branch of service.
Saturday’s ceremony was the second repatriation ceremony for a native of Bushong after Sgt. John Owen Herrick was laid to rest back in 2024. Herrick was also a member of the 149th Engineer Combat Battalion and died aboard the same craft as the Moreland brothers in 1944.
Click here for a YouTube Short recapping the Moreland Brothers’ repatriation.
Photos by Tagan Trahoon/KVOE News.

articles.title_orig: 'Take that light into the world': Interfaith group holds candlelight vigil for peace
articles.title_zh: 'Take that light into the world': Interfaith group holds candlelight vigil for peace
articles.content_orig:
In the shadow of a war memorial, a group of residents rallied for peace.
Wareham Faith in Action, an interfaith organization that works with Wareham Law and Democracy, gathered people at Center Park for its first peace vigil on Saturday, Oct. 10.
Vigil goers lit candles and listened to speeches and songs that called for an end to wars overseas and ICE detentions at home.
“Peace doesn’t mean the absence of tension, but it means the presence of justice,” said Wandra Harmsen in a speech. “And when we have justice, we will have peace.”
The vigil’s message was "Light a candle. Hold a hope. Stand for peace." Wareham Faith in Action organizers gave candles to everyone in attendance and had people light each other’s candles, spreading the flame throughout the park.
“We’ll ask you to take that light into the world,” Wareham Faith in Action Co-Chair Lisa Govoni told the attendees.
Those who attended had a common goal: change. “We’re here for change,” said Maria Rowley. “Justice and equality for all.”
“Our country needs a little boost of peace,” said Candy Johansen.
The Golden Rule was a core theme of the vigil. Keith Harvey, another co-chair and a Quaker, said that many of the world’s religions include some form of the rule directing people to treat everyone fairly. He said that Wareham Faith in Action wanted to bring people of all faiths together through their common beliefs.
The organization didn’t allow political messaging at the vigil. Harvey said that the organization keeps politics out of its events in order to bring more people in.
“There’s a center that all faiths are trying to move to. Let’s move there together,” Harvey said.
Henry St. Julien, a Wareham resident and the director of diversity, equity, inclusion and belonging at the Falmouth School District, talked about Anthony Burns, a slave who escaped to Boston but was arrested and returned to Virginia in 1854 under the Fugitive Slave Act. He said that 50,000 Bostonians protested the detention, shaming the officers arresting Burns.
He also said that a group of Bostonians raised thousands of dollars to buy Burns’ freedom.
St. Julien drew parallels between Burns’ story and the stories of families who have been detained and deported by ICE.
“History … it’s a mirror,” St. Julien said. “When we look at this mirror, we see a reoccurring history … where there’s a struggle for human dignity against systems.”
He said that as a school administrator, he needs to come up with a plan to help students in case their parents are detained. He said he’s seen fear creep into his schools.
“I’m compelled by my faith,” he said. “And every day, I ensure that every child walks through our doors, feels safe, seen, valued and protected, regardless of where they’re born, what language they speak … what status they have.”
St. Julien urged the vigil goers not to let their work end after the event. He said they should continue to make their voices heard. “Chaos flourishes when good people stay silent while vulnerable [people] are targeted,” he said.
Wareham Faith in Action gave attendees ways to help, promoting a GoFundMe to support Haitian families living in the area who had their temporary protected statuses removed over the summer.
The organization will continue hosting events promoting peace. It already hosted three peace walks this summer.
Harmsen said that the organization will “aim higher” with its coming events and try to involve local government and other parts of the community.

WLOS — As remnants of Hurricane Isaias moves through the South this weekend, western North Carolina is experiencing wet and windy conditions. The weather has caused disruptions in some areas, including power outages and downed trees.
According to a Duke Energy power outage map update , remnants of Isaias are bringing heavy rain, gusty winds and power outages to some areas in the Carolinas. Their crews are working to assess damage and restore power as safely and quickly as possible. The energy company advises staying away from downed power lines.

Officials also advise caution on roadways. The North Canton Fire Department posted on Facebook about a two-car crash on West Interstate 40, mile marker 32.5, saying to exercise extreme caution due to the amount of rain that has fallen and continues.
North Carolina Emergency Management activated Mooresville Fire-Rescue’s Swift Water Rescue team to western North Carolina, with 12 Mooresville Fire-Rescue members deploying to Yancey County.

articles.title_orig: House Republican, invoking Reagan, moves to block Trump's Russia oil deal
articles.title_zh: House Republican, invoking Reagan, moves to block Trump's Russia oil deal
articles.content_orig:
In brief: US Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon are preparing the bipartisan “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” to prohibit purchases of Russian petroleum, directly challenging Donald Trump’s commercial agreement permitting Russian diesel imports. Bacon condemned the administration’s move as a sign of weakness that finances the Russian military machine, calling on Congress to vote its conscience and reaffirm support for Ukraine ahead of the midterm elections.
Members of the US Congress are preparing bipartisan legislation to prohibit purchases of Russian petroleum, moving to challenge US President Donald Trump’s commercial agreement permitting Russian diesel imports onto American and global markets.
The legislative initiative, titled the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,” is being drafted by Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, with Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska confirming he will join as one of its initial co-sponsors.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The bill aims to establish a statutory ban on purchasing Russian oil and petroleum products, seeking to reverse the administration’s regulatory exemptions and curtail revenues funding the Russian military.
We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil.  It will be called the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.”  It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly. #PeaceThroughStrength
In comments to Ukrainska Pravda , Bacon criticized the administration’s diesel agreement, characterizing the decision as a grave policy misstep that projects weakness toward the Kremlin while providing financial lifelines to Moscow’s defense sector.
“Allowing the purchase of Russian diesel fuel gives money to the Russian economy and its war machine,” Bacon said.
“A year ago, the president criticized Europeans for purchasing Russian gas. I completely disagree with this decision, and I consider the president’s policy regarding Russia and Ukraine a failure. I and ‘old school’ Republicans, supporters of Ronald Reagan, are deeply disappointed.”
Bacon attributed the administration’s decision to domestic political calculations ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, noting that retail diesel prices approaching $6 per gallon have created pressure on voters. However, the lawmaker argued that the transactional approach undermines the nation’s strategic and moral standing.
Writing on X, Fitzpatrick also reaffirmed congressional backing for Kyiv, stating that President Volodymyr Zelensky maintains the overwhelming support of lawmakers and the American public.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine, a sovereign and freedom-loving nation, and Russia is squarely to blame for all damage and destruction, to both lives and treasure, that has resulted from Putin’s unprovoked attack,” Fitzpatrick stated.
“We have your back, and we will stand with you until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
The push for legislative intervention follows Trump’s announcement on Friday, Oct. 9, of a bilateral arrangement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to American and international buyers.
Under the terms announced by Trump following a telephone conversation with Putin, Moscow agreed to deliver 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter, with prospective deliveries scaling up to 3 million tons depending on the operational status of Russian refineries.
To enable the transactions, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was enacted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, a statute intended to expand secondary sanctions and tariff mechanisms across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The announcement drew condemnation from Ukrainian officials, who noted that the deal coincided with multilateral peace consultations in Miami involving US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. President Zelensky characterized the timing of the Miami talks as a “smokescreen” for bilateral energy concessions .
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that offering economic accommodations to the Kremlin signals Western weakness , arguing that the Russian leadership interprets concessions as appeasement rather than an incentive to negotiate.
Sybiha maintained that only an energy ceasefire – under which Russia halts attacks on Ukraine’s electrical and heating infrastructure in exchange for a pause in Ukrainian refinery strikes – can sustainably reduce fuel costs.
Lawmakers backing the new bill argue that allowing Russian refined hydrocarbons back into Western supply chains directly contradicts allied efforts to starve Moscow’s wartime budget.
The draft statute must be formally introduced in the House of Representatives and pass both chambers of Congress before it can be submitted to the president, setting up a potential legislative confrontation over executive sanctions waivers and energy trade with Russia.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Kalen DeBoer talks refs, injuries and more after Alabama loses to Georgia
articles.title_zh: Kalen DeBoer talks refs, injuries and more after Alabama loses to Georgia
articles.content_orig:
OutKick's Trey Wallace provides an update on the weather after Hurricane Isaias' remnants made its way through Tuscaloosa ahead of Saturday's Alabama-Georgia game.
TUSCALOOSA, AL- Don't tell Georgia or Alabama that Saturday night's game in Tuscaloosa was meaningless because of the current college football playoff format.
After a week full of drama surrounding Hurricane Isaias and whether we would see these two teams take the field on time, fans were treated to a heavyweight showdown inside Bryant Denny Stadium on Saturday in front of a soaked crowd watching from the stands.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
We did not need any extra hype for this one. The theatrical movies that schools release before kickoff were not going to do anything that the Bulldogs and Tide couldn’t do when they arrived around 5:40 p.m. EST on Saturday afternoon.
WATCH AS OUTKICK'S TREY WALLACE BRAVES HURRICANE ISAIAS' BEFORE ALABAMA-GEORGIA SHOWDOWN IN TUSCALOOSA
This was about Kirby Smart trying to buck the regular season trend against Alabama, while Kalen DeBoer looked to put his team back into the perceived national spot that some wanted to argue they had fallen out of.
What you got was two teams trading haymakers for a first half that ended with DeBoer going for a touchdown with just seconds remaining on the clock, taking a 14-10 lead into the locker room.
ALABAMA PROVIDES UPDATE FOR SHOWDOWN AGAINST GEORGIA, AS SCHOOL, SEC AND TRUMP PLAN FOR HURRICANE ISAIAS
This came after Georgia had found its way out of its own end of the field on two occasions for 10 points.
Running back EJ Crowell of the Alabama Crimson Tide gets around defensive back KJ Bolden of the Georgia Bulldogs for a touchdown during the first half at Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Ala., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Getty Images)
A late-arriving crowd inside a a misty Bryant Denny Stadium watched two coaches trying to outmaneuver each other for four quarters, while Keelon Russell and Gunner Stockton traded shots on offense.
What more could you ask for on a day filled with so much drama around college football?
Heck, in the fourth quarter alone this evening, Georgia missed a field goal that would have given it the lead against Alabama, while Kentucky missed a 26-yard chip shot that would have tied the game with LSU.
There were plenty of times in this game tonight where Georgia felt like the better football team, in all facets. But then, when you have such dynamic team like Alabama that can score on you within seconds, no lead seemed safe.
In reality, we were watching two of the best teams in college football in Tuscaloosa, and it doesn’t matter that they both come from the SEC. You can add Ohio State to that list, while taking Texas off of it at the same time.
Head coach Kirby Smart of the Georgia Bulldogs reacts after a penalty during the first half against the Alabama Crimson Tide at Bryant-Denny Stadium on Oct. 10, 2026, in Tuscaloosa, Ala. (Getty Images)
We are reaching that point in the season where the frauds are starting to show themselves, and there wasn’t one on the field in Tuscaloosa. We can talk about Alabama and this team moving past the Saban era until we're blue in the face, and some will still be doing 10 years from now.
ALABAMA CRIMSON TIDE NAMES STARTER FOR WEEK ONE: GET TO KNOW BAMA QUARTERBACK KEELON RUSSELL
While Georgia would retake the lead with a field goal on the ensuing drive, the officials would become part of the story late in the fourth quarter.
Chaos reigned on Alabama's drive, as Georgia was not called for an obvious pass interference that would have resulted in the Tide extending its drive by 15-yards. But, as the boos reigned down from the Bryant Denny Stadium stands, there was nothing left for the Alabama fans to cheer about after the Bulldogs sacked Keelon Russell on the ensuing play.
In that moment, tacked on with a personal foul against Dijon Lee that resulted in Georgia being able to take a knee and run the clock out, which once led to Kalen DeBoer being the most animated we've seen him during his time at Alabama.
Until somebody beats them, it's the Dawgs .
One way or the other, Kirby Smart has a football team that finds a way to win football games, which is not the case for other teams across the Southeastern Conference , or the sport.
"I didn’t come here to lose," Kirby Smart said after the game.
We witnessed a football team fighting through adversity, with the world wondering if Kirby Smart was going to get over some type of perceived hump.
Head coach Kirby Smart of the Georgia Bulldogs reacts during the second quarter against the Alabama Crimson Tide at Bryant-Denny Stadium on Sept. 28, 2024, in Tuscaloosa, Ala. (Getty Images)
The problem for those pushing that message: Kirby Smart really does not care any longer. Following the win, Smart bolted straight for the visitors section, slinging his visor around in the air while the Georgia fans and Kirby's wife waited to embrace his family.
"I'd rather make memories with my family, team and coaching staff ... I just wanted to celebrate with my wife..She deserved a kiss for all that she puts up with from me."
We are witnessing a new Kirby Smart, who is not worried about trying to silence critics or whatever is being written about him.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
That's a dangerous man, who seems to be fighting more for the respect from his family and those who encompass the football facility in Athens.
"Do I wanna win championships? Hell yeah, but I have a lot more respect for them (family and players) to understand that there's a lot more important things in life."
Welcome to the new era of Kirby Smart.

articles.title_orig: MacBook Pro overhaul: entry-level model to gain new design sooner than expected
articles.title_zh: MacBook Pro overhaul: entry-level model to gain new design sooner than expected
articles.content_orig:
Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected.
Normally, when Apple introduces a new MacBook Pro design, it takes a while to trickle down. For instance, the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M1 Pro and M1 Max was introduced in 2021, but the base model MacBook Pro stuck with the 13-inch design until 2023, when it gained the 14-inch chassis with the M3 chip .
Similarly, when Apple redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2016, it wasn’t until 2019 that the entry level model gained the Touch Bar. There’s also a similar story for the 2012 retina MacBook Pro redesign.
This time around though, there’ll only be a roughly 6 month gap before the redesign comes to the entry level.
According to Bloomberg , Apple will be introducing the redesign to the entry level MacBook Pro in early 2027, shortly after debuting it in the high end MacBook Pros, rumored to be called MacBook Ultra. From the report :
Apple is also preparing a revamped entry-level MacBook Pro, code-named K104, for as early as the first half of next year. The 14-inch laptop will adopt a new design in line with what Apple is preparing for higher-end MacBooks with touch screens due between the end of this year and early next year.
It’s worth noting that there’ll also be another entry level MacBook Pro with the current design and the M6 chip, which is currently on track to debut this fall alongside the redesigned high-end MacBook Pros.
To make things even weirder, those redesigned high-end MacBook Pros are also expected to debut with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, instead of M6 generation chips. Apple recently made a decision to abandon its plans for high end M6 chips to instead accelerate M7.
In short, it’ll look like this:
Of course, the redesign is expected to feature a slightly thinner chassis, OLED displays with touch support, and possibly even come with a Dynamic Island.
With the recent price hikes, this is excellent news for some people. I’m sure the redesigned 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro will likely cost over $2500, so if you’re looking to get something more in budget with the M7 chip and the redesign, you’ll only have to wait until the following spring.
I wish Apple would come back to the lines up it had years ago, one restyling of all the laptops, one of all the ipad at the same time and so on, in the last few years they have be releasing updates bits at the time, sometime the line up doesn't even make sense (M4 pro next to Basic M5). If i need to finally update a machine I'm stuck between waiting for a never arriving hardware or buying something already old. it really doesn't make sense. the only thing they kept similar is the iPhone line up each year where they change all the models at the same time, although they have the occasional basic model popping up here and there... also the've become very slow in their release, by the time a new ipad comes out there are already rumors and specs about the next model... it really doesn`t make sense commercially....
It’s certainly unfortunate that the $1,999 price point of the entry level MacBook Pro today is what the Pro chip versions cost just under a year ago , but that’s the inevitable reality of this memory shortage .

articles.title_orig: World Mental Health Day
articles.title_zh: World Mental Health Day
articles.content_orig:
Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia
Around the world, more than 1 billion people live with a mental health condition – most commonly anxiety or depression – and suicide remains a leading cause of death of young people. In the WHO South-East Asia Region, 208 000 people are lost each year to suicide, and an estimated 289 million people live with a mental, neurological, self-harm, or substance use condition.
This year, the theme of World Mental Health Day, “ Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change ,” reminds us that people with lived experience (PWLE) of mental health conditions must not only be recipients of care – their voices must help shape the care, policies, and services that affect their lives. PWLE are a source of knowledge and expertise, and a powerful force for change, helping challenge stigma and discrimination, and helping services become more responsive, respectful, and relevant. When PWLE participate as equal partners, mental health systems move closer to putting people first.
The Region has made progress. India has launched a nationwide tele-mental health initiative, and Bangladesh and Nepal are advancing WHO's Special Initiative for Mental Health . Bhutan and Sri Lanka are expanding community services, and Maldives is strengthening suicide prevention. Myanmar has reinforced psychosocial support, and Thailand is pioneering digital tools and workforce development. In 2025, the WHO South-East Asia Region launched a dashboard on mental, neurological, substance use, and self-harm conditions, to help accelerate and strengthen evidence-based planning, monitoring, and evaluation of mental health services and policies.
In 2024, WHO convened a mental health summit, “ Voices of People with Lived Experience in the WHO South-East Asia Region, ” in Nepal. PWLE and caregivers from eight countries shared perspectives on their rights, including access to health care, employment, housing, and education, and to identify opportunities for policy and systems reform. The resulting Kathmandu Charter for the Rights of People with Lived Experience of Mental Health Conditions is a guide for Member States to develop contextualized national charters of their own. It sets out rights to equal opportunities, autonomy in decision-making, community-based care, and participation in development of policies, programmes, and budgets.
The Region is guided by the Paro Declaration on universal access to people-centred mental health care and services , adopted in 2022. It commits to reorient mental health services around primary health care, to establish rights-oriented community mental health networks, and to combat stigma and discrimination through community empowerment and the active engagement of PWLE. The regional Mental Health Action Plan 2023–2030 puts these commitments into practice, making the involvement of PWLE in policy development, implementation, service evaluation, and research agendas a guiding principle. It further calls on Member States to support independent organisations of PWLE, and establishes regional targets including a 50% increase in government service coverage for mental health conditions, and a 15% reduction in the suicide rate by 2030.
Nevertheless, gaps remain. In many Member States, treatment gaps are as high as 90%. Services are concentrated in urban areas and institutions, out-of-pocket expenditure is high, and stigma and discrimination are widespread. Universal access requires addressing stigma and discrimination, strengthening community participation, supporting families and caregivers, and ensuring that PWLE have a meaningful voice in the design, implementation and evaluation of mental health policies, services, and budgets.
WHO is committed to working with Member States, PWLE, families, caregivers, civil society, health workers, and communities across the Region to transform mental health care and support, building systems where every voice matters, every person is treated with dignity, and everyone can access the mental health care and support they need, when and where they need it.

articles.title_orig: Mainland condemns Taiwan leader for playing up 'mainland threat'
articles.title_zh: Mainland condemns Taiwan leader for playing up 'mainland threat'
articles.content_orig:
The Chinese mainland on Saturday condemned Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te for clinging to a "Taiwan independence" stance and playing up the so-called mainland threat in a speech, saying his remarks misled the public and fueled confrontation across the Taiwan Strait.
Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said Lai's speech disregarded facts, distorted right and wrong, and exposed his ulterior motives, revealing his true colors as a so-called pragmatic worker for Taiwan independence.
ALSO READ: Mainland criticizes Taiwan authorities over 'defense' spending increase
Zhang criticized Lai for stubbornly adhering to a separatist "Taiwan independence" stance and playing up the so-called mainland threat. She also accused him of promoting the false narrative of "democracy versus authoritarianism" and seeking "Taiwan independence" through force and by relying on external forces.
Such moves stoke confrontation across the Taiwan Strait and undermine regional peace and stability, Zhang said.
"There is only one China in the world, and Taiwan is part of China," Zhang said, stressing that this remains the real status quo across the Taiwan Strait. She added that the one-China principle is a basic norm governing international relations, a broad consensus in the international community and an important part of the post-World War II international order.
READ MORE: Mainland slams DPP authorities for blocking job site serving Taiwan youth
"The future of Taiwan can only and must be decided jointly by all Chinese people, including Taiwan compatriots," she said.
Zhang said the mainland would uphold the one-China principle and the 1992 Consensus, unite people from all walks of life in Taiwan, resolutely combat separatist forces seeking "Taiwan independence", oppose external interference, and safeguard peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.
"As people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait are one family, we will deepen cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation, promote the peaceful and integrated development of cross-Strait relations, and advance the cause of national reunification and rejuvenation," she added.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Simon strengthens into Category 4 storm as it takes aim at Mexico's Pacific coast
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Simon strengthens into Category 4 storm as it takes aim at Mexico's Pacific coast
articles.content_orig:
Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane as it barrels toward Mexico's Pacific coast.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said Saturday that Simon's maximum sustained winds increased to 155 miles per hour.
The hurricane center said it expects Simon to approach Mexico's west-central coast on Sunday as a major hurricane, which is defined as a Category 3 storm or stronger, with winds of at least 111 mph.
Simon on Saturday night was just below a Category 5 classification, which requires maximum sustained winds of 157 mph. Forecasters said that Simon could weaken rapidly if its core moves fully onshore once it makes landfall.
The hurricane could bring as much as 10 to 20 inches of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches.
"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the center warned in a bulletin that also urged residents to take immediate action to prepare as tropical storm conditions arrived Saturday afternoon.
According to the hurricane center, Simon was about 65 miles south-southwest of Manzanillo, Mexico, on Saturday and moving slowly northward at 5 mph.
"Preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion in the hurricane warning area before conditions deteriorate later tonight," the hurricane center warned.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors were fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones by Friday afternoon.
Convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows Saturday morning, when few were walking the streets under overcast skies.
"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."
The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge "along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall." The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Meanwhile, Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who along with his wife still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do Saturday. "I just don't know what to expect."
Unlike the Atlantic, which saw just its first named hurricane of the season this week with Isaias, the Pacific season has been very active. Simon's arrival comes on the heels of Polo , which slammed Mexico last week as a Category 2 hurricane before reaching the southwestern U.S. and bringing heavy flooding to the region.

articles.title_orig: China retiree devotes life to photography after tumour shrinks post-bucket-list trip

articles.content_orig:
Driven by a new-found motivation to live, Wang has spent her pension on advanced gear, travelled to 30 countries to pursue bird photography
After spending all her savings on a month-long trip to Antarctica following a cancer diagnosis, a woman from southwestern China discovered that her tumour had shrunk.
Wang Ying, 67, is an amateur wildlife photographer who has photographed more than 1,200 bird species.
In 2013, as she was preparing to retire from her job as an administrator at a school in Kunming, the capital of southwestern China’s Yunnan province, Wang was diagnosed with a form of thyroid cancer. Doctors urged her to undergo surgery immediately, the Shanghai Morning Post reported.

articles.title_orig: Could Thai durian export duty mean higher prices, higher quality in China?
articles.title_zh: Could Thai durian export duty mean higher prices, higher quality in China?
articles.content_orig:
Proposed levy part of a draft bill aimed at establishing a fund for research and ‘sustainable’ development of the sector
A Thai government proposal to charge export duties on durians, a major cash crop, could raise prices for the fruit in China – its primary market – along with the quality, analysts said.
Thailand’s draft bill to establish a fund for research and “sustainable” development of the durian sector would include the collection of fees, the government’s public relations department said last month.
Southeast Asian media outlets and agricultural publications have tipped the export duty to be as high as 2 baht (5 US cents) per kilogram.

articles.title_orig: San Antonio DJ heads to London for world finals
articles.title_zh: San Antonio DJ heads to London for world finals
articles.content_orig:
by Yami Virgin, Photojournalist Paul Sanchez and Investigative Producer Natalie Medina
SAN ANTONIO — His dad, Rene Cardenas, is a famous San Antonio DJ now his son wants to take the city’s music scene international. Our Yami Virgin, who started out as a radio DJ while at UTSA, introduces us to an artist ready to make his own name on the world stage.
Two turntables, six minutes, and a chance to put San Antonio on the world stage.
"The DMC battle is the most prestigious DJ battle that has ever been on the planet," said Rene Cardenas, known as DJ RC3.
RC3 has won the U.S. Nationals.
Now, he's headed to London for the DMC World Finals.
"I'm going to go to London and show everybody how the USA Rolls and how we do it down here in the 210," Cardenas said.
He's competing in the classic category, showing off his scratching, beat juggling, and musical creativity.
Between practice sessions, he's studying business administration at St. Philip's College.
"I feel a lot more independent being that I'm really focusing on myself and I'm the one that's worried about myself and making sure that I am on top of everything," Cardenas said.
After competing in Tokyo last year, he says he's more comfortable taking the world stage.
"I make sure that I have fun while I'm doing anything related to DMC and especially when I'm out there," Cardenas said.
To help cover the trip, RC3 will showcase his battle routines at Pueblo Hall, Oct. 25, a chance for all of us in San Antonio to hear his skills before the world does.
