articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Rachel is behaving in unusual ways. What that means for SoCal this weekend
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Tropical Storm Rachel brings with it  a slew of potential hazards, including damaging coastal flooding.
The National Hurricane Center warned that Rachel could pick up some strength before arriving on the West Coast — an unusual occurrence for storms in the tropical eastern Pacific.
Typically, storms weaken significantly once they enter those cooler waters. But El Niño conditions and an ongoing marine heat wave have pushed ocean temperatures 10 to 13 degrees higher than normal, providing a far-more-conducive environment for Rachel.
“It’s notable that this is an unusual event that’s being made possible by both coincidence of this early arriving low-pressure trough off the coast of California and the record warm — and I do mean record warm — ocean temperatures off the coast of California right now,” UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said during a briefing  Friday.
Rachel is expected to make landfall either in northern Baja California or San Diego County as early as Saturday night.
In the modern record, only two storms  have passed through the state at tropical-storm strength.
The first — nicknamed El Cordonazo, or the Lash of St. Francis — hit Long Beach and San Pedro in September 1939 . It dumped 5.62 inches of rain on L.A. over three days, spawned wind gusts of up to 65 mph and resulted in 45 deaths from flooding, with an additional 48 deaths at sea.
There was also Nora in September 1997, which was briefly at tropical storm strength as its center passed along the California-Arizona border, but California was spared the kind of damage it delivered to Baja California. Street flooding was reported in Imperial County, the Coachella Valley and San Diego, while big waves boosted by Nora and another storm sent breakers crashing into beachfront properties in Seal Beach, seriously damaging three homes and resulting in minor damage to 45 others.
The blistering heat that has baked Southern California for days is coming to an end, with rain on tap for the weekend and early next week, along with a risk of potentially damaging coastal flooding.
The National Weather Service office in San Diego on Friday issued a rare tropical storm watch for most of San Diego County, including San Diego, Chula Vista, Carlsbad and Oceanside, meaning that tropical storm-force winds are possible over the next 48 hours. It’s only the second time a tropical storm watch has  been issued in California.
Coastal flooding will remain the biggest concern for the region in the coming days, particularly for south-facing shores, given the combination of high tides, a higher-than-typical water level and the arriving tropical storm. Swells will not only bring the potential for water intrusion, but also hazardous surf — ranging from 3 to 6 feet in some areas — and rip currents, according to the weather service.
Officials had predicted that tides in Southern California would be 1 foot to 1.5 feet above normal what would ordinarily be expected without the abnormally warm ocean temperatures wrought by El Niño .
Around 9 a.m. Friday, the high tide in San Diego and La Jolla was coming in 17 inches higher than the official prediction, which doesn’t account for hotter-than-normal ocean waters or swells from tropical storms, according to NOAA’s tide forecasts. Tides were coming in 16 inches higher than the official prediction in Santa Monica and 14 inches higher in San Francisco as of Friday morning.
“We’ve got water that’s already high and then we’re going to have periods of high tides each morning and evening and then on top of that we have high surf,” said Miguel Miller, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in San Diego. “We have all these things stacking up on each other and we’ve already seen in recent weeks how just the high tides, even without the large surf, is putting water into places where it doesn’t usually go.”
Forecasters are warning that south-facing beaches in Southern California could be particularly at risk of flooding on account of Tropical Storm Rachel this weekend.
A coastal flood advisory for Ventura, Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties — warning of the potential for flooding in beach parking lots, boardwalks and roads, with isolated road closures expected, along with minor coastal erosion — is expected to remain in effect through Tuesday afternoon.
Coastal cities including Laguna Beach, Newport Beach and Long Beach have already seen significant flooding. Long Beach issued a mandatory evacuation order for residents of Seaside Walk between 64th and 66th Place.
While tropical moisture from the remnants of Rachel is expected to deliver only light rain to much of Southern California between Sunday morning and Monday night, the Mojave Desert, the Inland Empire and portions of San Diego County could see more significant precipitation.
The weather service is warning that there is a moderate, or 40% chance, of excessive rainfall that could lead to flash flooding in places like San Diego, El Cajon, Chula Vista, Escondido, Palm Springs and Twentynine Palms. A moderate risk means that numerous flash floods are likely, and that many streams may flood. There is a chance that the San Diego River near Fashion Valley could reach minor flood stage.
There’s also a 15% chance of that occurring in Oceanside, San Clemente, Laguna Niguel, Riverside, San Bernardino, Las Vegas and the California-Arizona border; and a 5% chance in places like Huntington Beach, Santa Ana, Long Beach, Anaheim, Pomona, Victorville, Barstow, and most of Arizona and southern Utah.
Newport Beach was one of several coastal communities to see flooding Friday as residents braced for Tropical Storm Rachel, which is expected to cause more issues over the weekend.
In Los Angeles County, rain is expected to be light to moderate, ranging from about a quarter of an inch to an inch across much of the region. A bit more rain is expected in the San Gabriel Mountains, according to the weather service office in Oxnard. Rain rates are probably going to be a quarter of an inch per hour or less, making debris flow and landslides unlikely.
A bit more rain is expected in Orange County with coastal areas receiving from half an inch to an inch over the weekend and into early next week. Coastal sections of San Diego County could see between an inch and an inch and a half of precipitation with higher rain levels predicted farther inland.
Nora arrived during a “very strong” El Niño season. That pattern is linked to above-average hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific, and also is usually tied to above-average rainfall for Southern California in the winter.
That climate pattern sees the heating of ocean waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, which spur changes in the atmosphere that can affect weather around the world.
Strong surf across Southern California this weekend blasted through a seawall in Long Beach, caused a massive sinkhole at a celebrity’s Malibu home and damaged several Dana Point homes, among other issues.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center said  Thursday that there is virtually a 100% chance that the El Niño this season will be categorized as “very strong.” There’s also an 83% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest on record, which goes back to 1950, up from a 75% probability forecast last month.
“With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed,” the Climate Prediction Center said Thursday.
There have been only four “very strong” El Niños in the modern record — 1982-83, 1991-92, 1997-98 and 2015-16. Two of them — in 1982-83 and 1997-98 — deluged downtown Los Angeles with more than 30 inches of rain, more than double the area’s average annual rainfall.

articles.title_orig: China, EU talks show scope for cooperation despite disputes: expert
articles.title_zh: China, EU talks show scope for cooperation despite disputes: expert
articles.content_orig:
Our Privacy Statement & Cookie Policy
By continuing to browse our site you agree to our use of cookies, revised Privacy Policy and Terms of Use. You can change your cookie settings through your browser.
China and the European Union have the potential to deepen economic and trade cooperation by addressing their differences through negotiations and providing businesses with a more stable and predictable environment, a Chinese trade expert told CGTN on Saturday, following the two sides' latest trade talks in Beijing.
The remarks followed the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, co-chaired by Chinese Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic in Beijing from Thursday to Friday. A joint statement released on Friday said the two sides had agreed to maintain stable bilateral economic and trade ties and make them more balanced.
"The statement has made it very clear that both sides agree that we are going to negotiate in a better way," said Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.
China and the EU have complementary advantages in markets, innovation and businesses, Zhou said, adding that the two sides could better address uncertainties and restrictions through dialogue.
He said policy stability and predictability were crucial to encouraging businesses to invest and expand cooperation. "When enterprises are going to make investments, they have to understand that the situation will be stable."
Supply chains and industrial chains are built on collaboration and trust, Zhou said, adding that businesses would be more willing to strengthen ties if they believed cooperation would bring them further opportunities.
The joint statement outlined 16 areas of consensus, covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform. The two sides also agreed to continue exploring the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain goods within the framework of WTO rules and reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles.
Zhou said China and the EU could help restore confidence in global trade governance amid growing uncertainty and protectionism.
China and the EU are firm supporters of globalization, he said, calling for stronger support for the multilateral trading system, including through improvements to dispute settlement and efforts to address emerging issues such as e-commerce.
The two sides also identified potential cooperation in artificial intelligence, the digital economy and new energy. Zhou said turning that potential into concrete business and investment opportunities would depend partly on whether companies had confidence in policy stability and the prospects for cooperation.
China and the EU agreed to hold their next meeting under the trade and investment consultation mechanism in March 2027, with a ministerial video conference scheduled for January. Both sides also agreed to maintain close communication and promote the early implementation of the agreed outcomes.

articles.title_orig: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
articles.title_zh: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
articles.content_orig:
As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft , claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas.
The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers.
Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended.
The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad.
All eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45.
Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals.
The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

articles.title_orig: One year on, Gaza ceasefire exists ‘in name only,’ aid groups say amid near-daily Israeli strikes
articles.title_zh: One year on, Gaza ceasefire exists ‘in name only,’ aid groups say amid near-daily Israeli strikes
articles.content_orig:
A Palestinian mother mourns her son, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike just over a month into the ceasefire, at Al-Shifa Hospital, in Gaza City, on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.
GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.
Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.
That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.
NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.
Palestinians returned to the ruins of Gaza City after Israeli forces withdrew and ended their ground operation on the first day of the ceasefire, on Oct. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
In Khan Younis, families greet Palestinian prisoners who were freed in exchange for Israeli hostages on Oct. 13, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
At Al-Shifa Hospital on Oct. 23, 2025, Joud Al-Angar, 12, and his younger cousin are covered in dime-sized scabs after they were wounded by a piece of shrapnel from an Israeli munition. They found it in the rubble and thought it was coal they could use to help their family cook dinner. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The bodies of multiple people, including children, are covered in shrouds at a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital on Nov. 20, 2025, after Israeli airstrikes targeted homes and tents. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
People inspect the aftermath of a deadly Israeli airstrike that destroyed a home in Gaza City six weeks into the ceasefire on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A father and his son wade through flooded streets in Gaza City after picking up humanitarian aid on Nov. 25, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children wear virtual reality headsets as part of a TechMed Gaza initiative that aims to help provide children with psychosocial support for trauma, in Al-Zuweida, Gaza, on Dec. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Saqer Al-Ankah holds his dying 10-year-old granddaughter, Bayan, in his arms at Baptist Hospital in Gaza City on Dec. 10, 2025, after she was shot in her tent by Israeli troops who occupy northeast Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Makeshift tents like these in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025, offer little protection from the winter cold, but the U.N. says roughly 1.5 million people have only these for shelter after Israeli airstrikes destroyed nearly all the buildings in the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Raed el-Ghazawi and his children stand in a tent in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025. The family of five says the tent is freezing cold and damp from winter rainstorms. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
On Dec. 17, 2025, Palestinian Christian children decorate a Christmas tree inside the Holy Family Church in Gaza City for the first time since the beginning of the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Fresh produce returns to Gaza City's streets on Dec. 23, 2025, after U.N.-backed experts declared a famine there amid Israeli restrictions on aid during the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Patients sit in a clinic run by Doctors Without Borders in Gaza City on Dec. 31, 2025, a day before Israel banned more than 40 international aid organizations from bringing in staff or aid to Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian female artists gather at the beach in Gaza City for the first time since the war began to paint as a form of therapy, on Feb. 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian rescue workers begin the work of retrieving corpses from under the rubble of homes bombed by Israel during the war in Beit Lahia, Gaza, on Feb. 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The skeleton of Shawqi Abu Naser, 60, is retrieved from under the rubble on Feb. 16, 2026, more than a year after an Israeli airstrike killed 132 people from the same family in Beit Lahia. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A mother from the Abu Nasr family sits by her son's body in Beit Lahia on Feb. 17, 2026. The body was retrieved from under the rubble more than a year after 132 people were killed in a single Israeli airstrike on the family home. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians gather in an open space in Gaza City for early morning prayers that mark the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child smiles next to a man dressed as a clown on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, celebrations that mark the end of Ramadan fasting, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian boy shakes hands with Hamas militants on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, following the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians stand next to boxes of U.N. food aid in an area that aid groups need Israeli permission to enter in Jabalia, Gaza, on April 18, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A yellow block placed by Israeli forces marks the expanding territory controlled by the military in Bureij, Gaza, on May 7, 2026. Palestinians are barred from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Young Palestinian chess players gather at a coffee shop in Gaza City for the first tournament since the start of the war, on May 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child carries jugs of water as he passes by a mural of Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal that is painted on the rubble of a home destroyed by Israeli airstrikes, in Al-Shati refugee camp, Gaza, on May 14, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A building burns after an Israeli airstrike killed Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the leader of the military wing of Hamas, his wife, his daughter and a neighbor in Gaza City on May 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children jump on a trampoline during the Eid holidays on May 31, 2026, in Beit Lahia, which the Israeli military had deemed an "orange zone." Aid organizations are restricted from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child looks into a burned car that was targeted in an Israeli airstrike on a busy street in Gaza City on June 22, 2026. A teenage girl who was going to find internet access to take her final exams was killed in the strike. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A plume of smoke rises after an Israeli airstrike targeted a home in Gaza City nine months into the ceasefire on July 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Thousands of displaced Palestinians gather under Egyptian flags amid the rubble in Gaza City for a public screening of Egypt's match against Argentina in the World Cup on July 7, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
One-hundred corpses are wrapped in Palestinian flags in Gaza City on Aug. 4, 2026, after being retrieved from under the rubble of a building that was hit in an Israeli airstrike in October 2023. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child whose brother was killed in an Israeli airstrike cries at the door of a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Aug. 19, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian children form a chain for a global solidarity initiative called Swim With Gaza that raises money for swimming lessons in Khan Younis on Aug. 25, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

articles.title_orig: Palestinian Authority president postpones legislative elections another year, marking 20 years without a vote
articles.title_zh: Palestinian Authority president postpones legislative elections another year, marking 20 years without a vote
articles.content_orig:
President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas' party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas' presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas' Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority's control are both regularly reported.
Though the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.
Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.
"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

articles.title_orig: AI euphoria faces concern as bubble warnings intensify (OPENAI:Private)
articles.title_zh: AI euphoria faces concern as bubble warnings intensify (OPENAI:Private)
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It's not easy being a billionaire in the event that a stock market bubble bursts.
Just ask billionaire Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who sounds like he's worrying about potentially massive wealth destruction if the artificial intelligence trade goes south.
"Everybody says 'I'm worth a billion dollars' but, OK, try to spend that," Dalio said at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Wednesday. Bloomberg first reported his comments.
Dalio suggested that measures that force the ultrawealthy to liquidate their unrealized gains, such as a wealth tax, could hasten or contribute to a bubble popping.
"In order to spend that, you have to sell wealth in order to get money — and so the bubble usually pricks at that," he added.
Read more: How billionaires get away with paying less income tax
Dalio warned that AI speculation may be nearing its peak. "We're in the part of the cycle that is before that but approaching that," Dalio said on the bubble topic. "I think we're close to that."
To his point, the stock market is pretty much being kept afloat by three tech stocks , which is fueling fresh fears of an AI stock bubble bursting.
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has never been more concentrated in just three stocks than it is today, with Nvidia ( NVDA ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Microsoft ( MSFT ) representing over 21% of the index, per data from Creative Planning.
The importance of these three stocks to the S&P 500 has never been greater.
Only IBM ( IBM ), AT&T ( T ), and ExxonMobil ( XOM ) could hold a candle to the three tech stalwarts of today: In the mid-1980s, those three industrial giants at their peak made up 13.4% of the S&P 500.
We hope Dalio has his finances in order, should that bubble burst.

Apple reportedly plans to unveil an all-new smart home hub as part of the "Welcome home" product launch it announced for Tuesday, October 13.
Our image above is just a rough concept based on rumored design details, so be prepared for the device's actual appearance to be different.
The device will likely be unveiled in a press release shared on the Apple Newsroom website at around 9 a.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, as that is when Apple's private "Welcome home" experience in New York begins. At the experience, invited reporters and content creators will likely receive hands-on time with the home hub.
The hub is said to be designed for managing smart home accessories in the Apple Home app, home security monitoring, digital photo galleries, calendar appointments, music playback, FaceTime video calls, and more. As a user approaches the hub, or moves away from it, the size of the interface elements will reportedly adjust.
The device will be ideal for the kitchen, bedroom, and living room, and it will reportedly have multi-user support for families.
The hub reportedly has a 6-inch square display, and an A18 chip or newer for Apple Intelligence, with Siri AI expected to be a tentpole feature. A new operating system — potentially named "homeOS" — will feature clock faces, widgets, and more. There will be a tabletop version of the hub with a speaker base, plus a wall-mounted version.
Some of the preinstalled Apple apps that will apparently be available on the new platform include Calendar, Camera, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Apple News, Reminders, Notes, and the new Siri app with Siri AI conversation history. Do not expect third-party apps at launch, though, as the device reportedly lacks an App Store.
The device is often referred to as a "HomePad" in rumors because of expectations that it will be sort of a HomePod-iPad hybrid, but perhaps Apple will opt for a straightforward "Apple Home" name, or perhaps it will go with " HomeView " based on trademark filings that are potentially linked to the company. We will soon find out.

articles.title_orig: Flu season is already here. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu shots.
articles.title_zh: Flu season is already here. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu shots.
articles.content_orig:
Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?
Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.
The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.
"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.
"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."
Doctors say flu season is ahead of schedule this year as cases pop up across Ontario
1 dead, more than 400 confirmed flu cases ahead of vaccine availability in Alberta
But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.
Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.
According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.
Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.
It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.
But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.
"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.
B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign
He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.
"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."
Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.
In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.
You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year
"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.
"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."
Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.
The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.
This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.
Nova Scotia opens COVID-19, flu vaccine bookings ahead of respiratory illness season
Flu and COVID-19 vaccinations underway in B.C. as respiratory illness season arrives early
Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school
He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.
It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.
About 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)
Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 4.1 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.5 per cent at the same time in 2025.
The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.
Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.
New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.
Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.
In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26 .
In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20 . It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.
Updated COVID-19, flu vaccines available in N.B. on Oct. 13
Alberta now providing free RSV antibodies to newborns after calls from pediatricians to expand access
Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta , with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.
In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.

Customers are slowly getting power back as the total number of power outages across the US has trended down after hitting a peak of more than 850,000 earlier in the day. As of Saturday evening, it is hovering at about 630,000, according to poweroutage.com .

articles.title_zh: WWE Money in the Bank 2026 preview: LA Knight will never be world champion in WWE
articles.content_orig:
The megastar hasn’t won a singles match on Raw since June, so the idea that he can beat Roman Reigns is laughable.
WWE Money in the Bank 2026 takes place tonight (Sat., Oct. 10) from Smoothie King Center in New Orleans, Louisiana.
The show begins at 4 pm ET with the free Countdown show , leading right into the main course at 6 pm ET streaming HERE on ESPN Unlimited in the U.S., and on Netflix pretty much everywhere else.
World Heavyweight Champion Roman Reigns defends the gold tonight against LA Knight, and it’s actually the opening match of the night. Knight’s alliance with Solo Sikoa and their six-man tag team win over The Bloodline at SummerSlam has put the megastar in position to challenge Reigns on this PLE. It’s worth noting that LA hasn’t won a singles match on WWE programming since June, so WWE hasn’t gone out of its way to build him up as a major threat to Reigns.
In the promos leading up to tonight’s match, Knight keeps bringing up his last world title shot against Reigns from three years ago, where the Tribal Chief needed help from The Bloodline to retain the belt. Roman now wins matches on his own in 2026, and a clean fight is exactly what the megastar says he wants. He may not get it, though, because his other SummerSlam partner, Royce Keys, has gone on to create his own “946” heel faction that is causing all kinds of chaos for The Bloodline and Sikoa.
LA has admitted in interviews that this may be his last chance to win a world title in WWE. If that’s the case then he’s probably screwed, because it’s hard to see Roman dropping this belt to anybody other than Oba Femi. Even home country hero Penta couldn’t beat Reigns for the gold last month in Mexico City. It doesn’t help Knight’s chances that this match is now the opener. I have a very hard time time seeing a Roman Reigns title loss happening anywhere else besides the main event.
LA’s best hope to win the belt involves 946 interfering to attack the OTC without causing a disqualification, but it doesn’t seem like they’ll get a clean shot at Roman given that Sikoa and The Usos are standing in their way.
Will LA Knight back up his tough talk about being the most self-made man in WWE by finally winning a world title, or will he fall flat on his face when the Tribal Chief beats him clean this time? Tune into Money in the Bank to find out.
Here are the four other matches that are currently advertised for Money in the Bank:
Penta vs. Je’Von Evans vs. Trick Williams vs. Kevin Owens vs. CM Punk vs. Bron Breakker in the men’s Money in the Bank ladder match
A high risk spot fest with ladders is meant for younger bodies to endure, and there is plenty of new blood to be found with Je’Von, Trick, and Bron all looking to cement themselves as top stars in WWE. Penta is older but may be the hottest star of them all coming off his world title match against Roman Reigns in Mexico City. Then there is Owens and old man Punk, whose feud has helped Sami Zayn win the WWE championship and survive longer than nine days with the title this time. If Owens and Punk continue to cancel each other out in this match, Penta and Breakker stand out as being more likely to win than Evans and Williams.
Lola Vice vs. Sol Ruca vs. Tiffany Stratton vs. Lash Legend vs. Jacy Jayne vs. Roxanne Perez in the women’s Money in the Bank ladder match
The youth movement is even more apparent in the women’s Money in the Bank ladder match, where former winner Stratton is joined by five wrestlers who have never won a world title in WWE. That’s mostly because Jayne, Ruca, and Vice just joined the main roster in 2026, Legend’s call up happened less than one year ago, and Perez is closer to 1.5 years. Lash is the one who was standing tall over everyone else on last night’s go home show, so Reverse Momentum Theory might be working against her tonight. Perez is generally regarded as a favorite, which could create tension with her stablemate Liv Morgan, while WWE Women’s Champion Chelsea Green is hoping that her friend Stratton finds a way to win the MITB contract again.
Stephanie Vaquer (c) vs. Becky Lynch vs. Liv Morgan for the Women’s world championship
Becky Lynch and Stephanie Vaquer both returned to WWE to confront Women’s World Champion Liv Morgan on the August 3 episode of Raw. A rare house show title change happened when Vaquer beat Morgan for the belt in her home country of Chile, thanks to a major assist from special referee Lynch. Becky and Liv fought on Raw to see who gets this title match, and it had a very bad DQ finish where the babyface champ attacked them both to set up this 3-way title match. Vaquer looks like a dumbass, because now The Judgment Day can legally interfere and give Morgan the numbers game advantage to win back her belt.
Bronson Reed returned to WWE last month at Sunday Night’s Main Event to ruin Femi’s match against Bron Breakker and take out The Ruler with several Tsunami splashes. There was some drama added to the mix during The Vision’s next beatdown on Femi on Raw when Reed put his foot on Oba’s body. Femi quickly shoved Reed’s foot off in what looked like an unscripted moment. This is Oba’s chance to get revenge on Reed and step on him after the match is over. But how will Paul Heyman factor into the finish, if at all?
What will you be looking for at Money in the Bank? Let me know your thoughts on the card in the comments below, Cagesiders.

articles.title_orig: Tree rips through roof of Crestview family home during Hurricane Isaias
articles.title_zh: Tree rips through roof of Crestview family home during Hurricane Isaias
articles.content_orig:
CRESTVIEW, Fla. -- For one Crestview family, Hurricane Isaias hit harder than expected.
For Ashley Weeks and her family, the devastation is personal. A tree from their backyard split on top of their house, gutting their roof and bringing stormwater inside.
The owner says they are from the area, but have only lived in this home for two years. Destruction from Hurricane Isaias stretched more than 30 miles inland from the coast.
"Just scary, everything, my whole life is in the house," Weeks said. "We heard a loud like something, like a bomb went off in the house. It was so loud. And I got up and went and seen the tree through the roof and it was freaking out."
The tree landed on the roof near her daughter's bedroom. What was once their ceiling is now just piles of wet debris in their living room and kitchen.
Weeks  says she, Brian Johnson, her daughter, their four dogs, and a reptile were all inside the house at the time of the crash. Everyone made it out alive.
"I don't think anybody else would be good who experiences something like this," said Johnson. "But you never think it's gonna happen to you until it does."
Weeks says her family has called this house their home for the last two years. There's certain memories in the home she wanted to preserve.
"My daughter's father passed away a few years ago," Weeks said. "Her necklace with his ashes was in that house, and she was upset we came back at that like our pictures stuff that matters the most to us.
Outside the home, a second tree  collapsed in their front yard. The family is still processing the devastation, but are forced to think about next steps.
Weeks says the family spent the night at her fathers house. Her next steps are to figure out how to restore her home.

articles.title_orig: India cracks down on ‘Cockroach’ youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
articles.title_zh: India cracks down on ‘Cockroach’ youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
articles.content_orig:
NEW DELHI — Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth “Cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Police moved to break up the demonstration before it could begin, intercepting demonstrators on their way to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India’s capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several “Cockroach” movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.
The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators. Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.
Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.
Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Modi’s party, dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements.”
“Their flop show has been completely demolished,” Patra said.
The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the “Cockroach” movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi’s education minister to resign in July.
Leaders of the “Cockroach” movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the “Cockroach Janta Party” on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
“The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today’s peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site,” the movement said in a statement.
Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.
“We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn’t we fight for our rights,” said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. “Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?”
The police response marked an extraordinary show of force in a capital where Modi’s government has repeatedly sought to contain public dissent in the past. Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world’s largest democracy.
The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
“Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out,” opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press. Brittas was later detained by police.
The protests center on India’s Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Saturday’s planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.
Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi’s party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
For the “Cockroach” movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.
The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations , sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.
For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi’s home state, will test the party’s standing.

articles.title_orig: IsDB Group Chairman leads delegation at the 2026 World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok
articles.title_zh: IsDB Group Chairman leads delegation at the 2026 World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok
articles.content_orig:
Jeddah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, 10 October 2026 - H.E. Dr. Muhammad Al Jasser, Chairman of the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) Group, will lead a high-level delegation to the 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group (WBG) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), taking place in Bangkok, Thailand, from 12 to 19 October 2026.
Amidst a complex global economic landscape, Dr. Al Jasser will engage in strategic dialogues with finance ministers, leaders of multilateral development banks, and key international partners. The discussions will primarily focus on economic stability, trade resilience, scaling development finance, and deepening regional cooperation.
Dr. Al Jasser will hold a bilateral meeting with H.E. Mr. Ekniti Nitithanprapas, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance of Thailand, the host country.
On Wednesday, 14 October, he will feature as a panelist for the session, “Trade Diversification in Turbulent Times: Implications for Economic Stability and Growth.” The discussion will address how shifting global trade dynamics impact economic resilience, focusing on strategies for trade diversification and economic transformation in emerging markets and developing economies, particularly IsDB member countries.
Dr. Al Jasser will also deliver a keynote address at the high-level forum, “Islamic Finance: From Crisis Resilience to Transition Finance,” highlighting the sector’s vital role in contemporary economic transitions.
Additionally, Dr. Al Jasser will participate in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan (MENAP) Ministers and Governors Meeting with the IMF Managing Director, as well as the Arab Governors Meeting with the WBG President.
On the sidelines of the Annual Meetings, Dr. Al Jasser will conduct bilateral meetings with IsDB Governors and senior representatives from leading international development institutions. Expected meetings include leadership from the WBG, the IMF, the French Development Agency (AFD), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD).
These engagements provide a critical platform for exchanging insights on shared priorities and building stronger global partnerships to drive sustainable economic development across IsDB member countries. For media inquiries, please contact: media@isdb.org

articles.title_orig: Woman survives pancreatic cancer after routine heart scan catches early sign: "I feel so lucky"
articles.title_zh: Woman survives pancreatic cancer after routine heart scan catches early sign: "I feel so lucky"
articles.content_orig:
Bookstore owner Vicky Titcomb had no reason to suspect anything was out of the ordinary when she went to Mass General Brigham for a heart scan in March 2025.
The 72-year-old Cape Cod bookstore owner and great-grandmother felt healthy. The scan was just a routine errand she had to run before traveling to New York City to visit her son. After the test was complete, Titcomb drove to New York. She didn't think about the scan again until she received a call from her internist on the last day of her visit.
The doctor had alarming news: There was an abnormality on her pancreas. Further testing would be necessary, but she likely had pancreatic cancer , one of the deadliest types of cancer.
"I felt like my life just switched in that moment," Titcomb said. "It was a very weird feeling."
But it wasn't Titcomb's first experience with a scary diagnosis. She had been treated for breast cancer in 2012. Then, she had worried. This time, she decided to stay positive. When tests confirmed she had pancreatic cancer , she made the choice not to research the often-deadly diagnosis.
"I saw some terrible, terrible information about it," Titcomb said. "I shut it out pretty much completely, because it was too much to take in."
Pancreatic cancer is one of the most deadly forms of the disease, because it is often diagnosed after it has already spread to other organs. The 5-year overall survival rate for the disease is 13%. In its 2026 Cancer Progress Report , the American Association for Cancer Research noted that even as most cancer survival rates climb, pancreatic cancer statistics have seen little improvement despite advances in treatment .
In addition to the pancreatic cancer, Titcomb also had stage 1 breast cancer that needed treatment, and a mass on her ovary. The ovarian mass was handled first: Titcomb had the organ removed, and a test showed the mass was benign.
That left just the breast and pancreatic cancers. Cancer specialists at Mass General Brigham developed a plan to treat as much of Titcomb's disease as possible. It would start with chemotherapy and radiation to shrink the tumors.
"I was told the size of the (pancreatic) cancer was about the size of a grape. The goal, to me, was trying to make this cancer a raisin," Titcomb said. "That's the way I visualized it."
If all went well, Titcomb would undergo a procedure known as a Whipple, during which surgeons remove the head of the pancreas, the first part of the small intestine, the gallbladder, and the bile duct, then rejoin the organs to allow the digestive system to function. The operation is complex, but Titcomb was glad to be eligible for it: Only about 1 in 5 pancreatic cancer patients have disease that can be treated with a Whipple. Titcomb's early diagnosis had made it an option for her.
"If I had not had that scan when I did, the outcome would have been bad," Titcomb said.
Titcomb began chemotherapy in June, receiving eight doses over four months. That was followed by three weeks of radiation and more rounds of chemotherapy. Surgical oncologist Dr. Thomas Clancy, who oversaw Titcomb's care, said she tolerated the treatments "very well." The chemotherapy and radiation successfully shrank the cancer, he said, allowing him to schedule her for a Whipple.
On Nov. 4, Titcomb underwent a procedure to treat her breast cancer. Just over two weeks later, Clancy performed the robotic Whipple. The operation is difficult on a patient, Clancy said, though the robotic approach allows for smaller incisions and a faster recovery time. But Titcomb felt confident, because it was scheduled for World Pancreatic Cancer Day.
"I was sure that Dr. Clancy chose me for that day because he felt positive about the outcome, because you don't want somebody to do badly on World Pancreatic Cancer Day," Titcomb joked.
It turned out the scheduling was only a coincidence. Still, the surgery was a success. Titcomb said she was up and walking that night.
After several days in the hospital recovering, Titcomb went home. Two weeks later, she returned for a follow-up appointment. Clancy confirmed she was healing well. But because pancreatic cancer is so aggressive, Clancy recommended she receive two more months of chemotherapy.
"There was a lot going on," Titcomb said. "I just tried to cope with the day-to-day."
After several more rounds of treatment, Clancy was able to tell Titcomb in March 2026 that she had no evidence of cancer. She will continue to receive scans every three months, but his hope is for her to "spend as little time as possible thinking about this."
"She's living her life. I generally tell patients at this point, 'You're done with therapy ... you go about your days,'" Clancy said. "The goal is to not be thinking about it all the time."
Titcomb said she has been trying to do exactly that. She is getting back into the routine of running her bookstore, which family members helped steer while she was in treatment. She spends time with her children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. The ones who are far away inundate her with photos, videos and phone calls.
Titcomb is also working to raise awareness for pancreatic cancer and advancements in treatment. She has spoken to legislators on behalf of the American Cancer Society and is working with the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network to share her own story and uplift others.
"I have benefited from enormous advancements in cancer treatment. People kept telling me that 10 years ago it would have been a different story," Titcomb said. "There are advances being made that people who've worked a lifetime on pancreatic cancer have never seen. I feel so lucky. The luck trumps all."
Edited by Lucia I Suarez Sang

articles.title_orig: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
articles.title_zh: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
articles.content_orig:
Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets.
As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs.
In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs . In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%.
Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make.
When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems.
"If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly."
Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns.
Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue.
"Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price."
Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power.
Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years.
"Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer."
Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand.
Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level.
"It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel.
He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026.
Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June.
For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices.
Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business.
"When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel.
BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.
"That is sourcing sales growth as well and sort of giving us the formula where we can cut SKUs, and see sales go up, and see margin dollars go up," Eddy said on the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August.
In June 2025, Dollar General said the elimination of 1,000 SKUs from the previous year opened up more shelf space for its best-selling products and added to its top line. By March 2026, the company said, it had reduced up to 1,500 SKUs, providing benefits to the overall supply chain.
"Being more productive there means getting product to the shelf faster and being there for the consumer with the right amount of items and products that she's looking for as quickly as we possibly can," Dollar General CEO Todd Vasos said in the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August. "As we go forward, the team is looking at continued SKU rationalization, albeit probably more surgical in nature."
Successfully slashing products from shelves is difficult in practice.
Box stores risk losing customers to competitors that offer the products they scrapped. BJ's, for instance, acknowledged that a previous attempt to cut SKUs was unsuccessful.
"We just cut SKUs which cut sales, and then we added some SKUs back and so really what we're doing now is removing unnecessary choice," Eddy said on the company's earnings call in August. "Think about in traditional soda, we don't carry cans and one-liters and two-liters of the same product anymore."
Meanwhile, publicly traded brands that acknowledge sales need to decline in order for the business to grow still have answers to investors in the near term.
"It's hard for a company ever to say we need to shrink anything, but it's dramatically harder to say we need to shrink revenues," said Siegel. "Frequently we find that brands hit a peak, a healthy peak, extend past the peak by forcing it and then find their way back down pretty harshly."

articles.title_orig: These households could spend more to heat their homes this winter, federal outlook says
articles.title_zh: These households could spend more to heat their homes this winter, federal outlook says
articles.content_orig:
(WFSB) - Connecticut’s next governor will have to address the rising cost of home heating oil this winter. About half a million homes in the state use oil.
Republican candidate Ryan Fazio says suspending several taxes is the answer. Democratic candidate Ned Lamont says there is a special fund he plans to withdraw from.
Heating oil is more than $5.50 per gallon across Connecticut. As homeowners begin to turn on the heat, there is concern that many will not be able to afford it by the end of winter.
Connecticut is one of the most reliant states on home heating oil. After November’s election, the state’s next governor will have to address the issue.
Fazio said if he were governor, he would immediately suspend three different taxes at least through the end of the calendar year.
“I’ve called on the Governor to suspend the gas tax, the diesel tax, and the home heating oil tax through the end of the year,” he said. “It can be funded through the existing balance in the transportation fund. We have the money to do it.”
Lamont has pushed back on this, citing transportation funding. He said he tried to do it earlier this year, and said Republicans pushed back on it.
He said the state has set aside $500 million in what he calls a “Trump relief fund,” designed to help offset inflation and other rising costs.
“I’ll be asking legislative leadership to use some of that fund to give people a little bit of relief because the price of home heating could go up 70% or 80% this year, thanks to the war in Iran,” he stated.
When asked about how much of the fund Lamont is willing to withdraw from, he told voters to be confident that the state is taking care of them.
“We’re putting together those numbers right now. We ought to have something by early next week. People have some confidence we’re taking care of them,” he added.
“I think it was probably the wrong decision,” he said when asked if he believes the war in Iran, spearheaded by the Trump administration, has been worth the higher gas prices in oil.

articles.title_orig: Ranked: The World’s Top 25 Cities in 2026
articles.title_zh: Ranked: The World’s Top 25 Cities in 2026
articles.content_orig:
The world’s leading cities attract businesses, investment, and talent from across the globe. But even the most successful cities face challenges, from housing affordability to environmental risks.
This visualization ranks the world’s top 25 cities in 2026, showing how they perform across five categories and where their biggest strengths and weaknesses lie.
The data comes from Oxford Economics’ Global Cities Index 2026 , which evaluates 1,000 cities across Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment, and Governance.
Economics accounts for 30% of the overall score, while Human Capital and Quality of Life each contribute 25%. Environment and Governance account for 10% apiece. Governance is assessed at the national level, meaning cities within the same country receive the same ranking.
New York remains the world’s highest-ranked city, supported by its enormous $2.6 trillion metropolitan economy in 2025, the largest of any city in the index. Its strengths span finance, technology, media, and corporate headquarters, helping it rank first in Economics and fifth in Human Capital.
London follows in second place and leads the Human Capital category, thanks to its concentration of universities and highly educated workers. Around 40% of London’s residents are foreign-born, reflecting its ability to attract international talent.
Paris rounds out the top three with a different mix of advantages. Alongside its trillion-dollar economy, the French capital ranks 10th globally for Quality of Life, supported by high life expectancy, relatively strong incomes, and access to cultural amenities, including roughly 130 museums.
Seattle ranks fourth overall, benefiting from its technology sector anchored by Microsoft and Amazon, alongside major aerospace and retail companies.
San Francisco and San Jose rank fifth and eighth, respectively, highlighting Silicon Valley’s outsized economic influence.
San Jose has the highest GDP per person of all 1,000 cities, at an estimated $238,700 in 2025, reflecting the extraordinary productivity of its technology industry.
Yet economic success doesn’t guarantee strong performance across every category. San Jose ranks third for Economics but 121st for Human Capital, while Boston places ninth for Economics but 289th for Environment, partly reflecting its exposure to flooding.
Oxford Economics also highlights high housing costs, income inequality, and economic concentration among the challenges facing major U.S. technology hubs.
Economic size isn’t everything. Dublin, ranked sixth overall, stands out for its Environmental performance, placing ninth globally thanks partly to low pollution and a temperate climate, although housing affordability remains a major challenge.
Other European cities excel in different areas. Oslo ranks sixth for Quality of Life and eighth for Governance, while Copenhagen holds the top spot in Governance despite ranking 18th overall.
Zurich also places in the global top 10, supported by productive financial services, strong educational institutions, and high living standards.
Tokyo offers another striking contrast. Asia’s highest-ranked city places ninth overall and third for Human Capital, reflecting its deep pool of skilled workers and major educational institutions.
However, the Japanese capital ranks just 454th for Environment, the lowest placement in this category among the global top 10. Its exposure to earthquakes, typhoons, and other natural hazards weighs on its environmental performance.
Looking ahead, the rankings could become more competitive. Oxford Economics notes that eight of the 2025 top 10 cities remain in the top 10 this year, but forecasts that rapidly growing Asian cities will gain economic influence as they expand into advanced manufacturing, technology, and business services.
If you enjoyed today’s post, check out The World’s Most Populous Cities Over Time (1975–2050) on Voronoi .

The best cities for quality of life in 2026, led by Canberra, with Europe claiming 23 of the top 30 spots.
What makes a city one of the best places in the world to live? High incomes, affordable housing, safety, and access to recreation all play a role.
This graphic ranks the world’s leading cities for quality of life using data from Oxford Economics’ 2026 Global Cities Index , which evaluates 1,000 cities worldwide. Its Quality of Life category measures income equality, income per person, housing expenditure, life expectancy, crime, and access to recreation and cultural sites.
Canberra earns a perfect index score of 100, making it the highest-ranked city for Quality of Life in 2026. Oxford Economics attributes its performance to a combination of high salaries and relatively low income inequality, supported by the Australian capital’s concentration of stable, well-paying government jobs.
Canberra also performs well on life expectancy and benefits from a high number of recreation and cultural sites relative to its population. Interestingly, Canberra ranks only 45th in the overall Global Cities Index , showing how a city can excel in quality of life without ranking among the world’s top cities overall.
By region, Europe dominates the ranking, led by Bergen, Grenoble, Bern, and Oslo.
Germany has an especially strong showing, with Dresden, Berlin, Munich, Stuttgart, and Freiburg im Breisgau all appearing in the top 21. Switzerland places three cities in the top 14: Bern, Basel, and Zurich. Italy also contributes three cities to the top 30, including Venice, Padua, and Genoa.
Outside Europe, the leading cities include Canberra and Sydney in Australia, Singapore, San Jose and Seattle in the United States, and Hsinchu and Taipei in Taiwan.
The United States dominates several measures of global city competitiveness, but its performance in quality of life tells a different story.
According to Oxford Economics, U.S. cities generally excel in Economics and Human Capital, while European cities tend to perform better in Quality of Life, Environment, and Governance.
New York, for example, ranks 1st overall but 86th for Quality of Life . Oxford Economics notes that high housing costs weigh on the city’s score, even as New York benefits from high incomes and strong access to recreation and cultural sites.
Some cities commonly associated with high livability fall outside the top 30, largely because of housing costs.
Copenhagen, for instance, ranks 18th overall but 160th for Quality of Life, with Oxford Economics pointing to limited and expensive housing as the main drag. The city performs much better in Governance, where it ranks first globally, as well as Environment and Economics.
Vancouver shows a similar gap, ranking 24th overall but 215th for Quality of Life. Exceptionally high housing expenditure weighs on its score despite its outdoor amenities and long life expectancy.

The U.S. accounts for 27 of the 40 cities with the highest GDP per person, led by major technology hubs.
GDP per person offers a different perspective on urban economic strength than the overall size of a city’s economy.
The metric measures how much economic output a city generates relative to its population, highlighting places with especially high levels of production per resident.
This visualization ranks the top 40 cities by GDP per person among those featured in the 2026 Global Cities Index published by Oxford Economics. Figures are shown in U.S. dollars and are calculated using each city’s 2025 GDP and population.
