articles.title_orig: From 'cockroach' post to protest leader: India's Dipke tests Modi government
articles.title_zh: From 'cockroach' post to protest leader: India's Dipke tests Modi government
articles.content_orig:
These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us.
Below, you can review news from India from Saturday, October 10:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
That's all for today! Thank you for joining us.
There will be a fresh new India blog on Sunday. See you then!
Videos released by opposition leaders show that several senior figures were detained in New Delhi on Saturday.
They include Arvind Kejriwal, leader of the Aam Aadmi Party and former chief minister of Delhi .
"It's official... we are living under an absolute dictatorship," Kejriwal wrote on X.
Mamata Banerjee, who lost power as West Bengal's chief minister earlier this year, was also detained.
Pinarayi Vijayan, a communist leader who headed the southern state of Kerala until May, was among those detained.
Rahul Gandhi, leader of India's opposition Congress party , called the crackdown an act of "cowardice" and described Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah, right-wing, Hindu nationalist RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and National Security Adviser Ajit Doval as "the villains of this story" who were "slowly finding the space closing around them. We are closing that space."
Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Rahul Gandhi's sister and a Congress MP, wrote in a social media post: "India is not a democracy anymore. It is a dictatorship being run by Mr. Narendra Modi and Mr. Amit Shah."
Opposition parties and critics have warned that the electoral-roll revision exercise could strip millions of people of their voting rights and give an advantage to Prime Minister Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The Election Commission of India has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, saying the "special intensive revision" aims to remove duplicate and ineligible voters.
The protests echo the CJP's mass mobilization in July, which forced the then education minister to resign over an examination scandal.
This time, demonstrators are demanding the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.
Tens of thousands of security personnel have been deployed and roads barricaded across New Delhi to prevent the latest Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demonstration.
Police have detained thousands of protesters in a major crackdown. Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital.
Some protesters who turned back from Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site, have been waiting in different parts of central Delhi, determined to hold their ground.
The CJP has urged people who believe they or someone they know has been unlawfully detained to fill out an online form as soon as possible, saying it is collecting information to support affected volunteers and other individuals.
The protest targeted Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over voter list revisions that critics say favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
If you're joining us now, here's a helpful reminder about why India's youth are rising up this time.
DW Hindi's Adarsh Sharma, who is on the ground in New Delhi, spoke to protesters as they faced a security crackdown.
He caught up with one protester who managed to avoid detention.
"We were running back and forth. When the police are moving forward, we go back. When they are withdrawing, we are moving forward," the protester told DW.
The protester described the heavy police presence as a "game of perception."
"Where you have 20 protesters and 10 media persons, there are 100 police personnel standing. It seems like a joke, what they are doing with taxpayers' money," the protester said.
Another protester, Jasmine, described how the morning unfolded for the demonstrators.
"We have been playing a game of cat and mouse with the police, trying to stop them from picking us up," she said.
"I don't think we have ever seen something like this happening. Protesting is a fundamental right… it's such a convoluted idea to take permission to protest… you are protesting against a government, will you ask permission from the same government? They are not going to give it," she said.
Ajinkya Shinde, who was handed the responsibility of leading the Cockroach Janta Party's protest following the detentions of its main leaders, has made his first statement — calling for a continued march to Jantar Mantar.
"We appeal to everyone to march towards Jantar Mantar! If Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar," he said in a video post made by the CJP on X.
Indian media outlets, including Scroll and Newslaundry, reported that their journalists had been detained by police while covering the 'Cockroach' party protest. The journalists were later released.
Newslaundry reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports said journalists were physically assaulted.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an independent nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom and defends journalists' rights worldwide, has called on Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers.
It has also urged police to return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in New Delhi and the police response without interference.
In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), India ranked 157th out of 180 countries, down six places from 2025. Press freedom groups have raised concerns about the use of criminal laws against journalists and the impact of such measures on independent journalism.
Detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother is reported to have died on Saturday.
Indian media reports said that Dipke's paternal grandmother had been suffering from a prolonged illness and had been unwell in recent days. She died in her native village in Maharashtra, reports said.
News agency ANI, citing police sources, reported that the Delhi Police had informed Dipke of his grandmother's death. It was now up to the CJP leader to decide whether to continue his protest while under detention or travel back for the funeral rites.
Dipke was detained aboard his plane after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday morning, ahead of the protest. He was traveling from Mumbai.
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has indicated that it will press on with its protest despite its leaders and supporters being detained.
CJP's National Organization In-Charge Ajinkya Shinde will lead the protest at Jantar Mantar until Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remain in detention, the group said in a statement on X.
The CJP also shared a video of Dipke purportedly recorded on Friday night, anticipating a potential detention.
"If you are seeing this video, it means Ashutosh, Saurav and I have been arrested," Dipke says in the video.
"After us, Ajinkya will lead this movement," he says.
In a separate post, the CJP alleged that its three detained leaders had been taken to an undisclosed location, were being denied access to lawyers and had been cut off from "all contact with others."
The formal association of advocates at India's apex court called for urgent intervention by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant after several lawyers were detained by Delhi police.
This comes amid a reported crackdown on protesters attempting to reach the national capital, specifically central Delhi, to protest against India's chief election commissioner over alleged misconduct.

Eric Deters says US ambassador to Greece asked him to pay off American Express credit card bill in return for access
A Trump donor accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece and Trump family ally, of engaging in a “quid pro quo” by asking him to pay off her $100,000 debt in exchange for access to administration officials.
Eric Deters, a former congressional candidate and lawyer, told MS Now on Thursday that Guilfoyle had “ambushed” him last year with an offer to provide access to government officials if he paid her American Express credit card bill, before her US Senate confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece.
“It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” Deters told the network in response to a Wall Street Journal report that she had pushed him for the money.
“Kimberly Guilfoyle is a grifter,” he added.
The Guardian has asked Guilfoyle’s lawyer for comment.
Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages, but that she was “owed a balance” for travel and speaking at events before her nomination. Deters told the Journal that he did not owe Guilfoyle any balance.
The report is the latest allegation about Guilfoyle’s conduct as a US official. Deters shared messages he and Guilfoyle exchanged in which the US ambassador to Greece promised him “ride or die” access to Trump administration officials if he wired American Express $100,000.
Asked about the report during a press conference in Athens on Wednesday, Marco Rubio , the US secretary of state, said he would not address the allegations. He reaffirmed his support for the US embassy in Greece adding, “ Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” Asked again about the reports on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment.
The top Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees have asked Rubio to open an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct as an ambassador.
A spokesperson for the Democratic staff of the Senate foreign relations committee confirmed to the Guardian that they were requesting further information and continuing to investigate.
JD Vance similarly expressed hesitation, similar to Rubio, on Thursday when asked to respond to a US ambassador offering access to government officials in exchange for money to pay off debts.
“With that hypothetical, Jen, obviously I don’t love that,” the vice-president replied. “But I don’t know exactly who you’re talking about. I don’t know the full details. What I find with these stories is you never want to comment in a purely abstract way because a lot of times the details really matter,” he added.
Concerns about Guilfoyle’s conduct were first raised in September when the Wall Street Journal reported she had used her position to invite Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee, sent a letter to Rubio on Tuesday , asking him to look into the allegations against Guilfoyle.
“Such actions do not serve US credibility overseas and risk undermining US diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote. “In advance of your upcoming travel to Greece , I request an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.”
Separately, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, sent a letter to Rubio in September, requesting more information about Guilfoyle’s conduct, her relationship with the Greek construction and energy company and her relationship with the lobbyist.
“If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Meeks wrote.
Guilfoyle, 57, was once a member of the Trump family’s inner circle, having been engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest son, for roughly three years. The couple ended their engagement in 2024, and shortly after taking office, Donald Trump nominated Guilfoyle to be ambassador to Greece.
But now further allegations accuse Guilfoyle of promising a Trump donor, Eric Deters, access to the Trump administration in exchange for a $100,000 payment to American Express.
Deters shared messages exchanged between himself and Guilfoyle with the Wall Street Journal in which she reportedly pleaded: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”
Deters said Guilfoyle had promised him thatshe would “be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever” if he made the American Express balance. Deters said he never made the payment.
In other messages, Guilfoyle reportedly raised concerns about her communications with Deters becoming public and reprimanded him for not being discreet. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal,” she is said to have written in one message.
“What a nightmare, you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” Guilfoyle reportedly wrote in another message.
A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of messages Deters shared with the Wall Street Journal.
It is unclear whether Shaheen or Meeks will ask Rubio for further information about the latest report. The Guardian has asked Meeks and Shaheen for comment.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Syracuse stop showed us who we are right now: motivated and divided
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Syracuse stop showed us who we are right now: motivated and divided
articles.content_orig:
Get the best experience and stay connected to your community with our Spectrum News app. Learn More
President Donald Trump made a stop in Syracuse to rally in support of gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman.
Critics, however, held an event of their own.
Thousands filled Syracuse’s Clinton Square Friday evening, just blocks from where President Trump was set to make remarks. Their message for the president: Not in our house, Central New York resists.
“What Donald J. Trump stands for is not what we stand for, it’s not what real citizens of Syracuse and Central New York stand for,” said Judy Jerome, an organizer with the CNY Solidarity Coalition and Indivisible Onondaga County.
Protesters wanted to express their concern over the president and his administration’s policies.
“The president is not a friend of the environment, definitely not a friend in good immigration,” Jerome said.
David Clark is a proud veteran of the United States Army, but he says he would never serve under the current commander in chief.
“I would never ever volunteer to go into any military action with Trump as president and fight for corruption," Clark said. "I just wouldn’t do it."
And Dustin Eads with CNY Pride says the president’s policies have been impacting his community.
“Individuals within my community are passing away or they’re being attacked, they’re being mistreated and their rights are getting taken away on a daily occurrence,” Eads said.
Jerome, who helped organize the protest, says having so many come together to make their disapproval and disappointment known is an important part of their resistance.
“That means everything,” Jerome said. “I mean that means that we come together, that we are all part of resisting the corruption of this particular administration.”
After rallying at Clinton Square, protesters marched to the Oncenter.
Jerome says it doesn’t stop with the protest; organizers are also encouraging protesters to make their voice heard in a way that counts: to get out and vote.

articles.title_orig: The staggering numbers are in on the USS Abraham Lincoln's 321-day deployment: 93,000 nautical miles
articles.title_zh: The staggering numbers are in on the USS Abraham Lincoln's 321-day deployment: 93,000 nautical miles
articles.content_orig:
The US Navy aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned home this week after a long and difficult combat deployment. The numbers shared by the sea service for that deployment are staggering.
The warship left its homeport in San Diego in November 2025 and was deployed for 321 days, which included 286 consecutive days at sea without a port call. The lengthy deployment, extended by Operation Epic Fury that kicked off the Iran war, set a modern-day record .
As hostilities began at the end of February, the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group played a central role in the fight.
The carrier strike group's embarked Carrier Air Wing 9 — a naval aviation force consisting of nine squadrons of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, F-35C Lightning II Joint Strike Fighters, and EA-18G Growler electronic attack aircraft, among other assets— flew nearly 4,000 combat flights during the 40-day operation.
During the monthslong deployment, it flew 14,037 aircraft sorties and accumulated 31,460 forward-deployed flight hours. An estimated 20.5 million gallons of aviation fuel enabled the air wing's operations, the Navy said.
During Operation Epic Fury, the carrier air wing's mix of fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft launched 1,499 precision munitions, dropping over 1.37 million pounds of ordnance on priority targets such as missile sites, defense production facilities, military infrastructure, and Iranian naval capabilities. Air assets also shielded the strike group from enemy action.
The Navy said that the air wing, with its combination of stealth fighter jets and workhorse aircraft, effectively penetrated contested airspace and demonstrated the "Air Wing of the Future" concept in a real-world combat scenario.
Following the April ceasefire and the conclusion of Epic Fury, Carrier Strike Group 3 supported the Navy's blockade. When Iran began targeting commercial shipping, the group participated in strikes on Iranian coastal defenses and missile sites. It supported a second blockade before finally heading home. Over the course of its deployment, the Lincoln sailed over 93,000 nautical miles, supported by 72 at-sea replenishments.
For its actions during the deployment, the strike group received the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the military's highest unit awards.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The difficult deployment took its toll on the broader strike group, which also included three guided-missile destroyers. Multiple reports indicated that logistical strain caused by the war exacerbated the situation.
Business Insider obtained written responses submitted to Congress by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao late last month that revealed eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Cao said that multiple sailors attempted to jump overboard. There were no suicides, though.
Cao wrote that "the men and women of Carrier Strike Group THREE have demonstrated exceptional resolve under demanding conditions," emphasizing that "operational decisions to extend deployments are never made lightly." He said the Navy is committed to preserving crew morale, health, and safety, and overall fleet readiness.
Navy leadership has said that it is taking lessons from the deployment . The service has said that it is loading carriers up with more supplies to ensure self-sufficiency if logistics and support come under stress, adding quality of life improvements, and working to keep sailors and Marines better connected with loved ones.

articles.title_orig: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
articles.title_zh: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
articles.content_orig:
For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”
In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.
Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.
Volunteers went through the same four-part sequence twice, once sober and once on psilocybin. The sequence included putting participants in four different settings or contexts: eight minutes of lying at rest, a guided meditation, an 11-minute curated music playlist, and finally six minutes of eyes-open video of clouds moving across a sky. Each participant did all four inside an MRI scanner about 80 minutes after dosing, and again on EEG about 150 minutes after.
There were no cognitive tasks researchers routinely go for in brain studies, but there was a purpose behind this omission.
“We wanted ecological validity,” Stoliker says. “We wanted to know what the brain was like when somebody was having an authentic, uninterrupted psychedelic experience. If somebody took a psychedelic in a therapeutic setting, you wouldn’t have them completing tasks.” Stoliker also points out that there’s evidence that giving someone a task mid-trip pulls them out of the state—a phenomenon researchers sometimes call grounding. “Once you introduce these sorts of tasks, you’re actually interrupting the very phenomena you are seeking to measure.” And it worked.
Half of the participants ranked their session among the most meaningful experiences of their lives, and 24 put it in their personal top five. Stolkier and his colleagues started analyzing their brain scan data to find out why.
Measuring global functional connectivity—how much influence each patch of cortex exerts over the rest—the team found that, when participants had their eyes closed, sensory regions lost sway while associative regions gained. “It seems like the brain’s ability to construct reality, or imagination, or our associations, our beliefs, our sense of self—these faculties had more dominance over sensory areas,” Stoliker says, stressing that the interpretation is a hypothetical. “This could help explain why people have meaningful, complex imagery experiences, why they have mystical experiences with imagery that is personally relevant to them.”
Another observation the team made was that connections within each brain network weakened, connections between networks strengthened. The brain’s modularity, a parameter that describes how cleanly neurons stay sorted into specialist teams, dropped across all four parts of the experimental sequence.
What’s more, researchers found that, when sober, activity in a brain with its eyes shut looked very different from a brain watching a movie. Under psilocybin, that difference nearly evaporated. In the visual network, the gap between eyes-open and eyes-closed connectivity shrank by 85 percent. The results from the EEG session independently confirmed that, with alpha-band activity (normally a marker of the brain gating visual input) reduced by nearly half.
“When somebody takes a psychedelic and they’re able to close their eyes and see complex imagery, there seems to be less boundary between the internal and external world than we ordinarily experience,” Stoliker says.
Regardless of these details, the results rather accurately reproduced the chaos in the brain so many researchers claimed psychedelics caused. This chaos, though, turned into order when the team processed their data in a slightly unorthodox way.
Scientists usually do two acts of averaging in a standard brain imaging study. The first is averaging over time. An eight-minute brain scan comprises a few hundred successive images of the whole brain. To understand how two specific regions work together, researchers conventionally average all these images down to a single number describing how well the two regions’ activity matched up across the whole eight minutes.
The problem with this analysis is that it runs the risk of missing ordered structures that appear for a brief period and then disappear into chaos.
The second analysis is averaging over people. Having produced one such number per participant, the standard approach then pools all of them into a group average, on the assumption that individual differences are noise that will be canceled out. Stoliker’s study was focused on individual experiences, so he wanted to avoid that.
Instead, the team fed the moment-by-moment activity of 332 brain regions into CEBRA, a machine-learning tool that compressed the data down to its essential structure while preserving the order of events. For each individual, it produced a trajectory—a path traced through a three-dimensional space, one point for each moment of the scan.
“When they’re not under psilocybin, the brain activity is less differentiated by context,” Stoliker says. “But under psilocybin, we see that the activity becomes organized across time and more clearly differentiated by context.” The trajectories separated into four distinct clusters corresponding to rest, meditation, music, and the movie. A classifier could read a moment of brain activity and say which one the person was in.
It turned out the performance of that classifier scaled with how profound the participants described their experience as being.
To find out which parts of the brain were doing the work, the team replaced one network’s psilocybin activity with its sober version and checked how badly the classifier degraded. The default mode network and the visual network each accounted for over 20 percent of the effect. “The default mode network is strongly associated with the sense of self: daydreaming, mind wandering, thinking about yourself. It’s often been called the narrative self,” Stoliker explains. “On the other end of this gradient, more externally oriented, is the visual system.”
Under psilocybin, the two became less differentiated, which the team thinks explains why participants reported a subjective experience of the self and the external world becoming less separate, a state Stoliker calls “embeddedness.”
“Theoretically, we could suggest that psychedelics are temporarily altering the organization of brain networks that ordinarily help maintain this separation that we experience,” he says. “It really challenges the idea of whether the internal world and external world are separate and highlights the idea that the brain may be responsible for constructing both.”
The day after the session, participants rated whether various things had shifted, like sense of connection to themselves, to others, to nature, along with peace, acceptance, and creativity, all on a scale running from –100 to 100. “For the vast majority of our participants, we found they had positive psychological changes the next day,” Stoliker says. articles.title_orig: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
articles.title_zh: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
articles.content_orig:
A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.
The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.
Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.
It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."
The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".
Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.
She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.
There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.
The policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".
The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."
Appearing on BBC Radio 4 programme Any Questions on Friday, Lucas said she was not putting any blame on the party's current leader, Zack Polanski, who she said had done "great things" for the party.
"Our constitution was written decades ago, well before we had MPs, before we had mayors, before we had anything like the number of that we have today," the ex-leader said.
Lucas, who was for years the face of the Greens as its first and sole MP until 2024, added the party needed to be made "a welcoming place for Jewish people."
A Green Party spokesperson said: "Green Party membership has increased since Zack Polanksi announced his leadership bid in May 2025. Unlike other political parties, our members can bring and set policy.
"This is one motion alongside dozens of others that was discussed at our biggest-ever party conference. Every motion submitted to conference undergoes debate and no single interest group drives policy. "
Polanski, who is Jewish, previously told the BBC he would not have voted for the motion and instead would have voted for an amended version.
However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious".
Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
Ashok Kumar, a Green Party member and part of the Greens for Palestine group, voted for the motion and told the BBC last week it was about "Palestinian liberation."
He said he didn't feel the vote was harming the image of the Green Party, and that a growing number of people see this as a core issue.
"They see the violence that's (been) occurring over the last three years," he told BBC Politics Live. "So, I think the Zionist position is actually the marginal position.
Following Polanksi's by-election defeat in Holborn and St Pancras this week, the leader of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said he should resign.
She added it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.
Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on the motion or amendments. He left early to campaign for the north London by-election, which Labour won on Thursday with Greens coming second.
Following his defeat, Polanski told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.
He lost out to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.

articles.title_orig: Warren Buffett Is Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street With This Warning. Here’s What History Says May Happen Next.
articles.title_zh: Warren Buffett Is Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street With This Warning. Here’s What History Says May Happen Next.
articles.content_orig:
Investors always listen closely to comments from Warren Buffett -- and for good reason. The billionaire spent six decades at the helm of Berkshire Hathaway , and there, he drove market-beating gains. He helped Berkshire Hathaway deliver an average annual return of more than 19%, compared with the S&P 500's 10% over that period.
That's concrete proof of Buffett's clear understanding of the market, and investors, realizing this, aim to benefit from his wisdom. Buffett has been generous when it comes to sharing his thoughts on investing and secrets to success, and he's done this through his letters to shareholders, talks at events, and press interviews.
Today, Buffett no longer leads Berkshire Hathaway's investing decisions. He recently retired and now holds the position of chairman emeritus and a spot on the board of directors. However, Buffett remains involved in the Berkshire Hathaway investment process and also continues to share his thoughts with the public.
In fact, Buffett is sending shockwaves through Wall Street with the following warning, and history says this may happen next.
Image source: The Motley Fool. Image source: The Motley Fool.
First, let's consider the S&P 500 's path so far in 2026, after completing a 78% gain over three years. As the artificial intelligence (AI) boom gained momentum, investors turned to stocks operating in this space -- and since many are tech giants, heavily weighted in the S&P 500, they helped push the index significantly higher. Meanwhile, against the backdrop of interest rate cuts in 2024 and 2025, investors also favored other growth stocks, as they benefit in such environments.
This year, the S&P 500 has pulled back on occasion as investors worried about several headwinds, from rising inflation to the possibility that the AI revenue opportunity wouldn't be as significant as expected. Still, declines have been short-lived, and the index has continued to march higher, even closing at a record this week. And certain AI stocks have delivered mind-boggling gains -- for example, AI memory providers Sandisk Corp. and Micron Technology have climbed more than 600% and 200%, respectively, since the start of January.
Now, let's consider the Warren Buffett warning that's sending shockwaves through Wall Street. Speaking with CNBC during the Berkshire Hathaway shareholders' meeting in May, Buffett expressed concern about a high level of "gambling" in the stock market.
"We've never had people in a more gambling mood than now," he said, referring to the preference for betting to score a fast gain rather than investing for the long term.
At the same time, valuations have climbed to high levels, as we can see through the S&P 500 Shiller CAPE ratio. It considers stock price and earnings per share over 10 years to account for fluctuations in the economic environment.
S&P 500 Shiller CAPE Ratio data by YCharts
As we can see, the last time valuations reached -- and surpassed -- such levels was prior to the dot-com crash. So, history suggests that, following this period of "gambling," and with stocks at expensive levels, the next move could be a decline in stock prices — even if it's not a long-lasting movement or a crash, stocks could be heading for a pullback from today's levels.
What does this mean for you as an investor? Buffett's warning doesn't signal that investors should stop buying stocks. The billionaire has invested throughout market environments and has never lost faith in quality companies. Instead, this comment from Buffett shows us that some market activity -- the quest for quick gains -- may present a risk. And against this backdrop, it's important to refrain from getting caught up in that movement.
Instead, it's essential to stick to strong investing principles, as Buffett does, and continue to look for quality stocks that trade at reasonable valuations and hold onto them for the long term. By doing so, even if the gambling Buffett notes in the market leads to declines, you still will be well-positioned to win over time.

articles.title_orig: Scientists Detect Record-Breaking Radio Signal from the Ancient Universe
articles.title_zh: Scientists Detect Record-Breaking Radio Signal from the Ancient Universe
articles.content_orig:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that spotted a blast from the past, opened a portal between realms, yakked it up, and rose from the ashes.
First, scientists have spotted a mysterious radio signal from the primordial universe that could illuminate cosmic evolution (it’s not aliens… sorry). Then: a diamond in the quantum rough, the decline of a fine bovine line, and a second-generation planet.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files .
Caleb, Manisha et al. “A fast radio burst at redshift 2, three billion years after the Big Bang.” Science.
Scientists have discovered the most distant fast radio burst (FRB), a type of mysterious radio flare from space. This burst erupted when the universe was only three billion years old and sent radio waves across 10 billion light years before they reached Earth on March 4, 2024.
The distant signal, known as FRB 20240304B, hails from an ancient galaxy beyond “redshift 2,” which means it originated more than twice as far as the next-farthest known FRB. Redshift, represented by the variable “z,” measures how wavelengths of light get stretched out in their journeys across space, a phenomenon that shifts them to the red end of the spectrum. Generally speaking, the more distant the object from Earth, the higher the redshift.
“Approximately one hundred FRBs have identified host galaxies with measured redshifts, with the vast majority at redshifts z ≲ 0.5,” said researchers led by Manisha Caleb of the Sydney Institute for Astronomy. “Only a small number of FRB host galaxies have been identified at z ≳ 1. This observational bias is driven by the sensitivity limit of radio observations that are capable of detecting FRBs and localizing their coordinates.”
Caleb and her colleagues were able to capture the remote flash using South Africa’s MeerKAT radio telescope. Follow-up observations with the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed “a low-mass, clumpy, starforming galaxy” at redshift 2.148 as the host of the burst.
FRBs produce incredibly energetic radio pulses, but the exact mechanisms that generate them remain unknown. Given the diverse features of these bursts—for instance, some repeat, and some are one-offs—they might come from many different sources. In the case of FRB 20240304B, the team speculated that the burst is a magnetar, the highly magnetized remains of a massive star that went supernova.
“The low stellar mass, active star formation, and low metallicity of the host galaxy are consistent with a magnetar origin of the FRB,” the researchers concluded.
This milestone detection of such a distant and ancient FRB opens up the possibility of finding more bursts at high redshifts. In addition to pushing the limits of observation, future discoveries could allow scientists to extract clues about the evolution of the universe that become imprinted in these signals during their vast journeys. So bring on the bygone bursts!
Nayak, Anshuman et al. “Spin force from a nitrogen-vacancy ensemble drives a 100-mg levitated resonator.” Science Advances.
Time to shrink down from the largest cosmic scale to the tiny quantum realm. In a new study, scientists report that they successfully moved a centimeter-scale diamond with a force known as quantum spin, making it by far the largest object ever manipulated by a quantum effect. It represents a major breakthrough, as the diamond is the first object large enough to be subject to gravity to be moved in this way, further bridging the gap between the loopy quantum realm and regular, everyday physics.
A graphical representation of the observed movements. a) When the laser is off, the diamond slab has a small magnetic moment (blue arrow) induced by the latent spin-state inside the nitrogen-vacancy centers of the diamond. b) When the green laser is on, the spin-state is polarized, causing the magnetic moment to fluctuate weakly, pushing the diamond down towards the magnetic field (red arrows). Image: Nayak et al., 2026
In the new work, scientists worked with a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond containing electrons with “spin,” a form of angular momentum on the quantum scale. Then, they shot a laser at the diamond—as science often demands—which stimulated electrons to spin in a certain state that eerily moved the diamond.
“Experimentally observing this spin force for anything larger than atomic scales has proved challenging,” said researchers led by Anshuman Nayak of the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology. “We have demonstrated the motional driving of a massive diamagnetically levitated mechanical oscillator by the force of NV spins in a gradient magnetic field.”
Congratulations, humanity: We just earned our license to quantum-motionally drive. Proceed responsibly.
Oppenheimer, Jonas and Gillardet, Alexandre et al. “Ancient genomes reveal an extinct bovine species from mid-latitude Asia.” Current Biology.
Domestic cows are overwhelmingly the most common bovine species on Earth today, but this family of swole ungulates once contained a diversity of wild lineages that included aurochs, steppe bison, and oxen.
Now, scientists have discovered the remains of a distinct bovine species—named “yak X”—in Siberia’s Denisova Cave, which was also inhabited by many human species (hominins) during the Pleistocene era, which ended 12,000 years ago.
Yak X (cool name!) began diverging from extant yaks about 400,000 years ago, and had formed its own unique yak pack by 250,000 years ago, reports a team that sequenced its ancient genomes. The youngest bones from this mysterious animal date back about 27,200 years, so it must have died out sometime after.
“Yak X is a Pleistocene megafaunal species previously unknown to genomics,” said researchers co-led by Jonas Oppenheimer and Alexandre Gillardet of Stockholm University. “Yak X appears to have become genetically isolated from other bovines including bison and aurochs despite their apparent geographic proximity in Pleistocene mid-latitude Asia. This lack of gene flow is in notable contrast to hominins at Denisova Cave, which displayed complex patterns of admixture among multiple divergent lineages.”
In other words, hominins at this cave, including Neanderthals and Denisovans, appear to have interbred, while this yak didn’t cross with its fellow bovine relatives. This has been Yak News.
Williams, Jamie T. et al. “Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf.” Nature Geoscience.
Planets are frequently obliterated by the explosive deaths of their stars, but they can also be born out of those same stellar ashes. Scientists have now directly observed the first evidence of one of these so-called “second-generation” planets that formed around a type of dead star called a white dwarf.
Located about 270 light years from Earth, the white dwarf—known as HS 0209+0832—was once a star similar to the Sun. About five million years ago, it shed its red giant shell and collapsed into its current husk state.
Since its transition to the afterlife, a new planet has coalesced out those ejected embers, though this world is destined for an early grave. Scientists spotted telltale signs of second-generation elements—including zinc, copper, and niobium—in the spectrum of the white dwarf, which are distinct from first-generation planetary ingredients, such as the silicon and iron that make up Earth. The discovery exposes a dead star feeding on its posthumous offspring that was birthed from its own ghostly gas.
“Here we report the discovery of a white dwarf accreting material that is unlike any Solar System object,” said researchers led by Jamie Williams of the University of Warwick. “The discovery of this second-generation planet that is chemically distinct from first-generation material demonstrates that close-in planets around white dwarfs can form…Establishing a sizable sample of such systems will open a windo

âInsolvency cascadesâ are set off by depreciating GPUs. Collateral food fights and margin calls ensue. Quinn Emanuel is a litigation boutique, so itâs talking its book. But business-development brochures were never such grim reading.

articles.title_orig: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
articles.title_zh: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
articles.content_orig:
Shelley and Todd Engel. The Engel family hide caption
Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.
In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."
The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION , for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.
Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.
More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.
Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.
His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.
In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter .
The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.
When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it . The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.
The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events . It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.
In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.
Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.
That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.
It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."
Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."
NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)
Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."
Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.
That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.
He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.
"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."
The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.
Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.
"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.
These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.
But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed
"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.
NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Army caught off guard by Hegseth’s order to make firing squad execution public
articles.title_zh: Army caught off guard by Hegseth’s order to make firing squad execution public
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood mass shooter would be shown in public caught people across the Pentagon and the Army off guard, three sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
Hegseth made the announcement in an interview Wednesday with far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, where he welcomed the crew home from their monthslong deployment to the Middle East.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said during the interview.
That comment was the first time many in the Army and Pentagon heard about the idea of a firing squad’s execution of Nidal Hasan in Texas being made public, and there were immediately questions about what “public” would mean. There are Army regulations about who can watch a military execution, including family of the prisoner and of the victims, media representatives and a chaplain.
But it was decided by Hegseth, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, and Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell and his staff that “public” would mean it would be livestreamed, one source familiar said. The Pentagon then confirmed as much to the media, saying in a statement, “The Secretary is correct. It will be livestreamed. Details will follow.”
Hegseth wants America to watch a firing squad execution. It’s drawing backlash
The Army referred questions to the Pentagon, and a Pentagon spokesperson said they had nothing to add beyond Thursday’s confirmation that it would be livestreamed.
The idea has shocked many service members and veterans and provoked a bipartisan backlash . Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday that the livestream could ultimately go forward, saying he didn’t know “if that’s actually going to happen,” but said if it was, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
“It takes away everything America stands for when we do public executions,” one Army officer with multiple deployments to the Middle East told CNN. “The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable.”
President Donald Trump welcomed the idea of a firing squad execution throughout the week but on Saturday said he hasn’t decided whether to livestream it.
“We’re giving a man the death penalty who killed 14 soldiers a couple of years ago. Death penalty through firing squad — and he deserves it,” the president said to applause during a White House event Friday honoring Christopher Columbus.
Trump told reporters Saturday, “I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
Many of the details around the livestream have yet to be finalized, and multiple sources told CNN that officials have been working to find answers since it was announced. A second source familiar told CNN that great care is being taken to determine which soldiers would fire on Hasan, taking into consideration the potential psychological impacts of doing so. A specific unit has been selected to carry out the execution, the source said.
Showing the execution on a livestream presents more challenges, the source said, including any effort to obscure from the public the identities of the soldiers involved. It’s also unclear where and if the execution will be streamed beyond the Pentagon’s own website. Broadcasters and social media platforms have strict restrictions on violent and disturbing content.
The first source familiar said there are still questions about whether soldiers can decline to participate, given that the military is moving forward with this as a legal order.
The second source familiar echoed the same, saying while many soldiers may have “taken a life in combat,” this is a very different situation.
“This is a situation where the guy has done a very bad thing and hurt a lot of people, years removed,” the second source said. “He’s going to be immobile and put up like a target.”
This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title_orig: Pope: Art is not ‘mere aestheticism’ but a way to share the Gospel
articles.title_zh: Pope: Art is not ‘mere aestheticism’ but a way to share the Gospel
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV met with members of the Bizot Group, officially known as the International Group of Organizers of Major Exhibitions, at the Vatican on October 10. The Group brings together directors of the largest art and culture museums around the world.
The Pope highlighted how the Groupâs passion reveals that âevery museum is a place of memory, beauty and history, fostering encounters between generations and promoting culture and human creativity.â
Over the centuries, the Catholic Church has developed a deep connection with the arts in all forms. Art, Pope Leo stressed, âis the means by which persons, through their ingenuity, enhance and transfigure matterâthat is, the creation in which they dwell as made in the image and likeness of God.â
Centering on the theme of 'Materiality,' the Bizot Groupâs meeting invites a deeper exploration into the relationship between an object and art interpretation. Moreover, it plays a role in reflecting on how God chose to reveal himself in the specific quality of matter.
With this in mind, the Pope outlined three points regarding matter, beginning with how it is available to humanity as âa gift entrusted to our care.â Through an artistâs skill, they are able to turn matter into a gift for others.
He underlined that cultural activity can reveal the beauty of creation.
Furthermore, matter can be formed into whatever the artist is trying to express. Art, Pope Leo said, âis a creative process through which human beings, in imitation of Godâs work, shape matter and imbue it with a transcendent meaning.â
In this way, artwork becomes a sign of the beauty that stirs humanityâs hearts and minds, encouraging the person to look to what is above.
Thirdly, matter is memory. âThe works preserved in museums bear witness to a history that speaks to every person, from one generation to the next,â the Pope explained. Pieces in a museum offer the wisdom of the past to the present.
âThe Church, as a pilgrim through time, has understood art precisely in this way: not as mere aestheticism, but as a means of proclaiming the Gospel through beauty.â
Concluding, Pope Leo congratulated the Bizot Group for its work in directing and administering museums around the worldââsafeguarding a heritage that belongs to all humanity.â

articles.title_orig: China, Pakistan armies to conduct counterterrorism drills
articles.title_zh: China, Pakistan armies to conduct counterterrorism drills
articles.content_orig:
Chinese and Pakistani armies will conduct a joint training exercise in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, in mid-to-late October, a Chinese defense spokesman said on Saturday.
Chen Xi, a spokesman for the Ministry of National Defense, said at an online news briefing that the exercise, code-named Karakoram 2026, will focus on joint counterterrorism operations in high-altitude areas.
The training will include drone operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, as well as joint command exercises and live-force drills, Chen said.
He said the exercise will be the first joint army training between the two countries and will help deepen exchanges and cooperation while enhancing their ability to jointly respond to terrorist threats.

articles.title_orig: World Watch Day 2026: Time as Living Heritage
articles.title_zh: World Watch Day 2026: Time as Living Heritage
articles.content_orig:
Today marks the second annual World Watch Day , celebrated on October 10 in a clever nod to the familiar “10:10” depiction of watch hands. This year’s theme, “Time as Living Heritage”, puts the people of Sainte-Croix at the centre of the occasion.
A training course at Association Mec-Art
Marking the event, our founder SJX participated in a round-table discussion about preserving and passing on the skills of both watchmaking and mechanical art.
The panel included De Bethune co-founder Denis Flageollet and automaton maker François Junod, who helped establish the Association Mec-Art, watchmaker Vianney Halter, The 1916 Company’s Tim Mosso, and Karin Alexandrian of the Musée des Arts et Métiers. Europa Star ’s Pierre Maillard moderated the conversation.
Denis Flageollet of De Bethune co-founded the Association Mec-Art in 2016 with automaton-makers François Junod and Nicolas Court
The organisers, Association Mec-Art and the Musée de la Mécanique d’Art et du Patrimoine de Sainte-Croix (MuMAPS), work to safeguard the traditions explored in our earlier story on the unique skills being preserved in Sainte-Croix. These extend beyond watches to music boxes, mechanical singing birds, and automata.
Mec-Art helps keep the skills alive through creative projects and practical courses, while MuMAPS is the local museum dedicated to mechanical art and the town’s heritage. The shared challenge is to ensure that future generations can still make and repair these objects, and so that future artisans will continue to have a commercial outlet for their craft.
For more information visit worldwatchday.org and mec-art.ch .

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan President William Lai Ching-te says the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom” in a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office in Taipei.
Lai made the remarks on Saturday in front of thousands of people, including foreign guests and diplomats. Fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over Taipei before his speech.
“We are open to exchanges but will not accept subordination,” he said. “Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke; rather, it is to deter war.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office condemned Lai’s speech, saying it “disregards facts, ⁠distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives”.
It said ‌Lai “stubbornly clung to ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist thinking” and exaggerated the “threat from the mainland”.
“There is only one ⁠China in the ⁠world, and Taiwan is part of China – this is the ⁠true status quo in ⁠the Taiwan ⁠Strait,” it said.
Taiwan’s future “can and must be decided jointly by ‌all the Chinese people, including our compatriots in ‌Taiwan”, ‌it also said.
The holiday marks the 115th anniversary of a 1911 uprising that toppled China’s last imperial dynasty and led to the founding of the Republic of China.
Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory, has never renounced the use of force to take it and calls Lai a “separatist”.
Beijing has rebuffed his offers of talks.
Lai said China continued to “apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait”.
Grey-zone tactics are actions that stop short of open war. “Peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further,” he added.
Lai’s government has set aside a record 1.1 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($34.5bn) for defence in 2027, more than 3 percent of its gross domestic product.
China held war games around the island shortly after Lai’s first National Day speech in 2024 but not last year. Its last drills near Taiwan were in late December after news of an $11bn arms deal with the United States, the largest ever US weapons package for the island.
Lai said he welcomed talks between the US and China but insisted “there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist”.
He urged democracies in the Asia Pacific to join forces to preserve peace and stability in the region.
Lai also said China has exerted pressure to try to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait and the island’s “resolve” is not just about its own survival in the face of “authoritarian expansion”. It’s also about whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules, he added.
According to Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defence, 21 Chinese military aircraft and seven navy ships were operating around Taiwan in a 24-hour period ending at 6am on Saturday (22:00 GMT on Friday). Thirteen of the aircraft crossed the median line in the Taiwan Strait, which once served as an unofficial barrier between the two sides, and entered the island’s air defence identification zone.
Eswatini King Mswati III and Indiana Lieutenant Governor Micah Beckwith were among the foreign guests who offered their congratulations in Taiwan, Lai’s office said. Eswatini is Taiwan’s only diplomatic ally in Africa. A Japanese parliamentary delegation also visited the island and joined the National Day celebrations.
The US switched its official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago but remains Taiwan’s most important security backer.
Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump.
In May, after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, Trump suggested arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China, which set off alarm across the world.
Taiwan is now waiting for Trump to sign off on $14bn worth of weapons, including the US-made Patriot air defence system.
The dispute dates back to China’s civil war, when the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after defeat by Mao Zedong’s communists.
The Republic of China remains the island’s formal name.

articles.title_orig: From hunger to hope: Lettie's story on World Porridge Day
articles.title_zh: From hunger to hope: Lettie's story on World Porridge Day
articles.content_orig:
When Mary's Meals first met Leticia, known to many as Lettie, she was 11 years old. Recently orphaned and hungry, she had been forced to leave school and care for her two younger brothers. Her story was first shared in Child 31 , the award-winning 2012 documentary that introduced audiences around the world to the reality of child hunger in Malawi. Now, more than a decade later, Mary's Meals has returned to Lettie's story.
Their new documentary, Lettie , shares a new, very different chapter of her life.
Today, Lettie is an educated, working mother. She works for Mary's Meals Malawi, where she also serves as a Youth Ambassador, sharing the stories of children who, like her, receive a daily meal at school. Her son is thriving and neither he nor his mother are facing the hunger that once threatened to define her and her brothers' futures.
For Angela Chipeta-Khonje, Country Director of Mary's Meals Malawi, Lettie's story is both extraordinary and deeply familiar. "She is one of those children who went through hunger, but she overcame it thanks to a meal that she was getting every day at school". However, Chipeta-Khonje notes, the significance of her story goes beyond survival. "It is a story that is giving hope to so many other children in Malawi," she explains. "And it helps people understand the extent to which children are living in these situations."
World Porridge Day, marked each year on 10 October, draws attention to the importance of school meals in tackling childhood hunger and improving access to education. The day is closely associated with the work of Mary's Meals, which provides nutritious meals to children in some of the world's poorest communities. Although the documentary was released earlier this year, Lettie's story offers a reminder of the lasting difference that a daily meal can make in a child's life.
For children in Malawi, the challenges of hunger and food insecurity are particularly acute. According to the World Food Programme, 6.8 million people in the country are experiencing insufficient food consumption. Most families rely on smallholder farming and rain-fed agriculture, leaving them especially vulnerable to droughts, flooding and other climate-related shocks.
"Food insecurity has remained a significant challenge," Chipeta-Khonje explains. "Most families have been unable to recover from repeated climatic shocks and do not have adequate food production." Children are often the first to bear the consequences. Yet, in the midst of these challenges, a simple meal can become something far greater than food. Mary's Meals "is meeting immediate hunger needs," Chipeta-Khonje says, "but it is also providing the incentive and energy for education, which ultimately breaks the cycle of poverty."
Mary's Meals began serving school meals in Malawi in 2003. What started with around 200 children in a single school has grown into the charity's largest programme worldwide. Today, more than 1.3 million children receive a meal every school day across Malawi. They now operate in 16 countries worldwide. According to the organisation's 2025 impact study, 97 per cent of teachers reported improvements in literacy and numeracy linked to better attendance and reduced hunger. Every teacher surveyed reported reduced dropout rates and improved retention among pupils receiving school meals.
Chipeta-Khonje says these outcomes reveal something important. "Yes, we are alleviating hunger," she says. "But at the same time, it is an investment in human capital development." Education, she argues, is one of the most effective ways of addressing the challenges many African countries continue to face. "We need a population that is educated so that we can deal with the challenges we are seeing every day."
Lettie's story has captured international attention because her journey was documented. But Chipeta-Khonje insists that "there are so many Letties out there".
Over the last two decades, millions of children have passed through Mary's Meals programmes in Malawi. Many have returned years later to share how a daily meal at school enabled them to remain in education, find employment, support their families and build better futures. For Chipeta-Khonje, these stories reveal the true power of school feeding programmes. "They create conditions for hope," she says. "They create opportunity. They bring lasting change that is carried into adulthood and passed on to the next generation."
Chipeta-Khonje hopes that as people watch Lettie all across the world, they will see more than one woman's journey. She hopes they will recognise what can happen when people choose to respond to hunger with compassion. "It doesn't have to be huge," she says. "Small acts of love can do so much for so many children across the world".
It is a message that resonates strongly on World Porridge Day. Behind the simple act of providing a daily meal are opportunities for children to attend school, receive an education and build a better future. Stories like Lettie's remind us what this means in practice. Often, it means a future that once seemed impossible. As Lettie shows, a daily school meal may seem simple, but for millions of children, it can change everything.

The robot made its public debut at a recent seminar on wheat breeding, state-run China Science Daily reported on Friday.
Traditional wheat breeders rely on a wealth of accumulated experience to identify and select strains with superior traits from tens of thousands of hybrid offspring.
But this requires manual assessment in the field – a process that is both labour intensive and subjective.

articles.title_orig: China maintains stable employment growth, vows further policy support
articles.title_zh: China maintains stable employment growth, vows further policy support
articles.content_orig:
China's job market maintained stable growth in the first three quarters, and the government will continue taking active measures, including expanding vocational training programs, strengthening rights protection for gig workers and developing new occupations, to further promote employment.
Figures released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security on Saturday show that about 10.52 million people found jobs in urban areas in the first nine months of this year, achieving 87.7 percent of the annual target. The surveyed urban unemployment rate averaged about 5.2 percent in the first eight months.
To promote higher-quality employment, the ministry will step up financial and fiscal support in the coming years and actively address the impact of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, on the job market, said Li Zhong, vice-minister of human resources and social security, at a news conference in Beijing on Saturday.
The ministry will focus on stabilizing employment in labor-intensive and service industries to create more jobs, while expanding vocational training programs to address structural imbalances between labor supply and demand.
It will also improve public employment services and strengthen supervision of the human resources market to promote higher-quality employment, Li said.
"Administrative regulations and mechanisms for protecting the employment rights of workers in flexible employment and gig work will be further improved to ensure fairer recruitment, remuneration, social insurance coverage and rest periods," he said.
The ministry will also continue developing new occupations in response to technological advances and the evolving needs of industrial development, thereby expanding employment opportunities.
Vocational training is also key to addressing structural imbalances in the labor market. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), the ministry aims to provide government-subsidized vocational training to 10 million people annually and help 40 million people obtain government-recognized skills certificates over the five-year period.
