articles.title_orig: The iPhone Duo’s Unfolding Animation Is Giving Z Fold 8 Owners FOMO, but Not Me
articles.title_zh: The iPhone Duo’s Unfolding Animation Is Giving Z Fold 8 Owners FOMO, but Not Me
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
When I first got my hands on the iPhone Duo , I admittedly dismissed the unfolding animation that would soon become a highlight of online discourse. I was less interested in the smooth transition as content shifted from one screen to another and more focused on details such as the matte inner display and seemingly invisible crease.
But in the weeks since Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, which drops Oct. 23 , I’ve seen countless examples on social media of people trying to recreate that buzzed-about animation on their Android foldables. While the Play Store offers plenty of launchers for customizing Android phones — including ones that mimic the iPhone’s home screen — this appears to be one iOS design element that users are particularly eager to bring to their devices.
Sometimes, you really can’t predict what people will care about most — or the lengths they’ll go to imitate a feature.
The primary phone people have used to recreate the iPhone Duo’s cascading transition effect is Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 , which debuted in July with a passport-size foldable design ahead of Apple’s release . Unlike iOS, Samsung’s One UI interface, which runs on top of Android on Galaxy devices, doesn’t include a folding animation. Instead, content simply transitions from the Z Fold 8’s cover screen to its inner display once the phone is opened about halfway. I never considered this a deficiency until I saw the flood of positive reactions to the iPhone Duo’s fluid transition effect.
To bridge that gap, several creators have posted videos explaining how to use third-party apps and developer tools on GitHub to get a similar effect on the Z Fold 8, with caveats like “ the smoothness and quality won’t be the same ‘” and “ install it [at] your own risk .” (That’s encouraging!) The steps don’t seem particularly complicated, and some options appear to have cropped up in the Play Store as well.
I’ve chosen to forgo installing these Duo-copycat apps on my precious Galaxy Z Fold 8 for two reasons. First, I’m not much of a risk-taker. Second, I’m not interested in imitating an aesthetic element of Apple’s software with a derivative version, especially when the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a standout foldable device in its own right. While the value of the Duo’s sleek animation has since grown on me, I’m not quite desperate enough to retrofit it onto a foldable phone that’s just as functional without that flourish.
Don’t get me wrong: I think Apple’s combination of hardware and software expertise will elevate the iPhone Duo in a way that merits the attention the phone has received, despite being relatively “late” to the foldables game . But I also think it’s more tasteful for consumers to embrace what each phone-maker does best, rather than shoehorning in a competitor’s feature for something as superficial as an animation effect.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of my favorite phones I’ve tested this year, earning it a CNET Editors’ Choice Award. Its versatile design is optimized for both vertical and horizontal content : I can stream YouTube videos and movies on the 7.6-inch inner display, then rotate it to seamlessly scroll through social posts. The crease is barely noticeable, and the battery easily lasts all day. The 5.5-inch cover screen never feels cramped, while its sharp corners give the phone a highly polished look. And despite lacking a telephoto lens, the Z Fold 8’s dual rear cameras pull their weight, capturing crisp, vibrant photos.
The iPhone Duo shares many attributes with the Z Fold 8, including a palm-size design, 7.6-inch inner display and dual rear cameras. Those similarities prompted Samsung to post a series of salty tweets after Apple debuted its foldable last month, including one that reads , “Let us know when you’re done reheating our leftovers.”
That said, I am curious how app developers might optimize their platforms for the iPhone Duo in ways we haven’t seen with other foldable phones. While the Android operating system spans a wide range of devices and configurations, iOS developers only have to cater to a single foldable, potentially leading to a more tailored and streamlined experience. We got a glimpse of how Netflix is building its app for the Duo, and it’ll be interesting to see how both Apple and other third-party developers take full advantage of the phone’s 1.4:1 aspect ratio in ways that could make its predecessors seem behind the curve in that regard.
“Borrowing” features from each other is what phone-makers do best. Down the road, it’s possible companies such as Samsung will implement foldable capabilities that Apple rolled out first, and vice versa. Heck, Apple’s delayed entry into this space means it had time to analyze what worked well for its competitors before jumping in with its own rendition. It’s just how the industry works.
So maybe the Galaxy Z Fold 9 — or whatever Samsung decides to call the follow-up to the Z Fold 8 — will have its own nifty opening animation. But until Samsung itself embraces the idea, I’ll stick with using the standout foldable as-is.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX launches 21 data satellites for the Space Development Agency
articles.title_zh: SpaceX launches 21 data satellites for the Space Development Agency
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX launched a Falcon 9 rocket early Saturday carrying a batch of data satellites for the U.S. military’s Space Development Agency (SDA), five days after a last-minute abort scrubbed the first attempt.
Liftoff from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California is occurred at 12:39 a.m. PDT (3:39 EDT / 0739 UTC). The Falcon 9 took a southerly trajectory on departure from Space Launch Complex 4E, currently SpaceX’s only launch facility on the West Coast.
A launch attempt on Oct. 5 was halted by an auto-abort with 58 seconds remaining on the clock. The halt was triggered moments after the rocket’s onboard computers took control of the countdown. SpaceX said the hold was called due to “some off-nominal data on Stage Two”.
The vehicle was lowered to a horizontal position at the pad for troubleshooting the issue, and the launch was repeatedly pushed back a day at a time.
“Additional time throughout the week allowed for double checks on vehicle systems and range deconfliction,” said SpaceX launch commentator Atticus Vadera.
The range conflict is believed to have been a missile test from Vandenberg that occurred on Friday.
The mission, dubbed Tranche 1 Transport Layer A (T1TL-A), is the fourth mission sending production satellites into orbit for the SDA. This is one piece of a broad constellation — called the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA) — designed to support the U.S. military and its allies through space-based capabilities, like missile tracking and secure communications.
The mission will used Falcon 9 first stage booster B1103. This was its sixth flight following the launches of the SDA’s T1TL-E, NROL-179, and three batches of Starlink satellites.
About 7.5 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX landed B1103 at Landing Zone 4. This was the 37th landing at LZ-4 and the 668th Falcon booster landing to date.
The T1TL-A mission is one of 23 missions awarded to SpaceX as part of the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 2 contract awarded in August 2020, which is managed by the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command (SSC). The previous missions from the SDA have already been launched:
The T1TL-B and -E missions featured satellites manufactured by York Space Systems and the T1TL-C satellites were produced by Lockheed Martin. Space Force Col. Ryan Hiserote, SSC’s division chief in Assured Access to Space, told Spaceflight Now back in September 2025 that these initial T1TL missions could be launched in any order.
The 21 satellites flying as part of the T1TL-A mission were manufactured by Northrop Grumman and delivered to Vandenberg Space Force Base on Sept. 28.
Tranche 1 is the initial component of the PWSA constellation is expected to begin providing operational capabilities to the Department of Defense beginning in 2027. When complete, T1 will consist of 126 Transport Layer satellites, 28 Tracking Layer satellites, and four missile defense demonstration spacecraft.
With the three launches completed to date, there are 63 satellites in orbit.
“In close coordination with Space Systems Command (SSC) and Space Launch Delta 30, the deployment of Tranche 1’s proliferated capability will soon deliver continuous overwatch—neutralizing any first-mover advantage by delivering data to warfighters around the world, nearly instantaneously,” said GP Sandhoo, SDA Director and Space Force Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Missile Warning and Tracking following the T1TL-E launch in July.
The SDA said the Transport Layer will consist of between 300 to 500 satellites in low Earth orbit from 750 km to 1,200 km in altitude. The SDA said once complete, 95 percent of the globe will be in view of at least two of the T1TL satellites at any given time.
“The constellation will be interconnected with Optical Inter-Satellite Links (OISLs) which have significantly increased performance over existing radio frequency crosslinks,” the SDA wrote. “LEO orbits in conjunction with OISLs will reduce path loss issues but more importantly offer much lower latencies, which are deemed critical to prosecute time sensitive targets in today’s wartime environment.”
These satellites will be able to integrate with the Link-16 and Integrated Broadcast System (IBS) to allow for “timely threat warnings and situational awareness information”.
The launches of these satellites are managed by the SSC’s System Delta 80 (SYD 80) and the Space Fore Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Assured Access to Space.
The rocket carried an unspecified number of satellites to orbit. Liftoff from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base happened on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 6:07:56 p.m. PDT / 9:07:56 p.m. EDT on Sept. 16 (0107:56 UTC on Sept. 17).
A Falcon 9 rocket fired into a late-night sky Friday night over Cape Canaveral with a Dragon supply ship bound for the International Space Station. Eight minutes later, the booster returned to Florida’s Space Coast for SpaceX’s 50th landing of a Falcon first stage.
Marc Rayman is chief engineer on NASA’s Dawn mission, which has run out of fuel after a 11-year interplanetary journey that explored Vesta and Ceres, the two largest objects in the asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

articles.title_orig: Vos claims second gravel world title with impressive performance in Australia
articles.title_zh: Vos claims second gravel world title with impressive performance in Australia
articles.content_orig:
Marianne Vos has claimed the gravel world title for the second time in her career. The Team Visma | Lease a Bike rider was crowned world champion in Nannup, Australia, after a demanding race over gravel roads and challenging climbs. With her victory, Vos adds another rainbow jersey to her impressive palmarès.
“This victory really means a lot to me,” an emotional Vos said after the finish. This year marked the first time the UCI Gravel World Championships were held outside Europe. In and around Nannup, the riders faced a demanding 125.6-kilometer course with approximately 3,180 meters of elevation gain.
"I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here."
The succession of short climbs made the course particularly challenging, requiring not only physical strength but also technical skills and good race management. On the demanding course, Vos once again demonstrated her versatility. “There was more mud than I expected. As a result, there were also some slippery sections on the course, so we had to be careful at times. Rosa was incredibly strong, especially on the climbs, where I really had to dig deep to stay with her,” Vos explained.
“It was a fantastic course here in Australia. I’m really happy to have been able to secure the rainbow jersey here,” the Dutch rider concluded. This is Vos’s second gravel world title. In 2024, she had already claimed victory at the World Championships in Leuven. With this latest world title, Vos adds another chapter to her remarkable cycling career and brings a difficult season to a close on a high note.

articles.title_orig: A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled
articles.title_zh: A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled
articles.content_orig:
A Palestinian mother mourns her son, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike just over a month into the ceasefire, at Al-Shifa Hospital, in Gaza City, on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.
GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.
Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.
That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.
NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.
Palestinians returned to the ruins of Gaza City after Israeli forces withdrew and ended their ground operation on the first day of the ceasefire, on Oct. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
In Khan Younis, families greet Palestinian prisoners who were freed in exchange for Israeli hostages on Oct. 13, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
At Al-Shifa Hospital on Oct. 23, 2025, Joud Al-Angar, 12, and his younger cousin are covered in dime-sized scabs after they were wounded by a piece of shrapnel from an Israeli munition. They found it in the rubble and thought it was coal they could use to help their family cook dinner. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The bodies of multiple people, including children, are covered in shrouds at a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital on Nov. 20, 2025, after Israeli airstrikes targeted homes and tents. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
People inspect the aftermath of a deadly Israeli airstrike that destroyed a home in Gaza City six weeks into the ceasefire on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A father and his son wade through flooded streets in Gaza City after picking up humanitarian aid on Nov. 25, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children wear virtual reality headsets as part of a TechMed Gaza initiative that aims to help provide children with psychosocial support for trauma, in Al-Zuweida, Gaza, on Dec. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Saqer Al-Ankah holds his dying 10-year-old granddaughter, Bayan, in his arms at Baptist Hospital in Gaza City on Dec. 10, 2025, after she was shot in her tent by Israeli troops who occupy northeast Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Makeshift tents like these in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025, offer little protection from the winter cold, but the U.N. says roughly 1.5 million people have only these for shelter after Israeli airstrikes destroyed nearly all the buildings in the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Raed el-Ghazawi and his children stand in a tent in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025. The family of five says the tent is freezing cold and damp from winter rainstorms. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
On Dec. 17, 2025, Palestinian Christian children decorate a Christmas tree inside the Holy Family Church in Gaza City for the first time since the beginning of the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Fresh produce returns to Gaza City's streets on Dec. 23, 2025, after U.N.-backed experts declared a famine there amid Israeli restrictions on aid during the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Patients sit in a clinic run by Doctors Without Borders in Gaza City on Dec. 31, 2025, a day before Israel banned more than 40 international aid organizations from bringing in staff or aid to Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian female artists gather at the beach in Gaza City for the first time since the war began to paint as a form of therapy, on Feb. 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian rescue workers begin the work of retrieving corpses from under the rubble of homes bombed by Israel during the war in Beit Lahia, Gaza, on Feb. 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
The skeleton of Shawqi Abu Naser, 60, is retrieved from under the rubble on Feb. 16, 2026, more than a year after an Israeli airstrike killed 132 people from the same family in Beit Lahia. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A mother from the Abu Nasr family sits by her son's body in Beit Lahia on Feb. 17, 2026. The body was retrieved from under the rubble more than a year after 132 people were killed in a single Israeli airstrike on the family home. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians gather in an open space in Gaza City for early morning prayers that mark the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child smiles next to a man dressed as a clown on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, celebrations that mark the end of Ramadan fasting, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian boy shakes hands with Hamas militants on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, following the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians stand next to boxes of U.N. food aid in an area that aid groups need Israeli permission to enter in Jabalia, Gaza, on April 18, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A yellow block placed by Israeli forces marks the expanding territory controlled by the military in Bureij, Gaza, on May 7, 2026. Palestinians are barred from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Young Palestinian chess players gather at a coffee shop in Gaza City for the first tournament since the start of the war, on May 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child carries jugs of water as he passes by a mural of Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal that is painted on the rubble of a home destroyed by Israeli airstrikes, in Al-Shati refugee camp, Gaza, on May 14, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A building burns after an Israeli airstrike killed Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the leader of the military wing of Hamas, his wife, his daughter and a neighbor in Gaza City on May 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Children jump on a trampoline during the Eid holidays on May 31, 2026, in Beit Lahia, which the Israeli military had deemed an "orange zone." Aid organizations are restricted from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child looks into a burned car that was targeted in an Israeli airstrike on a busy street in Gaza City on June 22, 2026. A teenage girl who was going to find internet access to take her final exams was killed in the strike. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A plume of smoke rises after an Israeli airstrike targeted a home in Gaza City nine months into the ceasefire on July 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Thousands of displaced Palestinians gather under Egyptian flags amid the rubble in Gaza City for a public screening of Egypt's match against Argentina in the World Cup on July 7, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
One-hundred corpses are wrapped in Palestinian flags in Gaza City on Aug. 4, 2026, after being retrieved from under the rubble of a building that was hit in an Israeli airstrike in October 2023. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child whose brother was killed in an Israeli airstrike cries at the door of a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Aug. 19, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian children form a chain for a global solidarity initiative called Swim With Gaza that raises money for swimming lessons in Khan Younis on Aug. 25, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child's toys are stained with blood in Gaza City

articles.title_orig: ‘They’re here, they’re fit, they’re financially sound.’ At 80 and older, these travelers are still taking on the world.
articles.title_zh: ‘They’re here, they’re fit, they’re financially sound.’ At 80 and older, these travelers are still taking on the world.
articles.content_orig:
Suzanne Lipsky is a devoted traveler. She’s taken 40 trips over the last decade, including to Cuba, South Africa, and Oman, with plans to add Morocco this year and cruise the Danube next year.
“At this stage of life, travel has become my life,” said Lipsky, who lives in Jamaica Plain.
A spry retired architect, Lipsky is 88. That puts her among a fast-growing group of older travelers determined to continue seeing the world — and changing the way travel providers serve them.
With the front wave of the baby boomers this year turning 80, “I’m seeing a lot of people like me” out on the road, said Peggy Goldman, founder of the global tour operator Friendly Planet Travel , who is 81 herself. “They are people who view themselves as being young and not old. That’s how I feel.”
After all, over-80s are part of a generation that grew up backpacking, hosteling, and riding chicken buses with dog-eared copies of the Lonely Planet guidebooks, noted Jacinta Lim, cofounder of the travel advice and booking site Seek Sophie . Many have already been to Paris and London and now want to see less heavily visited and often more exotic places.
“Adventure is in them,” Lim said. “Just because they’re older doesn’t mean their curiosities and desires have changed. In a lot of cases, they have the money to spend, they have time on their hands, they’re healthy, and they still want to do what they’ve always wanted to do, but with a little more precautions.”
Those precautions mostly have to do with time — more leisurely connections, more time to recover from jet lag, later starts, more nights in one place, fewer activities during the days.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean doing less, Lim said.
“We see older travelers who still want to hike, sail into remote areas, or stay with local communities,” she said. “What changes is how they do it. They might spend four days sailing somewhere rather than squeezing it into a day trip, choose a private guide so they can set their own pace, or do a shorter walk rather than give up hiking altogether.”
In the Indian region of Ladakh, which borders Tibet, tour provider Junichiro Honjo builds in time for older travelers to adjust to the altitude.
“With older guests, we pay much more attention to the pace of the trip — more time to acclimatize, fewer one-night stays, shorter driving days where possible, and more flexibility in the schedule,” said Honjo, founder of the company Life on the Planet Ladakh .
It’s a pace that makes travel more rewarding for people of all ages, he noted, and that younger travelers are starting to request, too, with fewer destinations, more rest days, and longer stays.
The nonprofit educational organization Road Scholar , which serves people over 50, has just added slower-paced versions of 16 of its most popular trips, for over-80 travelers, with more planned.
“You might not do everything,” said Maeve Hartney, Road Scholar’s Boston-based chief program officer. “You might go to Greece and have a lecture at the Acropolis Museum, but you might not climb up the stairs to the Acropolis.”
The idea, said Hartney, “is to ensure that people can still do the things that have always been on their bucket list,” but in a way that’s comfortable for them.
Road Scholar’s slower itineraries were designed for older adults with some limitations, she said. But as travel hassles are made worse by everything from climate issues to crowding, “we’re also seeing our younger participants looking for that slower, more relaxed vacation, versus going, going, going all day long. They want to relax. They want a few afternoons on their own.”
So big is the over-80 market now that Firebird Tours, which caters to retirees, has produced an index of the countries most accommodating to them , based on such things as safety, transportation, walkability, and senior discounts. The top destination: Japan, whose own population is among the oldest in the world.
Other travel providers are also adapting to the over-80 market, said Hartney.
Tourist Japan has debuted slower-paced packages with more free time and lighter itineraries, for example, said Ben Julius, that company’s founder. “A lot of it comes down to older travelers, particularly retirees, not being limited by fixed vacation days, so there’s less pressure to cram a trip full of activities,” Julius said.
Theme parks, where older travelers often come with children and grandchildren, are adding more accessibility, transportation options, seating, and shade, said Jakob Wahl, president and CEO of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions.
Many older travelers seek out tours that can be customized. Instead of physically demanding hikes, for instance, Wayfairer Travel will adapt a Patagonia itinerary by moving glacier and wildlife viewing to accessible boardwalks and boats, said Jason Stevens, CEO.
Of course, over-80s with the money for it can book entirely customized experiences. High-end Asia specialist Remote Lands , which reports a 25 percent increase since the pandemic in the number of customers it serves who are 80+, spares them from the stress of commercial flying by arranging private jets.
“The boomer generation has the funds, and the time, and they are ready to travel,” said Catherine Heald, Remote Lands’ CEO and cofounder.
Luxury travel concierges such as Revigorate can tailor custom trips that build in the choice for older travelers of staying for more or less time in a given destination, said its CEO, Steven Vigor.
“If a place feels special, boomers are willing to adapt the whole itinerary once again just to allow a few extra days in a place they truly enjoy,” Vigor said.
The same slow pace, at a relatively lower price point, is among the draws of river and ocean cruises, whose passengers only have to unpack once.
Uniworld Boutique River Cruises , for example, offers shore excursions of varying activity levels, including aboard tour vans and buses that make pickups just a few feet from the gangplank. It also hands out portable audio headsets so that passengers can hear the guides.
Longer ocean cruises also appeal to older travelers, said Paul Grigsby, vice president of itinerary planning and deployment at Holland America Line . Those include that company’s 29-day Pacific crossing. Live music aboard ship spans generations, and activities include pickleball.
Over-80s also often seek out not necessarily fully accessible rooms, but grab bars in the shower, travel providers say. Some still join cycling tours and hikes, but use e-bikes and trekking poles. Those hearing assistance devices are a plus. So are more choices at breakfast.
“The best plans do not keep reminding people of their age. They help reduce tiredness and dependence while keeping travel enjoyable and free,” said Andrés Serra, head of operations at Optimise Travel .
Rather than ageism, tour providers said their older customers find typically gracious welcomes among natives who appreciate (and are sometimes surprised) that they’re still wandering the world — even in an era when overtourism can put locals in a sour mood.
“Rather than being impatient, people seem to respond in a very positive way,” said Goldman, the 81-year-old founder of Friendly Planet.
She said it’s another example of why everyone should slow down when they travel.
As for the rest of the industry, said Hartney, of Road Scholar, it should be paying more attention to the over-80 market.
“They’re here, they’re fit, they’re financially sound, and they want to travel,” she said. “Either we come up with things for them to do, or we’re going to lose their business.”
Jon Marcus can be reached at jonmarcusboston@gmail.com .

articles.title_orig: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
articles.title_zh: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
articles.content_orig:
Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.
The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists.
The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on calls for his resignation.
The protest comes just months after the movement brought thousands of young people onto Delhi's streets in July, in demonstrations that saw violent clashes with police and forced India's education minister to resign.
Police say they have denied permission for Saturday's gathering, and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed off with huge metal barricades.
The restrictions have caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads. A journey that would normally take 15 minutes took more than an hour this morning.
At Jantar Mantar, police and paramilitary personnel are stationed behind barricades and ropes, preventing people from entering the protest site. Drones could be seen flying overhead.
Some protesters who arrived early were stopped and questioned by security personnel. The BBC also saw at least five people being detained near the site.
Journalists covering the protest have been cordoned off into a designated area nearby.
At a nearby roundabout, loudspeakers repeatedly broadcast appeals for people to cooperate with the police.
Delhi Police has defended the measures, saying they were necessary to maintain public safety and prevent overcrowding at Jantar Mantar, which can accommodate only 1,000 people at a time.
Several trains to Delhi have also been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.
But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may".
"If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations demanding education reforms over the summer. The resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July was seen as a major victory for the group.
CJP protesters returned to the streets last week with a rally in Mumbai to demand Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held another large rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).
Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.
Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.
CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi.
In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.
Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP.
"Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said.
Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them.
"In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."
The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.
At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.
For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.
Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

articles.title_orig: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
articles.title_zh: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
articles.content_orig:
When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer.
But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history.
"Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it."
The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health.
Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby.
She says the whole process took its toll.
"I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits.
Days before Aaliyah's 25th birthday, a large unmarked envelope landed on the doormat of her home, in Birmingham.
"I rip it open, thinking it's an early birthday present," she says.
But what was inside was the response to her data request - pages and pages of her family history, including some medical details she had been painstakingly trying to track down for years.
The documents contained upsetting information alluding to the reason she was taken into care, alongside court records and a personal letter from her social worker.
"They were just given to me in a completely nondescript pile, and they contained completely earth-shattering information, of which I don't think I have ever recovered from," she says.
Aaliyah says knowing about her biological family's health could have helped her understand her own medical concerns.
"My biological mother struggled with eating disorders all her life," she says. "I had very severe anorexia in my teens and that would have been incredibly useful to know."
When a child is adopted in the UK, their NHS number - or equivalent health service identifier - is changed to protect their anonymity.
Their existing medical records should be merged with their new record, but this does not necessarily include their wider family medical history.
And while some local authorities offer specialist support for adoptees up to 21 or 25, the ease of access can vary across the country.
The BBC contacted Bradford Council, which said: "We are genuinely sorry that when Aaliyah received sensitive and personal information through her subject access request, we did not offer the support or signposting she needed. We recognise that we should have done more.
"Following Aaliyah's experience, we are strengthening our approach so that adults accessing their records are given clear information about the support available."
Bradford Children and Families Trust has now offered Aaliyah a meeting to further discuss her experience.
For Dr Chris Tennyson, a delay in getting information about his birth father's health could have put his life at risk.
The 40-year-old clinical psychologist, from Belfast, was adopted as a baby in the 1980s to "a really loving mum and dad, [in a] really comfortable family home".
But in his 20s, he became increasingly curious about his biological origins. He met his birth mother, but his attempts to find out about his father stalled after social workers warned him off asking questions.
Eight years later, Chris tried to trace him again, but it wasn't until he was 33 that a meeting was finally arranged.
Then, on the afternoon the father and son were due to meet, a social worker approached Chris.
"There's something that I need to share with you," the social worker told him. "Your father wants me to let you know that there's a genetic medical condition within your family."
A member of Chris's biological family died in 2000, when the condition came to light. At the time, other members of the family were offered testing. But Chris, who was then aged 14, was not contacted.
The condition, called malignant hyperthermia, causes a potentially life-threatening reaction to certain drugs used during anaesthesia.
While genes linked to it can run in families, not everyone who inherits one of these will necessarily experience a reaction with anaesthesia.
After undergoing genetic tests, Chris discovered his potential risk at the age of 37 - some 23 years after the condition had become known in his wider family.
He says a lack of understanding of how to support adopted adults resulted in the delay in him getting tested.
Chris, who now works with adoption and fostering services in Northern Ireland, says the lack of available information for adoptees is "a huge blind spot".
"There needs to be some kind of mechanism where adopted people's care records can be updated with family information that becomes available throughout the lifespan."
First-time mum Courtney-Grace says she is relieved her baby daughter, Tine, will have access to the crucial family medical history she lacked when she grew up.
Now living in the North of England, the 28-year-old was adopted as a baby and spent time in foster care as a teenager.
"The only thing we knew about my medical history is my biological mom was mentally ill, and had depression."
In her mid-20s, Courtney-Grace was diagnosed with a genetic mutation, which can be inherited and is associated with an increased risk of tumours.
Her symptoms had previously been misdiagnosed as asthma and anxiety, which she says was based off the little doctors knew about her mum.
Courtney-Grace believes allowing medical professionals access to familial history without interfering with data protection rules wouldn't just benefit adoptees, but the entire population.
"The system needs a bit of an overhaul as a whole," she says.
A government consultation on adoption support was launched in February 2026.
Josh MacAlister, the minister for children and families - who is responsible for adoption and children's social care in England - told the BBC that medical records was one of the issues being looked at.
"Adoption support and how it's set up at the moment isn't working well enough and there are obvious gaps in a number of areas that we're going to be looking at making changes to," MacAlister said.
He acknowledged that the current system did not strike the right balance between safeguarding biological relatives' medical privacy and enabling adopted people to access information relevant to their own health.
"We do need to change how we keep, retain, and share medical records," he said.
Authorities in England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all make provisions for adoptees to access their medical history, but the way this operates in practice can vary hugely in the different nations.
None of the four nations gives patients the legal right to that information.
But they advise that when a new clinical record is created for an adopted child, enough information must be kept to support continuity of care.
NHS England said depending on the circumstances of an adoption there may be a need to "protect from disclosure any information about a third party".
But it added that it is important any new NHS records, if created, contain sufficient information to allow for a continuity of care.
For Courtney-Grace, her own diagnosis means her five-month-old daughter will now be closely monitored.
Cord blood was collected when Tine was born, and it will be tested for the genetic condition when she is five. If she has inherited it, a plan will be put in place.
"She has the medical information," Courtney-Grace says. "She can say, 'My mum has this'".
A list of organisations in the UK offering support and information with some of the issues in this story is available at BBC Action Line

articles.title_orig: Trump hits International Criminal Court with sanctions after Nobel goes to former judge
articles.title_zh: Trump hits International Criminal Court with sanctions after Nobel goes to former judge
articles.content_orig:
When Payam Akhavan talks about the Trump administration's new, sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, the first feeling he brings up is despair.
"These institutions, which were once sacrosanct, are besieged," said Akhavan, a Canadian who was appointed as a special adviser on genocide at the ICC in 2021.
The United States government, in the words of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is now working to "dismantle the ICC, piece by piece."
But Akhavan says it's not too late to stand up for the court.
"Canada is at a historical juncture where it has to choose which side of history it's going to be on," he said.
"Will it continue not just to support the rule of international law, but to double down?"
On Friday, the U.S. announced it would cut off the ICC from American financial services, technology companies and even U.S. dollars within six months. The court investigates and tries individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity and the crime of aggression.
Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize for 'her commitment to justice and human dignity'
The U.S. has been pushing to dismantle the ICC over its investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel . U.S. President Donald Trump strongly opposes the ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The U.S. has long rejected the court's authority to investigate, charge and prosecute American service members, treating it as a threat to national sovereignty.
Neither the U.S. nor Israel are parties to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC.
After the sanctions were announced, Canada released a joint statement along with Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, expressing "unwavering support for the independence, impartiality and integrity of the ICC."
Akhavan says Canada must go further. He and other Canadian legal professionals are calling on the federal government to take action to strengthen the ICC through additional funding or other measures.
The initial joint statement did not mention any concrete actions being taken.
"We remain both united in our support for the ICC and committed to engaging in constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-states parties," it said.
Heidi Matthews, who has researched international law for two decades, is scratching her head about what that could mean.
"We would assume [non-state parties] means the United States here," said Matthews, who has worked in the international criminal tribunal prosecuting human rights violations in Sierra Leone.
Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay of International Court of Justice
But given "how aggressively the Trump administration has been moving against the ICC," she said holding constructive dialogue with the U.S. is "almost impossible to see."
The administration's previous moves against the court included sanctioning individual judges, such as Canadian Kimberly Prost .
Matthews says a stronger statement would have clearly recommitted the allies' support for their obligations under the Rome Statute, "including to arrest and surrender accused criminals."
The joint statement appears to instead be "an attempt to appease the Trump administration," said Matthews, and a signal that the independence of the court is up for discussion.
"If the independence of the court is on the table as something that Canada and others are willing to allow to be eroded in one manner or another, then the court is no longer worth the paper that the Rome Statute is written on."
Matthews agrees with Akhavan that Canada should put its money where its mouth is by increasing financial support for the court.
She'd also like the government to put in place legislation that would protect Canadian ICC staff by preventing Canadian companies from complying with the U.S. sanctions — similar to the EU blocking statute .
That legislation can be used to essentially stop a third party's laws from controlling activities on another sovereign territory.
Why the ICC is in the fight of its life with Trump | About That
She says Canada must provide a much stronger signal of its support for the court, whose roots go back to the Nuremberg trials that prosecuted the architects of the Holocaust.
"If we're no longer interested in prosecuting state officials who are engaged in mass atrocity, then I think we're no longer interested in what [Prime Minister Mark] Carney so happily refers to as the international rule of order."
Akhavan says the ICC does have room for improvement, such as its governance and increasing efficiency.
"The question is not that we cannot criticize the court," he said. "But to try and dismantle it as a whole I think is really an attack on the idea of the rule of international law."
Jennifer Yoon covers the latest national and international news for CBC News on television, radio and digital. You can reach her at jennifer.yoon@cbc.ca.

articles.title_orig: Large waves pummel Southern California coast, flooding homes
articles.title_zh: Large waves pummel Southern California coast, flooding homes
articles.content_orig:
A hurricane swell and an overlapping south swell, combined with high tide, flooded the streets of Newport Beach and Laguna Beach with salt water Friday morning, shutting down roadways and snarling traffic throughout the coastal towns.
City workers scrambled to pump the salt water back to the sea.
And the worst is likely yet to come. Waves are expected to get even bigger over the weekend, with tides even higher in the morning hours. Rain from Tropical Storm Rachel is also in the forecast this weekend.
The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood advisory for Orange County beaches that will remain in effect until 2 p.m. Tuesday, warning of flooding in low-lying coastal areas during high tides.
Both coastal towns have suffered severe erosion in recent months, as consistent swells have battered the coastline, eroding the beach buffer between the ocean and the roadways. Friday morning, seawater flooded nearby streets, despite city efforts to build berms, set up sandbags and hold back the ocean.
Newport Beach officials said they were declaring a local emergency Friday to get resources quickly and asked people to stay clear of the flooded areas on the Balboa Peninsula as water was drained and the aftermath of the flooding was cleaned up. Police were allowing only residents into the area.
City staffers were out Friday assessing any damage to homes, and about 40 to 50 workers had been tasked with pumping water out of the streets, city spokesperson Georgia Rios said.
Newport Beach maintains a network of 86 tidal valves designed to prevent rising ocean water from backing up through storm drains, along with 18 pumps used to remove standing water from streets near the harbor. The city has previously identified the Balboa Peninsula, Balboa Island, Newport Island and other low-lying harborfront neighborhoods as areas particularly vulnerable to flooding during unusually high tides.
Another six crews were rebuilding berms on local beaches, with more flooding anticipated through the weekend, Rios said.
Utilities Director Mark Vukojevic said an estimated 20 streets flooded Friday morning, similar to July 2020 when water from the ocean rushed into the streets during an episode of extremely high tide.
The water overtopped the beaches, flattening out the berms, then made its way to streets, he said.
Drains throughout the low-lying areas that feed out to the harbor were closed, because the tide was high. If they were opened, Vukojevic said, water would also rise up from the harbor into the streets.
“It would make the streets 10 times worse,” he said. “The water has nowhere to go, so we’re trying to pump it out. The relief comes when the tide goes down, that’s why it takes a couple hours after the tide goes down to drain out.”
A dozen more pumps have been added to the peninsula for the weekend and added crews will be on hand, he said.
Vukojevic was unsure Friday afternoon if homes flooded, but said he saw some water entering garages.
The city did not pump out any private properties, he said.
Councilmember Erik Weigand said he was stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic on Friday afternoon while trying to get onto the peninsula to meet with Brett Sanders, director of the UC Irvine Climate Collaboration, to assess the conditions that contributed to the flooding.
“We’re in a current situation that this will keep occurring the next few days,” Weigand said. “It may just be too much Mother Nature impacting us. We’re just going to keep trying everything we can. Our guys are going to be out there constantly in the next week, doing everything in their power to assist where we can.”
While the water was receding from some of the flooded areas by mid-afternoon Friday, sections from 6th to 17th streets were still underwater, he said.
Weigand wasn’t sure if homes were impacted by flooding, or how many, though he said he saw some online videos from areas around the Wedge and the upper 50th streets that showed water flooding into yards and possibly into homes.
“I think we’re doing everything in our power to make sure we can protect property if we can,” he said. “The city is doing the best it can to protect homes and utilize heavy equipment that can build up berms.”
Weigand remembered times growing up in Newport Beach when streets would flood. And then, there was July 4, 2020, when Balboa Peninsula streets flooded and cars were pushed around in the parking lot. There was also some similar summer flooding in 2010.
“But I haven’t seen it this severe,” he said of the latest flooding. “To the extent it is happening at more than one area, throughout our entire coastline, is definitely, I think, an effect of the Kelvin wave, meets swell, meets high tide. I think, overall, we have the perfect storm.”
A Kelvin wave is a warm-water anomaly that travels from around the equator and pushes water levels higher for extended periods.
And what’s on the horizon could make matters even worse — an inch of rain is forecast late Saturday through Monday morning.
Newport Beach Bike Rentals owner Dave Shaw said business was slow Friday all morning, but traffic was moving through the peninsula by the late afternoon.
One thing they aren’t renting out – electric bikes.
He’s bracing for the weekend, unsure of what is ahead. The beaches have been busy with Arizona schools out for fall break, and tourists coming to the beach to beat the heat.
“It’s going to happen all weekend,” he said of the flooding potential. “We’ll figure it out as it comes.”
Bill Sharp, who has lived in West Newport for 65 years, said he has seen streets in the low-lying areas flood over the decades. But Friday’s scene was something different.
“I’ve never seen it like this, ever,” Sharp said. “There’s been moments where it’s coming up and washed into the streets in certain spots. But this is from River Jetties to the Wedge, it’s coming over the berms and filling the streets.”
“It’s unprecedented,” he added.
Usually, the flooding comes when high tides, surf and rain combine in winter months — the rain raising the water levels — but rarely does the ocean water flow into the streets during dry summer months. The region is even on the tail end of a heat wave.
Sharp said he walked through the shin-deep water in the roadway at 51st Street Friday morning.
“It’s flowing heavily over, water rushing from the ocean to the street,” he said. “It’s going over the berms, all the way to the houses. A series of berms and dikes are diverting it to the streets.”
While houses weren’t “falling into the ocean,” he said a number of the homes had drenched front yards and water was flowing around structures and into the streets.
“There’s not massive destruction, but everyone is getting wet,” Sharp said.
At the Wedge, where the local surfing community has been sounding the alarm for months about the recent speed of erosio n, bodysurfer Sean Starkey showed videos on social media of water gushing into the yards of multi-million-dollar beachfront homes.
Starkey said he had warned the city that a steep, natural sand berm created by the waves was hard packed enough to keep the water at bay, but city crews flattened it out to create a slope. That allowed the water to run up the small sliver of sand left, he argued.
Weigand said crews have been out at the Wedge since June trying to move sand around. He wondered if there was enough sand to work with in the first place after recent erosion to create a big enough berm along the beaches.
And, beaches that have wide swaths of sand flooded over, like near Newport Elementary, he said.
“You can only protect so much with the manpower you have,” Weigand said. “We have 7 miles of shoreline; it’s impossible to protect it all, in a situation like this where it’s affecting everything. There’s swell, high tides and Kelvin waves. It’s a trifecta of trouble.”
Sharp has seen a thousand 6-foot swells, with 6-foot tides, like what showed up on Friday, he said. But this time, it was different, he said.
